items.title: Geodesics

milnor.label: §10, p. 55
milnor.statement: On a connected Riemannian manifold $M$, a parametrized path $\gamma : I \to M$, $I$ any interval of the real line, is called a *geodesic* if its acceleration field $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}$ is identically zero; that is, if the velocity field $\frac{d\gamma}{dt}$ is parallel along $\gamma$. Here $D/dt$ is the covariant derivative along a curve of §8, for the Levi-Civita connection of an abstract Riemannian manifold.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space (Milnor's $\mathbb R^K$) and $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold with the induced metric; $N$ need not be closed, compact or connected. A curve $\gamma : \mathbb R \to V$ is a geodesic on an open set $s \subseteq \mathbb R$ if it is $C^\infty$ on $s$, $\gamma(t) \in N$ for $t \in s$, and the acceleration $\gamma''(t)$ in $V$ is orthogonal to $T_{\gamma(t)}N$ for every $t \in s$. The velocity of a curve in $N$ is tangent to $N$, so the condition reads $P_{\gamma(t)}\gamma''(t) = 0$, $P$ the orthogonal projection onto the tangent space: this is $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt} = 0$ for the covariant derivative $D/dt = P \circ d/dt$ of Chapter 6, and for a smooth curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$ the equivalence of the two conditions is a theorem. Constant curves at points of $N$ are geodesics.

diff: Milnor's $M$ is an abstract Riemannian manifold. In Chapters 7–11 of the formalization it is a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space with the induced metric, and every row of these chapters is read in that setting; the narrowing is recorded here once rather than on every row. Every Riemannian manifold is of this kind by Nash's embedding theorem, which is quoted in the Lean files but neither proved nor used.

Mathlib has no Levi-Civita connection, geodesics or exponential map on an abstract manifold. In the embedded setting the connection is the tangential part of the derivative in $V$, and the Hausdorff property that Milnor uses silently is automatic.

Geodesics live on open sets: a geodesic on a closed interval, which Milnor allows, is represented by one on a slightly larger open interval. That the two notions give the same exponential map is proved later (V7.7).

Milnor's standing assumption that $M$ is connected is not made; it is assumed exactly where it is needed (finiteness of the distance, Theorem 10.9 for all pairs, Corollary 10.10, the Hopf–Rinow equivalence).

items.title: Constant speed and homogeneity

milnor.label: §10, pp. 55 and 57
milnor.statement: Since $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\frac{d\gamma}{dt}, \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle = 2\langle\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}, \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle = 0$, the length $\|d\gamma/dt\|$ of the velocity vector of a geodesic is constant, and the parameter $t$ is a linear function of arc length (p. 55). On p. 57 Milnor adds homogeneity: if $t \mapsto \gamma(t)$ is a geodesic, then so is $t \mapsto \gamma(ct)$ for every constant $c$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a geodesic on an open set $s \subseteq \mathbb R$. Then $\frac{d}{dt}\|\gamma'\|^2 = 2\langle\gamma'', \gamma'\rangle = 0$ on $s$. If $s$ is preconnected (an open interval), the speed $\|\gamma'\|$ is constant on $s$, and the length of $\gamma$ on every $[a, b] \subseteq s$ (V7.11) is $\|\gamma'(t_0)\|\,(b - a)$, for any $t_0 \in s$. For all real $a$ and $b$, the curve $t \mapsto \gamma(at + b)$ is a geodesic on $\{t : at + b \in s\}$.

diff: Milnor's homogeneity is for $t \mapsto \gamma(ct)$; the formal statement allows every affine change of parameter $t \mapsto at + b$, the case $a = 0$ giving a constant curve.
The length of a geodesic segment, which Milnor uses from Theorem 10.4 on without comment, is computed: speed times the length of the parameter interval.

items.title: The geodesic equation

milnor.label: §10, p. 55
milnor.statement: In terms of a local coordinate system $u^1, \dots, u^n$, the condition for $\gamma$ to be a geodesic becomes the system of second-order differential equations $\frac{d^2u^k}{dt^2} + \sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}\frac{du^i}{dt}\frac{du^j}{dt} = 0$, $k = 1, \dots, n$, with the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ of the connection. The existence of geodesics therefore rests on the existence theorem for such systems.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be $C^\infty$ on an open set $s$, with $\gamma(s) \subseteq N$. Then $\gamma$ is a geodesic on $s$ iff $\gamma'' = \mathrm{II}_\gamma(\gamma', \gamma')$ on $s$, $\mathrm{II}$ the second fundamental form, iff the lift $t \mapsto (\gamma(t), \gamma'(t))$, which lies in $TN = \{(x, v) : x \in N,\ v \in T_xN\}$, is an integral curve of the geodesic spray $(x, v) \mapsto (v, \mathrm{II}_x(v, v))$. In a slice chart with parametrization $x$ on an open set $T$ of the model space $Z$, put $A^+ = (A^{\mathsf T}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}$ for injective $A$ and $\Gamma(u)(w, w) = (dx_u)^+\big(d^2x_u(w, w)\big)$. The field $(u, w) \mapsto (w, -\Gamma(u)(w, w))$ is smooth on $T \times Z$, and if $(u, w)$ is a $C^\infty$ solution of $u' = w$, $w' = -\Gamma(u)(w, w)$ on an open set, with $u$ in $T$, then $x \circ u$ is a geodesic there.

diff: The global form of the equation lives in $V$: the acceleration of a geodesic is its normal part $\mathrm{II}(\gamma', \gamma')$, and the geodesics are the projections of the integral curves of a spray on $TN$.

In a chart, $(dx_u)^+d^2x_u(w, w)$ is the coordinate vector, in the basis $\partial x/\partial u^k$, of the tangential part of $d^2x_u(w, w)$, that is $(\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}w^iw^j)_k$ for the Christoffel symbols of the induced metric. The Lean files define no Christoffel symbols, so this identification is a remark, not a theorem.
Only the direction "solutions of the chart equation are geodesics" is stated in the chart, which is what existence needs (V7.6); uniqueness is proved from the global form (V7.5).
The scan shows only the $\Gamma$-term of Milnor's display; the missing $d^2u^k/dt^2$ is a defect of the scan, not a misprint.

items.title: Theorem 10.1: existence, uniqueness and smooth dependence for ODEs

milnor.label: §10, Theorem 10.1
milnor.statement: Given a point $(u_1, v_1) \in \mathbb R^{2n}$ and $C^\infty$ functions $F = (F^1, \dots, F^n)$ defined near it, there are a neighbourhood $W$ of $(u_1, v_1)$ and a number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every $(u_0, v_0) \in W$ the equation $\frac{d^2u}{dt^2} = F(u, \frac{du}{dt})$ has a unique solution $t \mapsto u(t)$, defined for $|t| < \varepsilon$, with $u(0) = u_0$ and $\frac{du}{dt}(0) = v_0$; moreover the solution is $C^\infty$ as a function of $(u_0, v_0, t)$ on $W \times (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. Milnor passes to the first-order system $du/dt = v$, $dv/dt = F(u, v)$ and quotes Graves.

lean.statement: *Existence and smooth dependence.* Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $U \subseteq E \times E$ open, $F : E \times E \to E$ smooth on $U$, and $z_1 \in U$. There are a neighbourhood $W$ of $z_1$, an $\varepsilon > 0$ and a map $(z, t) \mapsto u_z(t)$, smooth on $W \times (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$, such that for every $z = (u_0, v_0) \in W$: $u_z(0) = u_0$, $u_z'(0) = v_0$, and $(u_z(t), u_z'(t)) \in U$ and $u_z''(t) = F(u_z(t), u_z'(t))$ for $|t| < \varepsilon$. *Uniqueness.* Let $E$ be any real normed space and $G$ of class $C^1$ on an open $U \subseteq E$: two solutions of $x' = G(x)$ with values in $U$, defined on a common open preconnected set and agreeing at one of its times, agree on all of it. In particular, for $F$ of class $C^1$ on $U \subseteq E \times E$, two pairs with $u_i' = v_i$, $v_i' = F(u_i, v_i)$ and $(u_i, v_i) \in U$ on an open interval, with the same position and velocity at one time, have $u_1 = u_2$ on that interval.

diff: Milnor quotes the theorem; the formal one is proved. A bump function equal to $1$ near the base point turns the field into a compactly supported one, whose global flow is smooth in $(t, x)$; its bounded speed keeps the flow lines from nearby points, for a uniform time, where the bump function is $1$.

Uniqueness holds on every common open interval of definition, not only for $|t| < \varepsilon$, and needs only a $C^1$ equation on an arbitrary real normed space: Grönwall's inequality near each time, spread over the interval by connectedness.
Milnor's $\mathbb R^n$ is any finite-dimensional real normed space.

items.title: Uniqueness of geodesics in the large

milnor.label: §10, pp. 56–58
milnor.statement: Milnor never states uniqueness of geodesics on a whole interval. Theorem 10.1 gives it for small times in one coordinate system (p. 56); Lemmas 10.2 and 10.3 then speak of *the unique* geodesic on $(-2, 2)$, or of length $< \varepsilon$, and p. 58 asserts that $\exp_q(v)$, if defined at all, is uniquely defined. All of these use uniqueness of geodesics beyond a single chart.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: two geodesics on open sets $s_1$, $s_2$ containing $t_0$, with the same position and the same velocity at $t_0$, agree near $t_0$; and two geodesics on the same open interval (more generally, open preconnected set) $s$, with the same position and velocity at one time of $s$, agree on all of $s$.

chips: used by the book, never stated
diff: The book uses uniqueness in the large without stating it; the formal statement supplies it (the exposition's Lemma A). It is a connectedness argument from local uniqueness, and on an abstract manifold it would also need the Hausdorff property, which a subset of $V$ has.

Near $t_0$ both lifts $(\gamma_i, \gamma_i')$ solve $(x, v)' = (v, dQ_x(v)\,v)$, where $Q$ is a smooth extension of $x \mapsto P_x$ to an open set of $V$ given by a slice chart; this field is smooth, so the uniqueness of V7.4 applies.

items.title: Lemma 10.2: geodesics for small initial velocities

milnor.label: §10, Lemma 10.2
milnor.statement: For every point $p_0 \in M$ there are a neighbourhood $U$ of $p_0$ and a number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for each $p \in U$ and each tangent vector $v \in TM_p$ of length $< \varepsilon$ there is a unique geodesic $\gamma_v : (-2, 2) \to M$ with $\gamma_v(0) = p$ and $\frac{d\gamma_v}{dt}(0) = v$. The proof (pp. 56–57) takes $\varepsilon_1$, $\varepsilon_2$ from Theorem 10.1 in a coordinate system and rescales, $\gamma_v(t) = \gamma_{v/\varepsilon_2}(\varepsilon_2t)$, for $\|v\| < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for every $q_0 \in N$ there are an open set $U \ni q_0$ of $V$, an $\varepsilon > 0$ and a map $\Gamma : V \times V \times \mathbb R \to V$, smooth on $U \times \{\|v\| < \varepsilon\} \times (-2, 2)$, such that for every $p \in N \cap U$ and every $v \in T_pN$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$ the curve $\gamma_v = \Gamma(p, v, \cdot)$ is a geodesic on $(-2, 2)$ with $\gamma_v(0) = p$ and $\gamma_v'(0) = v$, and every geodesic on $(-2, 2)$ with this position and velocity at $0$ equals $\gamma_v$ on $(-2, 2)$.

diff: The formal statement adds that $\gamma_v(t)$ depends smoothly on $(p, v, t)$, which Milnor does not state here but uses on p. 58 to make $\exp$ smooth near the zero section (V7.8).

The step from the coordinate neighbourhood $W$ of Theorem 10.1 to the condition "$p \in U$, $\|v\| < \varepsilon_1$" needs a bound for the coordinates of $v$ by $\|v\|$ uniform for $p$ near $p_0$: here $\|d\sigma_p v\| \le \|d\sigma_p\|\,\|v\|$, $\sigma$ the slice chart, with $\|d\sigma_p\|$ bounded near $q_0$.
Uniqueness on all of $(-2, 2)$ is the uniqueness in the large of V7.5.

items.title: The exponential map

milnor.label: §10, pp. 57–58
milnor.statement: For $v \in TM_q$, suppose there is a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ with $\gamma(0) = q$ and $\frac{d\gamma}{dt}(0) = v$; then $\exp_q(v) = \gamma(1)$, and by homogeneity $\gamma(t) = \exp_q(tv)$ (p. 57). On p. 58 Milnor notes that $\exp_q(v)$ is defined when $\|v\|$ is small enough, in general not for large $v$, but is always uniquely defined when it is defined at all.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $q, v \in V$, a geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity $v$ is a geodesic on an open interval $(-\delta, 1 + \delta)$, $\delta > 0$, with $\gamma(0) = q$ and $\gamma'(0) = v$ (then $q \in N$ and $v \in T_qN$). The domain of $\exp$ is the set of pairs $(q, v)$ for which one exists, and $\exp_q(v) = \gamma(1)$ (off the domain $\exp_q(v)$ is set to $q$, a placeholder). Any two such geodesics agree on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$, so $\exp_q(v)$ is well defined. For $q \in N$, $(q, 0)$ is in the domain and $\exp_q(0) = q$; and for such a $\gamma$, each $s \mapsto \gamma(ts)$ with $t$ near $[0, 1]$ is a geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity $tv$, so $\exp_q(tv) = \gamma(t)$.

diff: Milnor's geodesic on the closed interval $[0, 1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the ends, is replaced by one on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$. Restriction gives a geodesic in Milnor's sense with the same value at $1$.

Conversely, a geodesic on $[0, 1]$ in Milnor's sense agrees there with $t \mapsto \exp_{\gamma(0)}(t\gamma'(0))$, which is a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$ (V9.9), so its initial data lie in the formal domain (V11.1): the two domains of $\exp$ coincide. This is proved in Chapters 9 and 11, not in Chapter 7.
Well-definedness is the uniqueness in the large of V7.5, and $\gamma(t) = \exp_q(tv)$ uses homogeneity (V7.2) together with it.

items.title: The tangent manifold, $\exp$ near the zero section, and $d(\exp_q)_0$

milnor.label: §10, p. 58
milnor.statement: The tangent manifold $TM$ is given a $C^\infty$ structure by the coordinates $(u^1, \dots, u^n, t^1, \dots, t^n)$, where $t^1\partial_1 + \dots + t^n\partial_n$ is a tangent vector at a point with coordinates $u$. Lemma 10.2 says that for each $p \in M$ the map $(q, v) \mapsto \exp_q(v)$ is defined throughout a neighbourhood $V$ of $(p, 0)$ in $TM$, and is differentiable there. In the Jacobian of $F(q, v) = (q, \exp_q(v))$ at $(p, 0)$, the column $F_*(\partial/\partial t^j) = \partial/\partial u_2^j$ amounts to $d(\exp_p)_0 = \mathrm{id}$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: $TN = \{(q, v) \in V \times V : q \in N,\ v \in T_qN\}$ is a slice submanifold of $V \times V$ (the companion project). (i) For every $q_0 \in N$ there are an open $U \ni q_0$, an $\varepsilon > 0$ and $F$ smooth on $U \times \{\|v\| < \varepsilon\}$ such that, for $p \in N \cap U$ and $v \in T_pN$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$, $(p, v)$ is in the domain of $\exp$ and $\exp_p(v) = F(p, v)$. (ii) There is one open $O \subseteq V \times V$ containing $(q, 0)$ for every $q \in N$ such that every point of $TN \cap O$ is in the domain of $\exp$, and $\exp$ is smooth on $TN \cap O$, both as a restriction of smooth maps on open sets of $V \times V$ and as a map on the manifold $TN$. (iii) For $q \in N$, $\exp_q$, as a map on the vector space $T_qN$, has derivative at $0$ the inclusion $T_qN \to V$.

chips: one neighbourhood of the zero section
diff: Milnor's tangent manifold, with its coordinates $(u, t)$, is the embedded $TN \subseteq V \times V$ of the companion project.
Milnor gives a neighbourhood of each $(p, 0)$; the formal statement gives one open neighbourhood of the whole zero section on which $\exp$ is defined and smooth.
The differentiability Milnor cites rests on the smooth dependence in Lemma 10.2, which his statement of that lemma omits (V7.6).

items.title: Normal radius

milnor.label: §10, Lemma 10.3 (3)
milnor.statement: Part (3) of Lemma 10.3 says that, for each $q$ in the neighbourhood $W$, $\exp_q$ maps the open $\varepsilon$-ball in $TM_q$ diffeomorphically onto an open set $U_q$. The book has no name for such an $\varepsilon$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $q \in N$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, let $B_\varepsilon(q) = \{v \in T_qN : \|v\| < \varepsilon\}$. Then $\varepsilon$ is a *normal radius* at $q$ if there are open sets $O, U \subseteq V$ and maps $F$ smooth on $O$ and $G$ smooth on $U$ with: $B_\varepsilon(q) \subseteq O$, $B_\varepsilon(q)$ in the domain of $\exp_q$ and $\exp_q = F$ there; $\exp_q$ maps $B_\varepsilon(q)$ into $U$ with $G(\exp_q v) = v$; and $G$ maps $U_q = N \cap U$ into $B_\varepsilon(q)$ with $\exp_q(G(y)) = y$. So $\exp_q$ is a bijection of $B_\varepsilon(q)$ onto the open subset $U_q$ of $N$, and it and its inverse are restrictions of smooth maps. A normal radius yields a diffeomorphism in Mathlib's sense: $\exp_q$ restricts to a `PartialDiffeomorph` of the open $\varepsilon$-ball onto $U_q$.

diff: The notion is the condition in Lemma 10.3 (3), given a name so that later statements can assume it of a single point.

"Diffeomorphically" is made precise in Milnor's own sense for subsets of Euclidean space (restrictions of smooth maps on open sets), and the diffeomorphism in Mathlib's sense, for the manifold structure of $N$, follows.

items.title: Lemma 10.3: uniformly normal neighbourhoods

milnor.label: §10, Lemma 10.3
milnor.statement: For each $p \in M$ there are a neighbourhood $W$ of $p$ and a number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that: (1) any two points of $W$ are joined by a unique geodesic in $M$ of length $< \varepsilon$; (2) this geodesic depends smoothly on the two points, in that if $t \mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, is the geodesic joining $q_1$ and $q_2$, the pair $(q_1, v) \in TM$ depends differentiably on $(q_1, q_2)$; (3) for each $q \in W$, $\exp_q$ maps the open $\varepsilon$-ball in $TM_q$ diffeomorphically onto an open set $U_q \supseteq W$. Proof (pp. 58–59): $F(q, v) = (q, \exp_q v)$ has nonsingular Jacobian $\begin{pmatrix} I & I \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix}$ at $(p, 0)$, and "the implicit function theorem" gives a local inverse.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for each $p \in N$ there are an open set $O \ni p$ of $V$ and an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that, with $W = N \cap O$: (1) for all $q_1, q_2 \in W$ there is exactly one $v \in T_{q_1}N$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$ and $\exp_{q_1}(v) = q_2$; and a geodesic from $q_1$ with initial velocity of norm $< \varepsilon$ ending at $q_2$ is $t \mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)$ for this $v$; (2) there are an open $O_2 \subseteq V \times V$ containing $W \times W$ and $G$ smooth on $O_2$ with $G(q_1, q_2)$ the vector of (1); (3) $\varepsilon$ is a normal radius (V7.9) at every $q \in W$, and $U_q \supseteq W$. In particular every point of $N$ has a normal radius, and $\exp_q$ restricts to a `PartialDiffeomorph` of an open ball of $T_qN$ onto an open neighbourhood of $q$ in $N$.

diff: In (1), "a unique geodesic of length $< \varepsilon$" becomes the unique initial vector $v$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$; the geodesic $t \mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)$ on $[0, 1]$ has length $\|v\|$ (V7.15), and the initial vector of a geodesic has norm equal to its length (V7.2).

The theorem used is the inverse function theorem (the companion project's, on manifolds), applied in the slice chart to $(u, w) \mapsto (u, E(u, w))$, whose derivative at $(u_0, 0)$ is $(a, b) \mapsto (a, a + b)$, Milnor's block matrix.

Taking the neighbourhood of $(p, 0)$ in the form $\{(q, v) : q \in U', \|v\| < \varepsilon\}$ needs such sets to be a neighbourhood base in $TM$, a comparison of $\|v\|$ with the coordinates of $v$ uniform near $p$; the formal proof supplies it.

items.title: The remark after Lemma 10.3: convex neighbourhoods

milnor.label: §10, Remark, p. 59
milnor.statement: Right after Lemma 10.3 Milnor remarks, without proof, that with more care it would be possible to choose $W$ so that the geodesic joining any two of its points lies completely within $W$, and refers to J. H. C. Whitehead, *Convex regions in the geometry of paths* (1932).

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: an open $O \subseteq V$ is a *good ball* if, for one $\delta > 0$, any two points $y, z$ of $N \cap O$ are at distance $\rho(y, z) < \delta$ and joined as in Corollary 10.8 at the scale $\delta$ (V7.20: a unique geodesic $\sigma_{yz}(s) = \exp_y(s\,v)$ with $\|v\| < \delta$, which is minimal and whose initial vector depends smoothly on $(y, z)$), and $\sigma_{yz}(s) \in N \cap O$ for $0 \le s \le 1$. For every $x \in N$ the balls $\{y : \|y - x\| < r\}$ of $V$ are good for all small $r > 0$; and for every compact $K \subseteq N$ there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ about each point of $K$ lies in a good ball.

diff: The verified Chapter 7 lists the remark as not formalized; it is proved in Chapter 10 (`Morse/Chapter10/GoodBalls.lean`), where the modified proof of Theorem 17.1 needs neighbourhoods convex for short geodesics (V10.17).

Milnor's $W$ is a set as in Lemma 10.3; a good ball is the intersection of $N$ with a small ball of $V$, and its scale $\delta$ plays the role of $\varepsilon$. Convexity is proved with the ambient distance, $(\|\gamma - x\|^2)'' = 2\|\gamma'\|^2 + 2\langle\gamma - x, \mathrm{II}(\gamma', \gamma')\rangle > 0$ along a geodesic near $x$, so no normal coordinates are needed.

That the good ball also satisfies Lemma 10.3 (3) for the same scale is not stated; what is proved is the convexity Milnor asks for, together with the minimality and smooth dependence of the joining geodesics.

items.title: Piecewise smooth paths and their lengths

milnor.label: §11, p. 67; used from p. 59
milnor.statement: A piecewise smooth path is a map $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ with a subdivision $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k = 1$ such that each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is $C^\infty$ (p. 67, where the notion is first defined). From Theorem 10.4 on (p. 59) such paths on intervals $[a, b]$, and their arc lengths $\int\|d\omega/dt\|\,dt$, are used without further comment.

lean.statement: Let $c$ be a curve in a real normed space (complete, for the statements involving $\int c'$) and $a \le b$. The length of $c$ on $[a, b]$ is $L(c|[a, b]) = \int_a^b\|c'(t)\|\,dt$, $c'$ being $0$ where $c$ is not differentiable. $c$ is *piecewise smooth* on $[a, b]$ if it is continuous there and, for a finite set $B$ of break points, $C^\infty$ (one-sided derivatives at the ends) on every $[s, t] \subseteq [a, b]$, $s < t$, with no point of $B$ in $(s, t)$. $c$ is *admissible* on $[a, b]$ if it is continuous there, differentiable off a countable subset of $(a, b)$, and $\|c'\|$ is integrable. Piecewise smooth paths are admissible. For admissible paths $\int_a^bc' = c(b) - c(a)$, so $\|c(b) - c(a)\| \le L$; length is additive under subdivision; a path of length $0$ is constant; and speed $k$ gives length $k(b - a)$. Restriction, concatenation at a common endpoint, reversal and translation of the parameter preserve piecewise smoothness; lengths add under concatenation and are unchanged by reversal and translation.

chips: break points as a finite set
diff: The subdivision is given as a finite set of break points, and a path is a map on $\mathbb R$ read on $[a, b]$.

The facts Milnor uses without comment are stated: integrability of $\|d\omega/dt\|$, additivity of length under subdivision and concatenation, invariance under reversal and translation, and $\|c(b) - c(a)\| \le L$.

The lower bounds for lengths (V7.13–V7.16) are proved for admissible paths, a class that contains the piecewise smooth paths and is closed under restriction, which is what the shell-crossing argument needs.

items.title: Lemma 10.5: the Gauss lemma

milnor.label: §10, Lemma 10.5
milnor.statement: In $U_q$ the geodesics through $q$ are the orthogonal trajectories of the hypersurfaces $\{\exp_q(v) : \|v\| = \text{constant}\}$. The proof considers the surface $f(r, t) = \exp_q(r\,v(t))$ for a curve $v(t)$ of unit vectors and shows that $\langle\partial f/\partial r, \partial f/\partial t\rangle$ is independent of $r$, hence zero.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $q \in N$ (V7.9) and regard $\exp_q$ as a map on the vector space $T_qN$. For $w, x \in T_qN$ with $\|w\| < \varepsilon$, $$\langle d(\exp_q)_w(w),\ d(\exp_q)_w(x)\rangle = \langle w, x\rangle;$$ in particular the radial velocity $d(\exp_q)_w(w)$ is orthogonal to $d(\exp_q)_w(x)$ when $x \perp w$. Moreover $d(\exp_q)_w$ is injective on $T_qN$, and $\|d(\exp_q)_{rw}(w)\| = \|w\|$ for $0 \le r \le 1$.

chips: the identity for every $x$, not $x \perp w$
diff: The identity holds for every $x \in T_qN$; Milnor's orthogonality of trajectories is its case $x \perp w$, the vectors $x \perp w$ forming the tangent space at $w$ of the sphere $\{\|v\| = \|w\|\}$.

That the sets $\{\exp_q(v) : \|v\| = \text{constant}\}$ are hypersurfaces with the expected tangent vectors uses that $\exp_q$ is a diffeomorphism on the ball, which the formal statement takes as the normal-radius hypothesis.

The proof is Milnor's, with $f(r, s) = \exp_q(r(w + sx))$; the symmetry of second derivatives in $V$ replaces Lemma 8.7, and the radial geodesic's normal acceleration kills $\langle\partial^2f/\partial r^2, \partial f/\partial s\rangle$.

items.title: Lemma 10.6: length and radius in a normal ball

milnor.label: §10, Lemma 10.6
milnor.statement: Let $\omega : [a, b] \to U_q - \{q\}$ be piecewise smooth, written $\omega(t) = \exp_q(r(t)v(t))$ with $0 < r(t) < \varepsilon$ and $\|v(t)\| = 1$. Then $\int_a^b\|d\omega/dt\|\,dt \ge |r(b) - r(a)|$, with equality only if $r$ is monotone and $v$ constant. The proof (p. 61) splits $d\omega/dt = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r}r'(t) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}$ into orthogonal parts by the Gauss lemma.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $q$, with $U_q$ and $G = \exp_q^{-1}$ as in V7.9, and let $c$ be admissible on $[a, b]$ (V7.11) with $c(t) \in U_q$ and $c(t) \ne q$ for $t \in [a, b]$; write $r(t) = \|G(c(t))\| \in (0, \varepsilon)$ and $v(t) = G(c(t))/r(t)$. Then $L(c|[a, b]) \ge r(b) - r(a)$, and if equality holds, $v$ is constant on $[a, b]$. Pointwise, at each $t \in (a, b)$ where $c$ is differentiable, $r$ is differentiable with $|r'(t)| \le \|c'(t)\|$, and $r'(t) = \|c'(t)\|$ forces $v'(t) = 0$.

diff: The bound is one-sided, $r(b) - r(a)$ rather than $|r(b) - r(a)|$, which is the case Theorem 10.4 uses; the two-sided form is not formalized.
The equality clause gives only that $v$ is constant; the monotone parametrization appears in the sharp equality case of Theorem 10.4 (V7.16) instead.

The paths are admissible rather than piecewise smooth. The step from $\partial f/\partial t = 0$ to $dv/dt = 0$ needs $d(\exp_q)$ injective (V7.12) and $r > 0$; the formal proof avoids the orthogonal splitting, using $\langle d(\exp_q)_w(w), c'\rangle = rr'$ and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

items.title: Paths leaving a normal ball: the shell crossing

milnor.label: §10, proof of Theorem 10.4, p. 61
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 10.4, Milnor observes that for every $\delta > 0$ a path from $q$ to a point of the shell of radius $r$ contains a segment that joins the shells of radii $\delta$ and $r$ and lies between them; by Lemma 10.6 that segment has length $\ge r - \delta$, and letting $\delta \to 0$ gives length $\ge r$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $q$ and $0 < s < \varepsilon$. The open normal ball $\exp_q\{\|v\| < s\}$ is the intersection of $N$ with an open set of $V$; the closed normal ball $\exp_q\{\|v\| \le s\}$ is compact, hence closed in $V$. If $c$ is an admissible path in $N$ on $[a, b]$ with $c(a) = q$ and $c(b)$ outside the open normal ball of radius $s$, there are $a \le t_1 < t_2 \le b$ with $c(t_1) = q$, $c(t) \in U_q \setminus \{q\}$ for $t_1 < t \le t_2$, $c(t)$ in the open normal ball for $t_1 \le t < t_2$, $\|G(c(t_2))\| = s$, and $L(c|[t_1, t_2]) \ge s$.

diff: The shells of radius $\delta \to 0$ are replaced by the last visit of $q$ before the first exit from the ball, the limit being taken inside the proof (the exposition's Lemma C).

A competing path may leave $U_q$ and come back; the segment exists because closed normal balls are closed in $M$, compact in a Hausdorff space, which puts the first exit point on the shell. Milnor's argument leaves this implicit.

items.title: Theorem 10.4: short geodesics are shortest

milnor.label: §10, Theorem 10.4
milnor.statement: Let $W$ and $\varepsilon$ be as in Lemma 10.3, let $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ be the geodesic of length $< \varepsilon$ joining two points of $W$, and let $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ be any other piecewise smooth path joining the same two points. Then $\int_0^1\|d\gamma/dt\|\,dt \le \int_0^1\|d\omega/dt\|\,dt$, where equality can hold only if the point sets $\omega([0, 1])$ and $\gamma([0, 1])$ coincide. Thus $\gamma$ is the shortest path joining its end points. Proof on p. 61.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $\varepsilon$ is a normal radius at $q$ and $v \in T_qN$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$, then $t \mapsto \exp_q(tv)$ is a geodesic near $[0, 1]$ with initial velocity $v$ and length $\|v\|$ on $[0, 1]$, and every admissible path in $N$, on any $[a, b]$, from $q$ to $\exp_q(v)$ has length $\ge \|v\|$, whether or not it stays in $U_q$. (ii) For each $p \in N$ there are an open $O \ni p$ of $V$ and an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for all $q_1, q_2 \in N \cap O$ there is $v \in T_{q_1}N$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$ and $\exp_{q_1}(v) = q_2$, the geodesic $\gamma(t) = \exp_{q_1}(tv)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, has length $\|v\|$, and every piecewise smooth path $c$ in $N$ on any $[a, b]$ from $q_1$ to $q_2$ has $L(c|[a, b]) \ge \|v\|$, with equality only if $c([a, b]) = \gamma([0, 1])$.

diff: Competing paths are parametrized on any interval $[a, b]$, not only $[0, 1]$, and in (i) they need only be admissible.
The proof needs the shell-crossing step (V7.14), because a competing path may leave the normal neighbourhood; the equality clause is the sharper V7.16.

items.title: The equality case of Theorem 10.4, sharp form

milnor.label: §10, Theorem 10.4, pp. 59 and 61
milnor.statement: Theorem 10.4 says that equality of lengths can hold only if the point sets $\omega([0, 1])$ and $\gamma([0, 1])$ coincide; on p. 61 Milnor adds that if the images differ, a strict inequality is "easily" obtained.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $q$, $v \in T_qN$ with $0 < \|v\| < \varepsilon$, and $c$ an admissible path in $N$ on $[a, b]$ from $q$ to $\exp_q(v)$ of length exactly $\|v\|$. Then $$c(t) = \exp_q(\rho(t)v),\qquad \rho(t) = L(c|[a, t])/\|v\|,\qquad a \le t \le b,$$ with $\rho$ continuous and nondecreasing, $\rho(a) = 0$ and $\rho(b) = 1$: $c$ is a monotone reparametrization of the geodesic $t \mapsto \exp_q(tv)$, $0 \le t \le 1$. Milnor's conclusion $c([a, b]) = \gamma([0, 1])$ follows.

diff: A monotone reparametrization replaces equal images. Equal images are too weak for Corollary 10.7: a path running along $\gamma$ at varying speed has the same image, and the proof of 10.7 needs the reparametrization form (V7.17).

The equality analysis that Milnor leaves to the reader is carried out: the path is constant before its last visit of $q$ and after its first arrival on the shell, and between them equality in Lemma 10.6 fixes the direction.

items.title: Corollary 10.7: shortest paths are geodesics

milnor.label: §10, Corollary 10.7
milnor.statement: If a path $\omega : [0, \ell] \to M$, parametrized by arc length, has length less than or equal to the length of any other path from $\omega(0)$ to $\omega(\ell)$, then $\omega$ is a geodesic. The proof applies Theorem 10.4 to each segment of $\omega$ that lies in a set $W$ of Lemma 10.3 and has length $< \varepsilon$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $c$ be a piecewise smooth path in $N$ on $[0, \ell]$ with $\|c'(t)\| = 1$ at every $t \in (0, \ell)$ where $c$ is differentiable, whose length is at most that of every piecewise smooth path in $N$, on any parameter interval, from $c(0)$ to $c(\ell)$. Then $c$ is a geodesic on $(0, \ell)$ (in particular smooth there, also at its break points), and $c$ agrees on $[0, \ell]$ with a geodesic defined on an open interval $(-\delta, \ell + \delta)$. On the way: being a geodesic is a local property, and a segment of $c$ inside a set of Lemma 10.3 agrees with a geodesic on an open set containing it.

diff: The formal statement adds that $c$ extends to a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, \ell]$.
As stated, the equality clause of Theorem 10.4 (equal images) does not make a segment a geodesic; the proof needs V7.16 together with unit speed, which makes the reparametrization affine.

Also needed: each segment is minimal between its end points (replacing it by the geodesic of Lemma 10.3 gives a competitor, by concatenation), the segments must contain the break points in their interiors, and being a geodesic is local.

items.title: The distance $\rho$

milnor.label: §10, p. 62
milnor.statement: For $p, q \in M$, $\rho(p, q)$ is the greatest lower bound of the arc lengths of the piecewise smooth paths joining $p$ and $q$, and this "clearly" makes $M$ a metric space.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $p, q \in V$, $\rho(p, q) \in [0, \infty]$ is the infimum of the lengths of the piecewise smooth paths $c$ in $N$, on any $[a, b]$, with $c(a) = p$ and $c(b) = q$ ($\infty$ if there is none, as when $q \notin N$). Then $\rho(p, q) \le L(c|[a, b])$ for every such path, $\rho(p, p) = 0$ for $p \in N$, $\rho$ is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality; if $\varepsilon$ is a normal radius at $p$ and $0 < s < \varepsilon$, every point outside the open normal ball of radius $s$ about $p$ is at distance $\ge s$; and for $p, q \in N$, $\rho(p, q) = 0$ implies $p = q$. So $\rho$ is a metric on $N$ with values in $[0, \infty]$.

chips: positivity is not clear: shell crossing
diff: $\rho$ is $\infty$ between points that no path joins, and $N$ need not be connected; finiteness needs Milnor's standing assumption that $M$ is connected (V7.21).
Positivity is not "clear": a path from $p$ to $q$ may leave every normal neighbourhood of $p$, and the lower bound needs the shell-crossing lemma (V7.14).

items.title: Metric balls and the topology

milnor.label: §10, p. 62
milnor.statement: The compatibility of the metric $\rho$ with the usual topology of $M$ follows "easily" from Theorem 10.4.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $p \in N$. For $v \in T_pN$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$, $\rho(p, \exp_pv) = \|v\|$; and for $0 < r \le \varepsilon$, $\rho(p, y) < r$ iff $y$ lies in the normal ball $\exp_p\{v \in T_pN : \|v\| < r\}$. Consequently, for every $p \in N$, the metric balls $\{y : \rho(p, y) < r\}$, $r > 0$, form a basis of the neighbourhoods of $p$ in $N$ for the topology of a subspace of $V$.

chips: small metric balls are normal balls
diff: Compatibility is stated as the neighbourhood-basis property at each point; the metric space structure it yields is V7.21.

The "easy" argument needs that small metric balls are normal balls (the shell crossing again) and that normal balls of small radius lie in any given neighbourhood of $p$ (continuity of $\exp_p$ at $0$).

items.title: Corollary 10.8: short joins on a compact set

milnor.label: §10, Corollary 10.8
milnor.statement: Given a compact set $K \subseteq M$ there is a number $\delta > 0$ such that any two points of $K$ with distance less than $\delta$ are joined by a unique geodesic of length less than $\delta$; this geodesic is minimal, and depends differentiably on its end points. Proof: cover $K$ by open sets $W$ as in Lemma 10.3 and let $\delta$ be small enough that any two points of $K$ at distance $< \delta$ lie in a common $W$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $K \subseteq N$ be compact. There is $\delta > 0$ such that for all $y, z \in K$ with $\rho(y, z) < \delta$: there is $v \in T_yN$ with $\|v\| < \delta$ and $\exp_y(v) = z$; the geodesic $t \mapsto \exp_y(tv)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, of length $\|v\|$, is minimal, $\rho(y, z) = \|v\|$; $v$ is the only $w \in T_yN$ with $\|w\| < \delta$ and $\exp_y(w) = z$; and there are an open $O_2 \ni (y, z)$ and a map $G$ smooth on $O_2$ with $G(y, z) = v$ such that for $y', z' \in N$ with $(y', z') \in O_2$ and $\rho(y', z') < \delta$, $G(y', z') \in T_{y'}N$, $\|G(y', z')\| < \delta$ and $\exp_{y'}(G(y', z')) = z'$.

diff: Uniqueness is stated for initial vectors: a geodesic from $y$ defined near $[0, 1]$ and ending at $z$ with initial velocity $w$ has length $\|w\|$ and $\exp_y(w) = z$ (V7.2, V7.7). "Depends differentiably" means that near each pair the initial vector is the restriction of a smooth map on an open set of $V \times V$, on the pairs at distance $< \delta$.

The choice of $\delta$ is a Lebesgue-number argument with a finite subcover; uniqueness among geodesics of length $< \delta$ needs $\delta$ at most the $\varepsilon$ of each set of the cover, else Lemma 10.3 (1) does not apply; minimality is Theorem 10.4, through $\rho(y, z) = \|v\|$.

items.title: Continuity and finiteness of $\rho$; the metric space $(N, \rho)$

milnor.label: §10, p. 62
milnor.statement: Milnor says that $\rho$ "clearly" makes $M$ a metric space, compatible with its topology by Theorem 10.4; finiteness rests on the standing assumption that $M$ is connected (p. 55). The continuity of $\rho$ is never stated, but the proof of Theorem 10.9 uses it (p. 63: a point of the compact shell $S$ at minimum distance from $q$, and an equality at the supremum $t_0$ "by continuity").

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for all $p, q \in V$, $\|q - p\| \le \rho(p, q)$. The function $(x, y) \mapsto \rho(x, y)$, with values in $[0, \infty]$, is continuous on $N \times N$ (topology of a subspace of $V \times V$). If $N$ is (pre)connected, $\rho(p, q) < \infty$ for all $p, q \in N$. Hence $\rho$ makes $N$ an extended metric space whose topology is that of $N$, and, for connected $N$, a metric space with distance $\rho$ and the topology of $N$; these structures are given by name, since $N$ already carries the metric of $V$.

diff: The continuity of $\rho$, which the book uses in the proof of Theorem 10.9 without stating it, is proved, from $|\rho(x, y) - \rho(x', y')| \le \rho(x, x') + \rho(y, y')$ and V7.19.

Connectedness is needed only for finiteness; in the formal statements "connected" is preconnected, which also admits $N = \emptyset$. The points at finite distance from $p$ form an open and closed subset of $N$.

items.title: Metric and geodesic completeness

milnor.label: §10, pp. 58, 62 and 64
milnor.statement: $M$ is *geodesically complete* if $\exp_q(v)$ is defined for all $q \in M$ and all $v \in TM_q$; this is "clearly" equivalent to the requirement that every geodesic segment $\gamma_0 : [a, b] \to M$ can be extended to an infinite geodesic $\gamma : \mathbb R \to M$ (p. 58, recalled p. 62). On p. 64: a subset of $M$ is bounded if it has finite diameter, and $M$ is complete as a metric space if every Cauchy sequence converges.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: $(N, \rho)$ is *complete* if every sequence in $N$ that is Cauchy for $\rho$ converges for $\rho$ to some point of $N$; for connected $N$ this is the completeness of the metric space of V7.21. A set $X \subseteq V$ is *bounded* if $\rho(x, y) \le d$ for all $x, y \in X$ and some real $d$ (a nonempty bounded set lies in $N$). $N$ is *geodesically complete* if $\exp_q(v)$ is defined for every $q \in N$ and $v \in T_qN$. If $\exp_q$ is defined on all of $T_qN$, then $t \mapsto \exp_q(tv)$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ for every $v$; and $N$ is geodesically complete iff every geodesic on a nonempty open interval (or preconnected open set) is the restriction of a geodesic on $\mathbb R$.

diff: Milnor's segments on closed intervals are replaced by geodesics on open intervals, as in V7.7.
The "clear" equivalence glues geodesics, which needs their uniqueness in the large (V7.5).

items.title: The geodesic flow, and the continuity of $\exp$

milnor.label: §10, pp. 57, 58, 62 and 64
milnor.statement: Milnor uses, without stating them as results: that a geodesic is $t \mapsto \exp_q(tv)$ (p. 57); that geodesics can be continued (pp. 58, 62); and, in the proof of Corollary 10.10 (p. 64), that $\exp_p$ maps the disk of radius $d$ in $TM_p$ onto a compact set, which needs $\exp_p$ continuous on the whole disk. Lemma 10.2 concerns small vectors only.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) a geodesic on an open interval containing $0$ is $t \mapsto \exp_{\gamma(0)}(t\gamma'(0))$ there. (ii) For $x_0 \in N$ and $R > 0$ there are an open $U \ni x_0$, a time $\tau > 0$ and a map $\Phi$ continuous on $U \times \{\|w\| < R\} \times (-\tau, \tau)$ such that for $y \in N \cap U$ and $w \in T_yN$ with $\|w\| < R$, $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ is a geodesic on $(-\tau, \tau)$ whose position and velocity at time $t$ are $\Phi(y, w, t)$. (iii) Geodesics $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ on an open interval $I \ni 0$ continue, from the position and velocity at any $s \in I$, by the geodesic with those initial data. (iv) The domain of $\exp$ is open in $TN$, and $\exp$ is continuous on it; in particular, if $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pN$, it is continuous there.

chips: global continuity of $\exp$, used on p. 64
diff: Corollary 10.10 needs the continuity of $\exp_p$ on a whole disk, a global dependence of geodesics on their initial data that Lemma 10.2 does not give; it is proved here, by covering the compact arc with finitely many sets of (ii) and continuing step by step with (iii).
Only continuity of $\exp$ on its open domain is proved in Chapter 7, which is all that Corollary 10.10 needs; smoothness on the whole domain is V11.1, proved in Chapter 11.
Maximal geodesics, which the exposition uses (its Lemma B), are not constructed: geodesics are glued by (iii) instead.

items.title: Minimal geodesics

milnor.label: §10, pp. 61–62
milnor.statement: A geodesic $\gamma : [a, b] \to M$ is *minimal* if its length is less than or equal to the length of any other piecewise smooth path joining its end points.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a curve $\gamma$ is a minimal geodesic on $[a, b]$, $a \le b$, if it is a geodesic on some open set containing $[a, b]$ and $L(\gamma|[a, b]) \le L(c|[a', b'])$ for every piecewise smooth path $c$ in $N$, on any $[a', b']$, with $c(a') = \gamma(a)$ and $c(b') = \gamma(b)$. Where $\exp_q(v)$ is defined it lies in $N$. If $v \in T_pN$, $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ and $\rho(p, \exp_pv) = \|v\|$, then $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ is a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$, of length $\|v\|$.

chips: a geodesic near $[a, b]$, not on it
diff: A geodesic on an open set containing $[a, b]$ replaces one on $[a, b]$, as in V7.7; competing paths may be parametrized on any interval.

items.title: The two steps of the proof of Theorem 10.9

milnor.label: §10, proof of Theorem 10.9, pp. 63–64
milnor.statement: In the proof of the Hopf–Rinow theorem: since every path from $p$ to $q$ passes through the shell $S$ of radius $\delta$ about $p$, $\rho(p, q) = \min_{s \in S}(\rho(p, s) + \rho(s, q)) = \delta + \rho(p_0, q)$ for a point $p_0 \in S$ (p. 63). Later (pp. 63–64) a broken geodesic from $p$ through $\gamma(t_0)$ is shown to have minimal length, so it is an unbroken geodesic by Corollary 10.7, "and hence coincides with $\gamma$".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $p \in N$, $0 < \delta < \varepsilon$, and $q$ with $\delta < \rho(p, q) < \infty$. There is $w \in T_pN$ with $\|w\| = \delta$ and $\rho(p, q) = \delta + \rho(\exp_pw, q)$. (ii) Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ with $\|\gamma'(0)\| = 1$, $0 < t_0 < t_1$, and $\sigma$ a geodesic on an open (preconnected) set containing $[t_0, t_1]$ with $\|\sigma'(t_0)\| = 1$ and $\sigma(t_0) = \gamma(t_0)$. If $\rho(\gamma(0), \sigma(t_1)) \ge t_1$, i.e. the broken path ($\gamma$ on $[0, t_0]$, then $\sigma$), of length $t_1$, is minimal, then $\sigma(t_1) = \gamma(t_1)$.

diff: In (i) the hypothesis $\delta < \rho(p, q)$ is needed, not only $\delta < \varepsilon$: otherwise $q$ lies inside the shell and paths from $p$ to $q$ need not meet it. That every path crosses the shell is V7.14, and the minimum exists because the shell is compact and nonempty and $\rho(\cdot, q)$ is continuous (V7.21).
In (ii), "coincides with $\gamma$" needs unit speed on both pieces, for Corollary 10.7, and the uniqueness of geodesics in the large (V7.5) from a time before the break.

items.title: Theorem 10.9: the Hopf–Rinow theorem

milnor.label: §10, Theorem 10.9
milnor.statement: If $M$ is geodesically complete, then any two points can be joined by a minimal geodesic. The proof (pp. 62–64, with Diagram 10) follows the geodesic from $p$ in the direction of the point of a small shell nearest to $q$, and shows by a supremum argument that it reaches $q$ at time $\rho(p, q)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) let $p \in N$ be such that $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pN$. Every $q \in N$ with $\rho(p, q) < \infty$ is $\exp_p(v)$ for some $v \in T_pN$ with $\|v\| = \rho(p, q)$, and $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ is a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$ (V7.24) from $p$ to $q$. (ii) If $N$ is (pre)connected and geodesically complete, any two points $p, q \in N$ are joined by a minimal geodesic $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$, $\gamma(0) = p$, $\gamma(1) = q$, whose length is $\rho(p, q)$.

diff: Part (i) uses completeness only at $p$, as the exposition remarks after the proof; Milnor assumes $\exp_q$ defined for every $q$.

The hidden hypotheses of V7.25 are used, together with $\delta' < r - t_0$ in the inductive step (otherwise the new time overshoots $r = \rho(p, q)$); the supremum argument is a continuous induction on $[\delta, r]$, closed by the continuity of $\rho$; connectedness gives $\rho(p, q) < \infty$.

items.title: Corollary 10.10: bounded sets and metric completeness

milnor.label: §10, Corollary 10.10
milnor.statement: If $M$ is geodesically complete, then every bounded subset of $M$ has compact closure; consequently $M$ is complete as a metric space. Proof: for $X$ of diameter $d$ and $p \in X$, $\exp_p$ maps the disk of radius $d$ in $TM_p$ onto a compact set which, by Theorem 10.9, contains $X$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $N$ is (pre)connected and $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pN$ for some $p \in N$, every bounded $X \subseteq V$ (V7.22) has compact closure, contained in $N$. (ii) If every bounded set has compact closure contained in $N$, then $(N, \rho)$ is complete. (iii) Hence, if $N$ is connected and geodesically complete, every bounded set has compact closure in $N$, and $(N, \rho)$ is complete.

diff: Part (i) needs completeness at one point only.

The proof uses the continuity of $\exp_p$ on the whole disk (V7.23 (iv)), which the book takes for granted; connectedness, so that distances are finite and Theorem 10.9 reaches all of $X$; and, for completeness, that a Cauchy sequence is bounded and converges once a subsequence does.
The closure is taken in $V$; as it lies in $N$, it is also the closure in $N$.

items.title: The converse of Corollary 10.10

milnor.label: §10, p. 64
milnor.statement: Conversely, if $M$ is complete as a metric space, then it is "not difficult, using Lemma 10.3" to prove that $M$ is geodesically complete. Milnor leaves the details to Hopf and Rinow.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: if $(N, \rho)$ is complete (V7.22), then $N$ is geodesically complete. No connectedness is assumed.

diff: Milnor states the converse and gives no proof; the formal statement is proved, and needs no connectedness of $N$ (Milnor's standing assumption).

The proof uses the uniform local existence of Lemma 10.2 (V7.23 (ii)), not Lemma 10.3: if $\gamma(t) = \exp_q(tv)$ existed only up to $T_0$, the points $\gamma(t_n)$, $t_n \uparrow T_0$, would form a Cauchy sequence, converging to some $x$ near which all geodesics of speed $\|v\|$ exist for a uniform time.

items.title: The Hopf–Rinow equivalence

milnor.label: §10, p. 64
milnor.statement: After Corollary 10.10 and its converse, Milnor no longer distinguishes geodesic from metric completeness, and calls such an $M$ simply a *complete* Riemannian manifold.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a (pre)connected nonempty $N$ the following are equivalent: (1) $(N, \rho)$ is complete; (2) $N$ is geodesically complete; (3) $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pN$ for some $p \in N$; (4) every bounded set has compact closure, contained in $N$. If $N$ is connected and $(N, \rho)$ complete, then $N$ is geodesically complete, every geodesic on an open interval is the restriction of a geodesic on $\mathbb R$, any two points are joined by a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$ whose length is their distance, and every bounded subset of $N$ that is closed in $N$ is compact.

diff: Condition (3), completeness of $\exp$ at a single point, and the compactness of closed bounded sets are not in the book; the equivalence of (1) and (2) is what Milnor's usage presupposes.
Connectedness is assumed, as Milnor does throughout; the proof is (2) ⇒ (3) since $N \ne \emptyset$, then V7.27 (i), V7.27 (ii) and V7.28.

items.title: Closed submanifolds are complete; the sphere

milnor.label: §10, cf. p. 65
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. On p. 65 Milnor shows that the geodesics of the unit sphere $S^n$ are the great circles and discusses which arcs are minimal; the exposition (Chapter 7, §5) notes that compact Riemannian manifolds are complete.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: convergence in $N$ implies convergence for $\rho$. If $N$ is closed in $V$, then $(N, \rho)$ is complete. Hence a (pre)connected $N$ that is closed in $V$, in particular a connected compact one, is geodesically complete, every geodesic extends to $\mathbb R$, and any two of its points are joined by a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$ whose length is their distance. The unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$ (the companion project's slice submanifold), is geodesically complete, and any two of its points are joined by a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$ of length their distance.

chips: the source of complete manifolds here
diff: In the embedded setting closedness in $V$ is the practical source of complete manifolds: compact manifolds, spheres and compact matrix groups. Later chapters assume closedness of $N$ where Milnor assumes completeness (V10.22).
Chapter 7 does not identify the geodesics of $S^n$ with the great circles; that is done in Chapter 10 for the geodesics between two given points (V10.23).

items.title: Familiar examples of geodesics: $\mathbb R^n$ and $S^n$

milnor.label: §10, pp. 65–66
milnor.statement: In Euclidean space $\mathbb R^n$ the equations for a geodesic become $d^2x_i/dt^2 = 0$, whose solutions are the straight lines. The geodesics on $S^n$ are precisely the great circles, the intersections of $S^n$ with the planes through its centre: reflection in such a plane is an isometry fixing the great circle, hence fixing the unique minimal geodesic between two nearby points of it, and there is a great circle through any point in any direction. Antipodal points are joined by a continuum of minimal geodesics; any other two points by a unique minimal geodesic and an infinite family of non-minimal ones. Meridians of a surface of revolution are geodesics, and on a right circular cylinder the geodesics are the generating lines, the circles and the helices, two points being joined by infinitely many.

lean.statement: (i) On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$, with the induced metric: for unit vectors $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, the great circle $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$; and for any $p, q$, every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(S^n; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with such a great circle, with $L \ge 0$. For $q \ne \pm p$ the geodesics from $p$ to $q$ are, up to their values off $[0, 1]$, the arcs $\gamma_0, \gamma_1, \dots$ of V10.23, with strictly increasing energies: infinitely many geodesics. (ii) If every tangent space of $N \subseteq V$ is $V$ (an open subset of $V$, with the flat metric) and the segment from $p$ to $q$ lies in $N$, then $t \mapsto p + t(q - p)$ is a geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ and every geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees with it on $[0, 1]$: the geodesics of $V$ are the straight lines.

diff: The verified Chapter 7 lists the examples as not formalized; the sphere and flat open sets are treated in Chapter 10, for the index computation of Corollary 17.4 (V10.23) and the counterexample to Corollary 17.5 (V10.27).

Not formalized: the continuum of minimal geodesics between antipodal points; the minimality of the short arc $\gamma_0$, which follows from V7.30 and the list of geodesics but is not stated; meridians of surfaces of revolution; the cylinder.
The great circles are found from the uniqueness of geodesics with given initial data (V7.5, V9.9), not by Milnor's reflection argument.

items.title: The path space and its “tangent spaces”

milnor.label: §11, p. 67
milnor.statement: $\Omega(M; p, q)$ is the set of piecewise smooth paths $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ from $p$ to $q$, each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ of class $C^\infty$ for some subdivision. Milnor thinks of $\Omega$ as "something like an infinite dimensional manifold", to be topologized only in §16, and defines its "tangent space" $T\Omega_\omega$ as the vector space of piecewise smooth vector fields $W$ along $\omega$ with $W(0) = 0$ and $W(1) = 0$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric ($P_x$ the projection onto $T_xN$, extended by $P_x = 0$ off $N$): for $p, q \in V$, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is the set of maps $\omega : \mathbb R \to V$ that are piecewise smooth on $[0, 1]$ (V7.11), with $\omega(t) \in N$ for $t \in [0, 1]$, $\omega(0) = p$ and $\omega(1) = q$. For a map $\omega$, $T\Omega_\omega$ is the real vector space of maps $W$ that are piecewise smooth on $[0, 1]$ and tangent along $\omega$ ($P_{\omega(t)}W(t) = W(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$), with $W(0) = W(1) = 0$; it depends only on $\omega$ on $[0, 1]$.

chips: $\Omega$ has no manifold structure, here too
diff: As in the book, $\Omega$ carries no topology or manifold structure here; $T\Omega_\omega$ is *defined* as a space of fields and is related to $\Omega$ only through variations (V8.2–V8.3).
Paths and fields are maps on $\mathbb R$ considered on $[0, 1]$, and the subdivision is a finite set of break points; the break points of a field need not be those of $\omega$.
Smoothness on a closed piece means one-sided derivatives at its ends, which the book leaves implicit.

items.title: Variations and variation fields

milnor.label: §11, p. 68
milnor.statement: A variation of $\omega$ keeping the end points fixed is a map $\bar\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to \Omega$ with $\bar\alpha(0) = \omega$ and a subdivision $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_k = 1$ such that $\alpha(u, t) = \bar\alpha(u)(t)$ is $C^\infty$ on each strip $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [t_{i-1}, t_i]$; an $n$-parameter variation replaces $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ by a neighbourhood of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$. The variation vector field is $W_t = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$, and "clearly" $W \in T\Omega_\omega$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $P$ be a real normed space (Milnor's $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb R^n$) and $U \ni 0$ open in $P$. A map $\alpha(u, t)$ is a variation with break points $B$ (a finite set) if $\alpha(u, t) \in N$ for $u \in U$, $t \in [0, 1]$; $\alpha(u, 0)$ and $\alpha(u, 1)$ do not depend on $u \in U$; and $\alpha$ is $C^\infty$ on every closed strip $U \times [s, t]$, $0 \le s < t \le 1$, with no point of $B$ in $(s, t)$. Every $\alpha(u, \cdot)$ then lies in $\Omega(N; \omega(0), \omega(1))$, $\omega = \alpha(0, \cdot)$, and composing with a smooth map into $P$ sending $0$ into $U$ gives a variation again. For $P = \mathbb R$, $W_t = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ lies in $T\Omega_\omega$, and every $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(u, t)$ is tangent to $N$ at $\alpha(u, t)$.

chips: any open parameter set, any normed space
diff: The parameter set is any open set containing $0$ in any real normed space, which covers Milnor's $1$- and $n$-parameter variations at once.

Behind "clearly": $W$ is continuous at a break point because both adjacent strips compute the velocity of the same curve $u \mapsto \alpha(u, t_i)$, tangent because that curve lies in $N$, and zero at the ends because they are fixed.

items.title: Lemma 11.A: every family of tangent fields comes from one variation

milnor.label: §11, pp. 68 and 74
milnor.statement: Given $W \in T\Omega_\omega$ there is a variation with $\bar\alpha(0) = \omega$ and $\frac{d\bar\alpha}{du}(0) = W$: "in fact one can set" $\bar\alpha(u)(t) = \exp_{\omega(t)}(uW_t)$ (p. 68). On p. 74, 2-parameter variations with prescribed variation fields $W_1$, $W_2$ are chosen without comment.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $P$ a real normed space, and $\Lambda$ a family, piecewise smooth on $[0, 1]$, of continuous linear maps $\Lambda(t) : P \to V$ with values in $T_{\omega(t)}N$ and $\Lambda(0) = \Lambda(1) = 0$. There are $\varepsilon > 0$ and a finite set $B$ such that $\alpha(u, t) = \exp_{\omega(t)}(\Lambda(t)u)$ is a variation with break points $B$ on the ball $\|u\| < \varepsilon$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \omega(t)$ and derivative $\Lambda(t)$ in $u$ at $u = 0$, for $t \in [0, 1]$. In particular every $W \in T\Omega_\omega$ is the variation field of $\exp_{\omega(t)}(uW_t)$, $|u| < \varepsilon$, and any $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\omega$ are the variation fields of the 2-parameter variation $\exp_{\omega(t)}(u_1W_1(t) + u_2W_2(t))$.

diff: Any number of parameters (the exposition's Lemma 11.A); Milnor states the one-parameter case and uses the two-parameter case.

$\exp$ is defined only near the zero section (V7.8), so $\varepsilon$ must be chosen uniformly along $\omega$, by the compactness of $\omega([0, 1])$ and a bound for $\|\Lambda\|$; completeness of $N$ is not needed.
The derivative in $u$ at $0$ is $\Lambda(t)$ because $d(\exp_q)_0$ is the inclusion of $T_qN$ (V7.8).

items.title: Critical paths of the energy

milnor.label: §11, p. 69
milnor.statement: A path $\omega$ is a critical path of a function $F : \Omega \to \mathbb R$ if and only if $\frac{dF(\bar\alpha(u))}{du}\big|_{u=0}$ is zero for every variation $\bar\alpha$ of $\omega$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a map $\omega$ is a critical path of the energy $E$ (V8.5) if for every 1-parameter variation $\alpha$ with $\alpha(0, t) = \omega(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$, the function $u \mapsto E(\alpha(u, \cdot))$ is differentiable at $0$ with derivative $0$.

diff: Critical paths are defined for the energy only, the case of Corollary 12.3; Milnor's definition is for any function on $\Omega$.
The definition asks that the derivative exist; for $E$ it always does (V8.9).

items.title: Energy and length

milnor.label: §12, p. 70
milnor.statement: For $\omega \in \Omega$ and $0 \le a < b \le 1$, the energy from $a$ to $b$ is $E_a^b(\omega) = \int_a^b\|d\omega/dt\|^2\,dt$, $E = E_0^1$, and $L_a^b$ is the arc length. By Schwarz's inequality $(L_a^b)^2 \le (b - a)E_a^b$, with equality if and only if $\|d\omega/dt\|$ is constant, that is, if and only if the parameter $t$ is proportional to arc length.

lean.statement: For a map $c$ into a real normed space and $a \le b$, $E_a^b(c) = \int_a^b\|c'(t)\|^2\,dt$, $E = E_0^1$, and $L_a^b(c)$ is the length of V7.11. If $c$ is piecewise smooth on $[a, b]$, then $(L_a^b(c))^2 \le (b - a)E_a^b(c)$, with equality iff $\|c'\|$ takes one and the same value at every point of $(a, b)$ where $c$ is differentiable. An admissible path of constant speed $k$ there has $E_a^b = k^2(b - a)$.

diff: Any $a \le b$ and any normed target, where Milnor has $0 \le a < b \le 1$ and paths in $M$.

For a speed that is only piecewise continuous, "constant" can only mean constant off the break points; the formal equality condition says so. The proof is the variance identity $(b - a)\int_a^b(g - \bar g)^2 = (b - a)E_a^b - (L_a^b)^2$, $g = \|c'\|$ (the exposition's Lemma 12.A).

items.title: Lemma 12.1: the energy at a minimal geodesic

milnor.label: §12, Lemma 12.1
milnor.statement: Let $M$ be complete and $p, q \in M$ at distance $d$. Then the energy function $E : \Omega(M; p, q) \to \mathbb R$ takes on its minimum $d^2$ precisely on the set of minimal geodesics from $p$ to $q$. The proof is the chain $E(\gamma) = L(\gamma)^2 \le L(\omega)^2 \le E(\omega)$ for a minimal geodesic $\gamma$, with the equality cases.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a path $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ is *minimal* if $L(\gamma) \le L(\omega)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$. If $\gamma$ is minimal and a geodesic of $\Omega$ (V8.10), then $E(\gamma) \le E(\omega)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$.

diff: Only the inequality is formalized. Neither the value $d^2$ of the minimum nor the converse (a path of energy $d^2$ is a minimal geodesic, which needs the equality cases of V8.5 and of Corollary 10.7) is stated.
Completeness serves only to make a minimal geodesic exist (V7.26); the inequality holds on any $N$.
Minimality is among the paths of $\Omega$, parametrized on $[0, 1]$; by affine reparametrization this is Milnor's notion (V7.24), an equivalence not stated formally.

items.title: Velocity jumps, acceleration and the first variation

milnor.label: §12, p. 71
milnor.statement: For $\omega \in \Omega$, Milnor writes $V_t = d\omega/dt$ for the velocity, $A_t = \frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\omega}{dt}$ for the acceleration, and $\Delta_tV = V_{t^+} - V_{t^-}$ for the discontinuity of the velocity at $t$, which is zero for all but finitely many $t$ in $(0, 1)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a map $f$ into $V$, the jump $\Delta_tf' = f'(t^+) - f'(t^-)$ is the difference of the right and the left derivative of $f$ at $t$; it vanishes where $f$ is differentiable. Along a path $\omega$, $\frac{DX}{dt}(t) = P_{\omega(t)}X'(t)$, $V = \omega'$ and $A = \frac{D}{dt}V$. The first variation of $\omega$ in the direction $W$ is $-\sum_{0 < t < 1}\langle W_t, \Delta_tV\rangle - \int_0^1\langle W_t, A_t\rangle\,dt$, the sum being finite: for $\omega$ differentiable off a finite set $B$, it is the sum over the points of $B$ in $(0, 1)$. It depends only on $W$ on $[0, 1]$.

diff: The sum is written over all of $(0, 1)$, its terms vanishing off the break points; the formal statement shows it is the finite sum over the break points.

items.title: Calculus on closed strips

milnor.label: §§12–13, pp. 71–76
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. In the proofs of Theorems 12.2 and 13.1 Milnor differentiates under the integral sign, integrates by parts on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ and adds up, and interchanges partial derivatives of a variation, which is smooth only on closed strips, all without comment.

lean.statement: For $F$ smooth on a closed strip $U \times [a, b]$, $U \subseteq \mathbb R$ open, $a < b$: the partial derivatives $\partial F/\partial u$, $\partial F/\partial t$ computed within the strip are smooth on it, are one-sided $t$-derivatives on the edges, and the mixed partials agree on the whole closed strip, edges included. If $F$ and $F'$ are continuous on the strip and $F'$ is the $u$-derivative of $F$ inside it, then $u \mapsto \int_a^bF(u, t)\,dt$ has derivative $\int_a^bF'(u_0, t)\,dt$ at every $u_0 \in U$, also for integrands that are $C^1$ only piece by piece. If $\int_s^tg = F^-(t) - F^+(s)$ on every piece $[s, t]$ of $[a, b]$ with break points $B$, then $\int_a^bg = F^-(b) - F^+(a) - \sum_{x \in B \cap (a, b)}(F^+(x) - F^-(x))$.

chips: mixed partials up to the edges
diff: These are the analytic facts behind "differentiate under the integral sign" and "integrate by parts on each interval": smoothness on the closed strips, compactness for the domination bound, and the symmetry of second derivatives on the edges, where the $t$-derivatives are one-sided.
The last statement is the bookkeeping by which the boundary terms of the pieces telescope into the jump terms of the first and second variation formulas.

items.title: Theorem 12.2: the first variation formula

milnor.label: §12, Theorem 12.2
milnor.statement: Let $\bar\alpha$ be a variation of $\omega$ with variation field $W$. Then $\frac12\frac{dE(\bar\alpha(u))}{du}\big|_{u=0} = -\sum_t\langle W_t, \Delta_tV\rangle - \int_0^1\langle W_t, A_t\rangle\,dt$. The proof differentiates under the integral sign, uses Lemma 8.3 and "Lemma 8.5" to replace $\frac{D}{\partial u}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t}$ by $\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}$, integrates by parts on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ and adds up.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\alpha$ be a 1-parameter variation (V8.2) with parameter set $U \subseteq \mathbb R$. For every $u_0 \in U$, $u \mapsto E(\alpha(u, \cdot))$ is differentiable at $u_0$, and $\frac12\frac{d}{du}E(\alpha(u, \cdot))|_{u_0}$ is the first variation (V8.7) of $\alpha(u_0, \cdot)$ in the direction $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(u_0, \cdot)$: $$-\sum_t\Big\langle\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}, \Delta_t\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t}\Big\rangle - \int_0^1\Big\langle\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}, \frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t}\Big\rangle\,dt$$ at $(u_0, t)$. At $u_0 = 0$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \omega(t)$ on $[0, 1]$, this is Milnor's formula.

diff: The formula holds at every value of the parameter (the exposition's formula (12.2′)), which is what §13 differentiates; the existence of the derivative is part of the conclusion.

Milnor's reference to Lemma 8.5 should be to Lemma 8.7 (8.5 is the definition of a symmetric connection). The scan loses the leading minus sign of the displayed statement; the end of the proof on p. 72 has it.

Hidden: differentiation under the integral sign and the symmetry of mixed partials on the closed strips (V8.8); the boundary terms telescope into the jump terms because $\partial\alpha/\partial u$ is continuous in $t$.

items.title: Geodesics of $\Omega$, and criticality through the first variation

milnor.label: §12, p. 73
milnor.statement: The path $\omega \in \Omega$ is a geodesic if and only if $\omega$ is $C^\infty$ on the whole interval $[0, 1]$ and its acceleration $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\omega}{dt}$ is identically zero along $\omega$. "Clearly" a geodesic is a critical point of $E$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a map $\omega$ is an (unbroken) geodesic if it is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the ends, and a geodesic on $(0, 1)$ in the sense of V7.1, so that $A = 0$ there. For $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$: $\omega$ is a critical path (V8.4) iff its first variation (V8.7) vanishes in every direction $W \in T\Omega_\omega$. For a geodesic, the first variation vanishes in every direction.

diff: The acceleration is required to vanish on $(0, 1)$; at the ends it then vanishes by continuity.
The converse direction of "critical iff the first variation vanishes on $T\Omega_\omega$" needs every field to be a variation field, Lemma 11.A (V8.3).

items.title: Corollary 12.3: the critical paths of $E$ are the geodesics

milnor.label: §12, Corollary 12.3
milnor.statement: The path $\omega$ is a critical point for the function $E$ if and only if $\omega$ is a geodesic. Proof: a variation with $W(t) = f(t)A(t)$, $f$ positive except at the $t_i$, gives $A = 0$ on each piece; one with $W(t_i) = \Delta_{t_i}V$ gives $\Delta_{t_i}V = 0$, so $\omega$ is $C^1$; then $\omega$ is $C^\infty$ "from the uniqueness theorem for differential equations".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a path $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ is a critical path of $E$ iff it is a geodesic (V8.10). The steps, for $\omega$ critical and smooth on the pieces of a finite set $B$: the acceleration vanishes at every $t \in (0, 1) \setminus B$; the one-sided velocities and their jumps are tangent to $N$, and every jump $\Delta_tV$, $0 < t < 1$, vanishes; through every $q \in N$ with any $v \in T_qN$ at any time $x$ there is a geodesic on an interval around $x$; and a path that is a geodesic on both sides of $x$, smooth up to $x$ from each side and differentiable at $x$, is a geodesic near $x$.

diff: The test variations exist only by Lemma 11.A (V8.3); $W = fA$ must be continuous at the $t_i$, where the one-sided accelerations differ; and a field with the prescribed values $\Delta_{t_i}V$ has to be constructed. The formal proof uses bump functions at one point at a time.

The last step needs the lift $(\omega, \omega')$ to solve the geodesic equation at the former break point itself (a derivative-extension argument) before uniqueness for the first-order geodesic system (V7.3, V7.4) applies.

items.title: The curvature identity (13.3), and jumps under differentiation

milnor.label: §13, pp. 75–76
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 13.1, the curvature formula $\frac{D}{\partial u_1}\frac{D}{\partial t}V - \frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial u_1}V = R(V, W_1)V$ (Lemma 9.2) and $\frac{D}{\partial u_1}V = \frac{D}{\partial t}W_1$ (Lemma 8.7) give (13.3): $\frac{D}{\partial u_1}\frac{D}{\partial t}V = \frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V$. On p. 75 the second term of the differentiated first variation formula is "rearranged", which differentiates the velocity jumps in $u$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric, $R$ Milnor's curvature tensor with his sign ($0$ off $N$): (i) for $F(u, t)$ smooth on an open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^2$ with values in $N$, at every point of $O$, $$\frac{D}{\partial u}\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} = \frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial F}{\partial u} + R\Big(\frac{\partial F}{\partial t}, \frac{\partial F}{\partial u}\Big)\frac{\partial F}{\partial t},$$ with $\frac{D}{\partial u}X = P(\partial X/\partial u)$, $\frac{D}{\partial t}X = P(\partial X/\partial t)$. (ii) For a 1-parameter variation $\alpha$, $u_0 \in U$ and $0 < x < 1$, the jump $\Delta_x\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t}(u, \cdot)$ is differentiable in $u$ at $u_0$, with derivative $\Delta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(u_0, \cdot)$.

chips: on strips, up to the edges
diff: (i) is (13.3) for a surface, with $x = t$, $y = u$ in Lemma 9.2.

Lemmas 8.7 and 9.2 are applied by Milnor to a surface defined only on strips; Chapter 6 states them for surfaces on all of $\mathbb R^2$, so the identity is proved near interior points, and differentiating a one-sided $t$-derivative in $u$ needs the symmetry of mixed partials on the edges (V8.8).

items.title: Theorem 13.1: the second variation formula

milnor.label: §13, Theorem 13.1
milnor.statement: Let $\bar\alpha : U \to \Omega$ be a 2-parameter variation of the geodesic $\gamma$ with variation fields $W_i = \frac{\partial\bar\alpha}{\partial u_i}(0, 0)$, $i = 1, 2$. Then $$\frac12\frac{\partial^2E(\bar\alpha(u_1, u_2))}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0) = -\sum_t\Big\langle W_2(t), \Delta_t\frac{DW_1}{dt}\Big\rangle - \int_0^1\Big\langle W_2, \frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V\Big\rangle\,dt.$$ It is introduced on p. 74 to show that $E_{**}$ is well defined, and proved on pp. 75–76 from 12.2, the vanishing of $\Delta_tV$ and $\frac{D}{dt}V$ along a geodesic, (13.2) and (13.3).

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a path $\gamma$ with velocity $V$ and fields $W_1, W_2$ along it, let $\Phi(W_1, W_2)$ be the right side above, where $\Delta_t\frac{DW_1}{dt} = P_{\gamma(t)}(\Delta_tW_1')$ is the jump of $\frac{DW_1}{dt} = PW_1'$. Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic (V8.10) and $\alpha(u_1, u_2, t)$ a 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ ($\alpha(0, 0, t) = \gamma(t)$ on $[0, 1]$) with variation fields $W_1, W_2$. Then $u_1 \mapsto \frac{\partial}{\partial u_2}E(\alpha(u_1, u_2, \cdot))|_{u_2 = 0}$ is differentiable at $u_1 = 0$, with derivative $2\Phi(W_1, W_2)$. Two 2-parameter variations of $\gamma$ whose variation fields agree on $[0, 1]$ give the same value.

diff: Milnor's $\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0)$ is the iterated derivative $\partial/\partial u_1$ of $\partial E/\partial u_2$ along $u_2 = 0$, which is what his proof computes; its existence is part of the conclusion, and $E \circ \bar\alpha$ is not assumed to be of class $C^2$.
The proof needs formula (12.2′) at every $(u_1, 0)$ (V8.9), and differentiation of the jump and integral terms in $u_1$ (V8.8, V8.12).
The scan drops the $-\sum_t$ in front of the first term of the displayed statement; (13.2) on the same page has it.

items.title: The Hessian $E_{**}$

milnor.label: §13, p. 74
milnor.statement: For a geodesic $\gamma$, the Hessian $E_{**} : T\Omega_\gamma \times T\Omega_\gamma \to \mathbb R$ of $E$ at $\gamma$ is defined by analogy with the Hessian $f_{**}$ of a function on a manifold: given $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$, choose a 2-parameter variation with these variation fields and put $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = \frac{\partial^2E(\bar\alpha(u_1, u_2))}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 2\Phi(W_1, W_2)$ ($\Phi$ as in V8.13) is a bilinear form on $T\Omega_\gamma$, depending only on the values of the fields on $[0, 1]$. The variation fields of a 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ lie in $T\Omega_\gamma$. If $\gamma$ is a geodesic, every 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ with variation fields $W_1, W_2$ has $\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0) = E_{**}(W_1, W_2)$ (in the sense of V8.13), and every pair $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ arises (V8.3). So Milnor's definition is well defined and agrees with $E_{**}$.

diff: $\Omega$ has no manifold structure, here as in the book, so $E_{**}$ is defined by the second variation formula and identified with Milnor's definition through variations: every pair of fields comes from a variation (Lemma 11.A), and every such variation computes it (Theorem 13.1).

items.title: Corollary 13.4: $E_{**}$ is symmetric and bilinear

milnor.label: §13, Corollary 13.4
milnor.statement: The expression $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = \frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0)$ is a well defined, symmetric, bilinear function of $W_1$ and $W_2$: well defined and bilinear by the second variation formula, symmetric because $\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2} = \frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_2\partial u_1}$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $E_{**}$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $T\Omega_\gamma$. For tangent vectors $v, w_1, w_2$ at $x \in N$, $\langle R(v, w_1)v, w_2\rangle = \langle R(v, w_2)v, w_1\rangle$.

items.title: Remark 13.5: the second derivative along a 1-parameter variation

items.title: Lemma 13.6: the Hessian at a minimal geodesic

milnor.label: §13, Lemma 13.6
milnor.statement: If $\gamma$ is a minimal geodesic from $p$ to $q$, then the bilinear pairing $E_{**}$ is positive semi-definite. Hence the index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is zero. Proof: $E(\bar\alpha(u)) \ge E(\gamma) = E(\bar\alpha(0))$ forces $\frac{d^2E(\bar\alpha(u))}{du^2}(0) \ge 0$.

items.title: Linear equations have global solutions (Lemma 14.A)

milnor.label: §14, p. 77
milnor.statement: The Jacobi equation, a linear second-order differential equation, has $2n$ linearly independent solutions, each of which is "defined throughout $\gamma$" and of class $C^\infty$; a Jacobi field is determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$. Milnor gives no proof.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a complete real normed space and $t \mapsto A(t)$ a continuous map from $\mathbb R$ to the continuous linear maps $E \to E$. (i) For every $t_0 \in \mathbb R$ and $x_0 \in E$ the equation $x' = A(t)x$ has a solution on all of $\mathbb R$ with $x(t_0) = x_0$, and the solution with value $\xi$ at $s$ depends linearly on $\xi$. (ii) If $a < b$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and solves the equation on $(a, b)$, then for every $s \in [a, b]$, end points included, $f$ agrees on $[a, b]$ with the solution whose value at $s$ is $f(s)$. (iii) If $A$ is $C^\infty$ on $[a, b]$ (one-sided derivatives at the ends) and $f'(t) = A(t)f(t)$ at every $t \in [a, b]$, then $f$ is $C^\infty$ on $[a, b]$.
