It is proved by truncating the equation radially and bounding the solution by Grönwall's inequality in both time directions, so that the truncation is never active.
The coefficients may be any continuous family on any complete space, extending the skew-adjoint case of Chapter 6.

items.title: Jacobi fields and the Jacobi system

milnor.label: §14, p. 77
milnor.statement: A vector field $J$ along a geodesic $\gamma$ is a *Jacobi field* if it satisfies the Jacobi differential equation $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0$, $V = d\gamma/dt$. In terms of orthonormal parallel fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $\gamma$, writing $J = \sum f^iP_i$, it becomes a linear system with coefficients $\langle R(V, P_j)V, P_i\rangle$; a Jacobi field is completely determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric. A *smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$* is a map $\gamma : \mathbb R \to V$ that is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the ends, and has values in $N$ there; every geodesic of $\Omega$ is one. A map $J$ is a *Jacobi field along $\gamma$* if it is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, tangent along $\gamma$, and $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0$ on $(0, 1)$, $D/dt$ the covariant derivative of V8.7. With $S = P'P - PP'$ and $K(t)v = R(V, P(t)v)V$, the Jacobi system is the linear system $J' = SJ + Y$, $Y' = SY - KJ$ for $(J, Y)$ in $V \times V$; its solution with any value at any time exists on $\mathbb R$. If $s \in [0, 1]$ and both initial values are tangent at $\gamma(s)$, both components stay tangent on $[0, 1]$, the first is a Jacobi field and the second its covariant derivative. Conversely every Jacobi field $J$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with the solution whose value at $s$ is $(J(s), \frac{DJ}{dt}(s))$; in particular $J(s) = 0$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(s) = 0$ force $J = 0$ on $[0, 1]$.

chips: no parallel frame: a system in $V \times V$
diff: No frame is used: the unknown is $(J, \frac{DJ}{dt})$ in $V \times V$, and the term $S$ keeps solutions with tangent initial values tangent, their normal parts solving a homogeneous linear system and vanishing at $s$.
Parallel frames along $\gamma$ (Lemma 8.2) are formalized only for curves on all of $\mathbb R$; the frame-free system avoids extending $\gamma$.
The definition and the solution theory hold along any smooth curve in $N$, not only along a geodesic, with initial values at any $s \in [0, 1]$; the global existence is V9.1.

items.title: The space of Jacobi fields (Corollary 14.B)

milnor.label: §14, p. 77
milnor.statement: The Jacobi equation has $2n$ linearly independent solutions, and a Jacobi field is completely determined by $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ (V9.2) and $n = \dim N$. $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ is the vector space of the Jacobi fields along $\gamma$ that are constant off $[0, 1]$; every Jacobi field agrees on $[0, 1]$ with one of them. For every $s \in [0, 1]$, $J \mapsto (J(s), \frac{DJ}{dt}(s))$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathcal J(\gamma) \to T_{\gamma(s)}N \times T_{\gamma(s)}N$: every pair of tangent vectors at $\gamma(s)$ is the value and covariant derivative at $s$ of exactly one field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$; and $\dim\mathcal J(\gamma) = 2n$.

diff: The isomorphism holds at every $s \in [0, 1]$, along any smooth curve in $N$; that every pair of initial values occurs is the global existence of V9.1.
Fields are normalized to be constant off $[0, 1]$, so that the space is finite-dimensional on the nose; its elements are maps on $\mathbb R$.

items.title: Conjugate points and their multiplicity

milnor.label: §14, p. 77
milnor.statement: For $a \ne b$, the points $p = \gamma(a)$ and $q = \gamma(b)$ are *conjugate* along $\gamma$ if there is a non-zero Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ which vanishes for $t = a$ and $t = b$; the multiplicity of $p$ and $q$ as conjugate points is the dimension of the vector space of all such fields. A footnote warns that if $\gamma$ has self-intersections one should rather say that the parameter values $a$ and $b$ are conjugate.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. Parameters $a$ and $b$ are *conjugate along $\gamma$* if $a, b \in [0, 1]$, $a \ne b$, and some Jacobi field along $\gamma$ vanishes at $a$ and at $b$ without vanishing identically on $[0, 1]$. Their *multiplicity* is the dimension of the space of fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $a$ and $b$, finite by V9.3; for $a \ne b$ in $[0, 1]$ they are conjugate iff the multiplicity is positive.

diff: Conjugacy is a relation between parameter values, as Milnor's footnote recommends; throughout §15, "the conjugate points $\gamma(t)$" are read as the conjugate parameters $t$.

items.title: Theorem 14.1: the null vectors of $E_{**}$ are the Jacobi fields

milnor.label: §14, Theorem 14.1
milnor.statement: A vector field $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ belongs to the null space of $E_{**}$ if and only if $W_1$ is a Jacobi field. Proof (pp. 78–79): a Jacobi field vanishing at the ends is null by the second variation formula; conversely, testing against $W_2 = f(t)(\frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V)$, $f$ vanishing exactly at the break points, makes $W_1$ a Jacobi field on each piece, testing against a field with values $\Delta_{t_i}\frac{DW_1}{dt}$ at the break points removes the jumps, and the pieces "fit together" since a solution is determined by $W_1(t_i)$ and $\frac{DW_1}{dt}(t_i)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic (V8.10) and $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$. Then $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for every $W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ iff $W_1$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$; in particular such a $W_1$ is $C^\infty$ on all of $[0, 1]$. On the way: for a Jacobi field $J$ along any curve, $\Phi(J, Y) = 0$ for every field $Y$; for a null vector the Jacobi operator vanishes off the break points and every jump of $W_1'$ is tangent and zero; and for a smooth tangent field the Jacobi equation is a second-order equation in $V$.

The test field with prescribed values at the break points has to be constructed, and Milnor's fitting together needs Jacobi fields along all of $\gamma$ with given initial values (V9.2), stated in the book without proof. The formal proof joins the pieces by a local argument instead: a smooth second-order equation holds on both sides of a former break point with a right side continuous across it.

items.title: Theorem 14.1: the null space and the nullity

milnor.label: §14, Theorem 14.1, pp. 77–79
milnor.statement: The null space of $E_{**}$ is the space of $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2$, the nullity $\nu$ is its dimension, and $E_{**}$ is degenerate if $\nu > 0$ (pp. 77–78). Theorem 14.1 continues: hence $E_{**}$ is degenerate if and only if the end points $p$ and $q$ are conjugate along $\gamma$, and the nullity of $E_{**}$ equals their multiplicity as conjugate points. On p. 79: the nullity is always finite.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, the *null space* of $E_{**}$ is the space of the restrictions to $[0, 1]$, extended as constants, of the $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$, and the *nullity* is its dimension. If $\gamma$ is a geodesic, the null space is the space of fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$; so the nullity is the multiplicity of $0$ and $1$ as conjugate parameters (V9.4), in particular finite, and it is positive iff $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma$.

Finiteness needs the identification with a subspace of the $2n$-dimensional $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ (V9.3).

items.title: Remark 14.2: the nullity is less than $n$

milnor.label: §14, Remark 14.2
milnor.statement: Actually the nullity satisfies $0 \le \nu < n$: the Jacobi fields vanishing for $t = 0$ form a space of dimension precisely $n$, and $J_t = tV_t$ is a Jacobi field vanishing for $t = 0$ but not for $t = 1$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: along a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, the fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $0$ form a space of dimension $n = \dim N$. If $\gamma$ is moreover a geodesic on $(0, 1)$, then $t \mapsto tV(t)$ is a Jacobi field, and $\gamma$ is constant on $[0, 1]$ if $V(1) = 0$; along a constant curve, $t \mapsto ty$ is a Jacobi field for every tangent vector $y$. Hence, for a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ and $n \ge 1$, the nullity of $E_{**}$ satisfies $\nu < n$.

$\nu < n$ requires $n \ge 1$: for $n = 0$, $\nu = 0 = n$.

items.title: Example 1: no conjugate points in a flat space

milnor.label: §14, Example 1
milnor.statement: Suppose that $M$ is "flat", in the sense that the curvature tensor is identically zero. Then the Jacobi equation becomes $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} = 0$; in parallel fields, $J = \sum f^iP_i$ with $\frac{d^2f^i}{dt^2} = 0$. Evidently a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ can have at most one zero; thus there are no conjugate points, and $E_{**}$ is non-degenerate.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq V$ be a slice submanifold every tangent space of which is all of $V$ (for instance an open subset of $V$, which is a slice submanifold of codimension $0$). Then the induced metric is flat ($R = 0$); along a curve in $N$ every Jacobi field is affine, $J(t) = J(0) + t(J(1) - J(0))$ on $[0, 1]$; no two parameters are conjugate along any curve in $N$; and at every geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ the index and the nullity of $E_{**}$ are $0$.

Milnor's hypothesis is $R \equiv 0$; the formal one is that $N$ has codimension $0$. A flat manifold embedded with positive codimension, such as a flat torus in $\mathbb R^4$, has $R = 0$ but is not covered, since its Jacobi fields are not computed without parallel frames.
The formal statement also gives index $0$ at every geodesic, which Milnor does not state here.

items.title: Example 2: antipodal points of $S^n$

milnor.label: §14, Example 2, pp. 79–80
milnor.statement: Suppose that $p$ and $q$ are antipodal points on the unit sphere $S^n$, and let $\gamma$ be a great circle arc from $p$ to $q$. Then $p$ and $q$ are conjugate with multiplicity $n - 1$, so the nullity of $E_{**}$ takes its largest possible value. Proof (p. 80): rotating the sphere about the axis through $p$ and $q$ gives variations through geodesics, whose variation fields are Jacobi fields vanishing at $p$ and $q$ (Lemma 14.3); rotating in $n - 1$ different directions gives $n - 1$ linearly independent ones.

lean.statement: On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$, with the induced metric: for unit vectors $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$; for every $e \perp p, u$, $t \mapsto \sin(Lt)\,e$ is a Jacobi field along $c$; and for $L > 0$ and $0 < t \le 1$, the multiplicity of $0$ and $t$ as conjugate parameters along $c$ is $n - 1$ if $Lt$ is a multiple of $\pi$, and $0$ otherwise. For $L = \pi$, $t = 1$ this is Milnor's statement for the great semicircle from $p$ to $-p$.

The formal statement covers every great circle and every parameter: the conjugate parameters along $c$ are exactly the $t$ with $Lt \in \pi\mathbb Z$, each of multiplicity $n - 1$, which is what the index computation of §17 needs.

The Jacobi fields are checked directly with $R(x, y)z = \langle x, z\rangle y - \langle y, z\rangle x$ rather than through rotations and Lemma 14.3; the upper bound $n - 1$ comes from Remark 14.2 (V9.7), as in the book.

items.title: Lemma 14.3: variations through geodesics give Jacobi fields

milnor.label: §14, Lemma 14.3
milnor.statement: A variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics, not necessarily keeping the end points fixed, is a $C^\infty$ map $\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1] \to M$ with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and each $\bar\alpha(u)$ a geodesic (p. 79). Lemma 14.3: its variation vector field $W(t) = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$. Proof: apply $\frac{D}{\partial u}$ to $\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t} = 0$ and use Lemmas 9.2 and 8.7.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\alpha(u, t)$ be $C^\infty$ on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$ (one-sided derivatives along the edges $t = 0, 1$), with values in $N$ there, such that each $t \mapsto \alpha(u, t)$, $|u| < \varepsilon$, is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$. Then $W(t) = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ is a Jacobi field along $\alpha(0, \cdot)$. Being a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ depends only on $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$.

items.title: Lemma 14.4: every Jacobi field comes from a variation through geodesics

milnor.label: §14, Lemma 14.4
milnor.statement: Every Jacobi field along a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ may be obtained by a variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics. Proof: in a neighbourhood $U$ of $\gamma(0)$ where any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points, with $\gamma(t) \in U$ for $0 \le t \le \delta$, minimal geodesics between the points of two curves $a(u)$, $b(u)$ give Jacobi fields along $\gamma|[0, \delta]$ with arbitrary values at $0$ and $\delta$; so $J \mapsto (J(0), J(\delta))$ is onto, hence an isomorphism (both spaces have dimension $2n$); "using the compactness of $[0, 1]$", the geodesics extend over $[0, 1]$ for small $u$.

(ii) A smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ that is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto \exp_{\gamma(0)}(tV(0))$, a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$. (iii) Geodesics $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ with smooth initial data depend smoothly on $(u, t)$ over any compact time interval on which the one at $u = 0$ exists. (iv) **Lemma 14.4:** for such a $\gamma$ and a Jacobi field $J$ along it, there are $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\alpha$ satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 14.3 (V9.8) on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t) = J(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$.

items.title: A Jacobi field is determined by its values at two non-conjugate points

milnor.label: §14, p. 81
milnor.statement: In the proof of Lemma 14.4, in parentheses and without proof: more generally a Jacobi field is determined by its values at any two non-conjugate points.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and $a \ne b$ in $[0, 1]$ parameters that are not conjugate along $\gamma$ (V9.4). items.title: Remark 14.5: Jacobi fields along short geodesics

milnor.label: §14, Remark 14.5
milnor.statement: The argument of Lemma 14.4 shows that in any such neighbourhood $U$ the Jacobi fields along a geodesic segment in $U$ are uniquely determined by their values at the end points of the segment.

items.title: Remark 14.6: no conjugate points near the start

milnor.label: §14, Remark 14.6
milnor.statement: The proof of 14.4 also shows that there is a neighbourhood $(-\delta, \delta)$ of $0$ such that $\gamma(t)$ is not conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$ for $t \in (-\delta, \delta)$; and, by 15.2, the points conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along an entire geodesic have no cluster points.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for every smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that no $t \in (0, \delta)$ is conjugate to $0$ along $\gamma$.

chips: no statement along an entire geodesic
diff: Only $t > 0$, $\gamma$ being given on $[0, 1]$; the statement that the conjugate points along an entire geodesic have no cluster points is not formalized (the reparametrization of a geodesic to $[0, 1]$, the exposition's Lemma 14.C, is not formalized).

It holds along any smooth curve in $N$, with $\delta$ the explicit mesh of V9.16, since no two parameters closer than it are conjugate; Milnor's neighbourhood $U$, which needs $\gamma|[0, t]$ to be the minimal geodesic between its ends, is not used.

items.title: The index and the nullity of a bilinear form

milnor.label: §15, p. 83; §2, p. 5
milnor.statement: The index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is the maximum dimension of a subspace of $T\Omega_\gamma$ on which $E_{**}$ is negative definite (p. 83); for a bilinear functional on a vector space, the index and the nullity are defined in §2 (p. 5).

lean.statement: Let $B$ be a bilinear form on a real vector space $X$. $B$ is negative (positive) definite on a subspace $S$ if $B(x, x) < 0$ ($> 0$) for every $x \ne 0$ in $S$. The *index* of $B$ is the supremum, in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\} \cup \{\infty\}$, of the dimensions of the finite-dimensional subspaces on which $B$ is negative definite; a finite index is the dimension of such a subspace. A linear map $L$ with $B'(Lx, Ly) = B(x, y)$ does not decrease the index, so an isomorphism carrying $B$ to $B'$ preserves it; on a finite-dimensional space the index is Mathlib's negative index of inertia of $x \mapsto B(x, x)$. The *nullity* is the dimension of $\{x : B(x, y) = 0 \text{ for all } y\}$; for $E_{**}$ the null space is read on $[0, 1]$ (V9.6).

diff: Milnor's "maximum dimension" presupposes that the maximum exists; here the index is a supremum over finite-dimensional subspaces, possibly $\infty$, and its finiteness for $E_{**}$ is part of Theorem 15.1, as in the book. A negative definite subspace of infinite dimension contains finite-dimensional ones of every dimension, and so also gives $\infty$.

milnor.label: §15, pp. 85–87

items.title: The second variation formula for piecewise Jacobi fields

milnor.label: §15, pp. 84 and 87
milnor.statement: In the proof of Lemma 15.3 (p. 84), for a broken Jacobi field $W_1$ and a field $W_2$ vanishing at the break points, the second variation formula reduces to its jump terms; on p. 87 the values of $E_{**}(J_h, \cdot)$ are seen "easily" from the second variation formula.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $X, Y \in T\Omega_\gamma$, and $B$ a finite set such that near every $t \in (0, 1) \setminus B$ the field $X$ agrees with some Jacobi field along $\gamma$ (the zero field is one). Then $$E_{**}(X, Y) = -2\sum_{b \in B \cap (0, 1)}\Big\langle Y(b), \Delta_b\frac{DX}{dt}\Big\rangle,$$ $\Delta_b\frac{DX}{dt} = P_{\gamma(b)}(\Delta_bX')$. $\gamma$ need not be a geodesic.

diff: The reduction that Milnor performs twice inside proofs is stated once: the integrand of the second variation formula (V8.13) vanishes off the finite set $B \cup \{1\}$.

items.title: Positivity near zeros, and fine subdivisions

milnor.label: §15, pp. 83–84
milnor.statement: Each $\gamma(t)$ lies in an open set $U$ in which any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points (§10), and the subdivision $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k = 1$ is chosen "sufficiently fine" that each $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ lies in such a $U$ and is minimal. Milnor uses two consequences: along each segment the Jacobi fields are determined by their end values, which can be prescribed (Remark 14.5); and each segment has smaller energy than any other path between its end points (p. 84).

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $C \ge 0$ a bound for $\|P'(t)\|^2 + \|K(t)\|$ on $[0, 1]$ ($K$ as in V9.2), and $h_0 = 1/(C + 1)$. (i) *Poincaré estimate:* if $X \in T\Omega_\gamma$ and every $t \in [0, 1]$ has a zero $s \in [0, t]$ of $X$ with $t - s \le h_0$, then $\int_0^1\|X\|^2\,dt \le \frac12E_{**}(X, X)$; so $E_{**}(X, X) \le 0$ forces $X = 0$ on $[0, 1]$. (ii) If $0 \le a < b \le 1$ and $b - a \le h_0$, a field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $a$ and $b$ is $0$, and $J \mapsto (J(a), J(b))$ is an isomorphism onto $T_{\gamma(a)}N \times T_{\gamma(b)}N$: no two parameters at distance at most $h_0$ are conjugate. (iii) A finite set $B \subseteq (0, \tau)$ is *fine for $[0, \tau]$* if consecutive points of $\{0\} \cup B \cup \{\tau\}$ are at most $h_0$ apart; for every $\tau > 0$ there is one whose last point is within $h_0/2$ of $\tau$.

diff: "Sufficiently fine" becomes the explicit mesh $h_0$, which depends only on bounds for $P'$ and the curvature along $\gamma$; $\gamma$ need not be a geodesic, and neither $\exp$ nor minimal geodesics enter.

The existence of Milnor's subdivisions needs a Lebesgue number of a finite cover and a length bound for minimality (Theorem 10.4), which the book does not spell out; the Poincaré estimate replaces both of his uses.

items.title: Broken Jacobi fields and $T'$

milnor.label: §15, pp. 83–84 and 86
milnor.statement: $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, t_1, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of vector fields $W$ along $\gamma$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$ such that each $W|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$: a finite-dimensional space of broken Jacobi fields (p. 83). $T'$ is the space of fields with $W(t_0) = W(t_1) = \dots = W(t_k) = 0$, and "it follows from §14.5" that the broken Jacobi field with given values at the $t_i$ exists and is unique (p. 84). On p. 86, along $\gamma_\tau$, the broken Jacobi fields for $0 < t_1 < \dots < t_i < \tau$ form a space isomorphic to $TM_{\gamma(t_1)} \oplus \dots \oplus TM_{\gamma(t_i)}$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. For $\tau \in \mathbb R$, the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ are the fields of $T\Omega_\gamma$ vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$. Let $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ be fine for $[0, \tau]$ (V9.16). A map is a *broken Jacobi field* on $[0, \tau]$ for $B$ if on each piece between consecutive points of $\{0\} \cup B \cup \{\tau\}$ it agrees with a field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$. Milnor's $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ that are broken Jacobi fields, and $T'$ the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ vanishing at the points of $B$. $W \mapsto (W(b))_{b \in B}$ is a linear isomorphism from the broken Jacobi fields onto $\bigoplus_{b \in B}T_{\gamma(b)}N$.

diff: Everything is along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$, as fields on $[0, 1]$ vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$; Milnor uses $\tau = 1$ here and $\gamma_\tau$ on p. 86.

A piece is the restriction of a Jacobi field along all of $\gamma$, which is equivalent to being a Jacobi field along the segment by V9.1–V9.2, an equivalence not stated formally. Existence is by induction over the division points with V9.16 (ii); Milnor's "follows from §14.5" also needs the gluing of the pieces.

items.title: Lemma 15.3: the splitting of $T\Omega_\gamma$

milnor.label: §15, Lemma 15.3
milnor.statement: $T\Omega_\gamma = T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k) \oplus T'$, the two subspaces are mutually perpendicular with respect to $E_{**}$, and $E_{**}$ restricted to $T'$ is positive definite. Proof (pp. 84–85): $W = W_1 + (W - W_1)$; perpendicularity from the second variation formula; $E_{**}(W, W) \ge 0$ on $T'$ because each segment is minimal, and $E_{**}(W, W) = 0$ puts $W$ in the null space, so $W$ is a Jacobi field, and $T'$ contains no Jacobi field other than $0$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ fine for $[0, \tau]$. (i) The fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ are the direct sum of the broken Jacobi fields and $T'$ (V9.17). (ii) For a broken Jacobi field $W_1$ and every field $Y$ along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$, $E_{**}(W_1, Y) = -2\sum_{b \in B}\langle Y(b), \Delta_b\frac{DW_1}{dt}\rangle$; in particular $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for $W_2 \in T'$. (iii) $E_{**}(W, W) > 0$ for every $W \ne 0$ in $T'$.

diff: Stated along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$, for fine subdivisions in the sense of V9.16; Milnor's lemma is $\tau = 1$ for his subdivisions.

(iii) departs from Milnor's proof: a field of $T'$ has a zero within $h_0$ before every point, so the Poincaré estimate gives $E_{**}(W, W) > 0$ directly, without minimal geodesics, variations or Theorem 14.1.

items.title: Lemma 15.4: the index on the broken Jacobi fields

milnor.label: §15, Lemma 15.4
milnor.statement: The index (or the nullity) of $E_{**}$ is equal to the index (or the nullity) of $E_{**}$ restricted to the space $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ of broken Jacobi fields; in particular the index $\lambda$ is always finite. Milnor adds only that "the proof is straightforward".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$, $\tau$ and $B$ be as in V9.18. The index (V9.13) of $E_{**}$ on the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ equals its index on the broken Jacobi fields; the null space of $E_{**}$ on the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ is the null space of its restriction to the broken Jacobi fields, and the latter has dimension $\nu(\tau)$, the multiplicity of $0$ and $\tau$ (V9.4), because a broken Jacobi field without jumps agrees on $[0, \tau]$ with a single field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$. In particular the index is at most the dimension of the broken Jacobi fields, hence finite, for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$.

diff: The "straightforward" proof is the abstract Lemma 15.B (V9.14 (4)) applied to Lemma 15.3.
Stated along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ (Milnor states $\tau = 1$ and applies it to $\gamma_\tau$ on p. 86), for subdivisions fine in the sense of V9.16; the theorem needs only one fine subdivision.
The nullity on the broken Jacobi fields is identified with $\nu(\tau)$ directly; Milnor gets this on p. 86 from Theorem 14.1 for $\gamma_\tau$.

items.title: $\lambda(\tau)$, and Assertions (1) and (2)

milnor.label: §15, p. 85
milnor.statement: For $0 < \tau \le 1$, let $\gamma_\tau = \gamma|[0, \tau]$, a geodesic from $\gamma(0)$ to $\gamma(\tau)$, and let $\lambda(\tau)$ be the index of the associated Hessian $(E_0^\tau)_{**}$; so $\lambda(1)$ is the index we are trying to compute. Assertion (1): $\lambda(\tau)$ is a monotone function of $\tau$, because a field along $\gamma_\tau$ vanishing at both ends extends by zero to one along $\gamma_{\tau'}$. Assertion (2): $\lambda(\tau) = 0$ for small $\tau$, because $\gamma_\tau$ is then a minimal geodesic (Lemma 13.6).

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and $\tau \in \mathbb R$, $\lambda(\tau)$ is the index of $E_{**}$ (of $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$) restricted to the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$, i.e. vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$ (V9.17); $\lambda(1)$ is the index of $E_{**}$ on all of $T\Omega_\gamma$. (1) $\lambda(\tau) \le \lambda(\tau')$ for $\tau \le \tau'$. (2) $\lambda(\tau) = 0$ for $0 < \tau \le h_0$ (V9.16).

diff: $\lambda(\tau)$ is the index of a restriction of $E_{**}$, not of a Hessian along $\gamma_\tau$ on its own interval: the fields along $\gamma_\tau$ vanishing at $0$ and $\tau$, extended by zero as in Milnor's proof of (1), with $\frac12E_{**}$ given on them by the integral over $[0, \tau]$ (V8.15). With this definition (1) is immediate, and no rescaling of $\gamma_\tau$ to $[0, 1]$ (the exposition's Lemma 13.B) is needed.

(2) comes from the Poincaré estimate (V9.16 (i)): $E_{**}$ is positive definite on the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ when $\tau \le h_0$. Milnor's route needs short geodesics to be minimal (Theorem 10.4) and Lemma 13.6.

items.title: The forms $H_\tau$ and their continuity (Lemma 15.C)

milnor.label: §15, p. 86
milnor.statement: With the subdivision chosen so that $t_i < \tau < t_{i+1}$, $\lambda(\tau)$ is the index of a quadratic form $H_\tau$ on the broken Jacobi fields along $\gamma_\tau$ for $0 < t_1 < \dots < t_i < \tau$, a space isomorphic to $\Sigma = TM_{\gamma(t_1)} \oplus \dots \oplus TM_{\gamma(t_i)}$, which is independent of $\tau$. "Evidently" $H_\tau$ varies continuously with $\tau$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and $B$ a finite set; $\tau$ is *valid* for $B$ if $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ is fine for $[0, \tau]$. For valid $\tau$, $H_\tau$ is the symmetric bilinear form on $\Sigma = \bigoplus_{b \in B}T_{\gamma(b)}N$ given by $E_{**}$ on the broken Jacobi fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ with these values at the points of $B$ (V9.17). For valid $\tau$, the index of $H_\tau$ is $\lambda(\tau)$ and its nullity is $\nu(\tau)$. For $x, y \in \Sigma$, $\tau \mapsto H_\tau(x, y)$ is continuous on the set of valid $\tau$; and if $B$ is fine for $[0, \tau]$ with its last point $m$ within $h_0/2$ of $\tau$, every $\tau' \in (m, \tau + h_0/2)$ with $\tau' \le 1$ is valid.

diff: The continuity needs that the subdivision stays fine for $\tau'$ near $\tau$, that the last division point and $\tau$ are not conjugate (so that the Jacobi field with prescribed values there exists), the linear dependence of Jacobi fields on their initial values, and the continuity of the solution of an injective linear system; all are supplied.

The formal proof reads $H_\tau$ through its jump terms (V9.18 (ii)), where only the covariant derivative at the last division point depends on $\tau$; this replaces Cramer's rule in the exposition's proof.

items.title: Assertion (3): $\lambda$ is continuous from the left

milnor.label: §15, Assertion (3)
milnor.statement: $\lambda(\tau - \varepsilon) = \lambda(\tau)$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$. Proof (p. 86): $H_\tau$ is negative definite on a subspace of $\Sigma$ of dimension $\lambda(\tau)$, hence so is $H_{\tau'}$ for $\tau'$ near $\tau$, giving $\lambda(\tau') \ge \lambda(\tau)$, and Assertion (1) gives the reverse inequality for $\tau' < \tau$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and $0 < \tau \le 1$, $\lambda(\tau') = \lambda(\tau)$ for all $\tau' < \tau$ close enough to $\tau$, $\lambda$ as in V9.20.

items.title: Theorem 15.1: the Morse index theorem

milnor.label: §15, Theorem 15.1
milnor.statement: (Morse.) The index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is equal to the number of points $\gamma(t)$, with $0 < t < 1$, such that $\gamma(t)$ is conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$, each such conjugate point being counted with its multiplicity. The index $\lambda$ is always finite. On p. 87 the theorem "clearly follows" from Assertions (2), (3) and (4).

chips: the identity along any smooth curve
finiteness of the set proved first

(ii) holds along any smooth curve in $N$; when $\gamma$ is not a geodesic, $E_{**}$ is the form of V8.14, not the Hessian of the energy.

"Clearly follows" hides a step: the finiteness of the set of conjugate parameters has to be proved first, from Assertions (1) and (4) and the finiteness of $\lambda(1)$, before the jumps can be added up; then $\lambda(\tau) - \sum_{t < \tau}\nu(t)$ is locally constant on $(0, 1]$, and it vanishes for small $\tau$.

items.title: Corollary 15.2: finitely many conjugate points

milnor.label: §15, Corollary 15.2
milnor.statement: A geodesic segment $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ can contain only finitely many points which are conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$; an "immediate consequence" of Theorem 15.1.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, the set of parameters conjugate to $0$ along $\gamma$ is finite.
