items.title: Milnor's metric on $\Omega$

milnor.label: §16, p. 88
milnor.statement: The path space $\Omega$ can be topologized by the distance $d(\omega, \omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t)) + \big[\int_0^1(\frac{ds}{dt} - \frac{ds'}{dt})^2dt\big]^{1/2}$, where $s(t)$ and $s'(t)$ are the arc lengths of $\omega$ and $\omega'$ from $0$ to $t$, and $\rho$ is the distance of §10.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric and its distance $\rho$ (V7.18): for $\omega, \eta \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, with speeds $\dot s_\omega = \|\omega'\|$ and $\dot s_\eta = \|\eta'\|$, $$d(\omega, \eta) = \sup_{0 \le t \le 1}\rho(\omega(t), \eta(t)) + \Big(\int_0^1(\dot s_\omega - \dot s_\eta)^2\,dt\Big)^{1/2}.$$ This is an extended pseudometric on $\Omega$ (values in $[0, \infty]$, symmetric, with the triangle inequality), and two paths that agree on $[0, 1]$ are at distance $0$. From now on $\Omega$ and its subsets carry the topology of $d$.

chips: a pseudometric on maps $\mathbb R \to V$
diff: Paths are maps on $\mathbb R$ whose values off $[0, 1]$ play no role, and $d$ sees only $[0, 1]$, so it is a pseudometric; on paths $[0, 1] \to N$ it is Milnor's metric. Three conventions follow throughout the chapter: identities between paths hold on $[0, 1]$, homeomorphisms become homotopy equivalences up to paths at distance $0$, and geodesics are counted by their values on $[0, 1]$.
The triangle inequality for the second term is Minkowski's inequality in $L^2$; $\frac{ds}{dt}$ exists except at finitely many points.

items.title: The energy is continuous for $d$ (Lemmas 16.A and 16.B)

milnor.label: §16, p. 88
milnor.statement: The last term of $d$ is added so that the energy $E_a^b(\omega) = \int_a^b(\frac{ds}{dt})^2dt$ is a continuous function on $\Omega$. Hence $\Omega^c = E^{-1}([0, c])$ is closed and $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c = E^{-1}([0, c))$ is open.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) for $\omega, \eta \in \Omega$ and $0 \le a \le b \le 1$, $|\sqrt{E_a^b(\omega)} - \sqrt{E_a^b(\eta)}| \le (\int_0^1(\dot s_\omega - \dot s_\eta)^2dt)^{1/2}$; hence $\sqrt{E_a^b}$ is $1$-Lipschitz for $d$, $E_a^b$ is continuous on $\Omega$, $\Omega^c$ is closed and $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$ is open. (ii) (Lemma 16.B) If $\omega_n \to \omega$ in $\Omega$, then for every $\epsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $E_a^b(\omega_n) < \epsilon$ for all $n$ and all $0 \le a \le b \le 1$ with $b - a < \delta$.

chips: uniformly small energy on short intervals
diff: $\sqrt{E_a^b} = \|\dot s\|_{L^2[a, b]}$, and Minkowski's inequality on $[a, b]$ makes it $1$-Lipschitz for $d$; with the uniform term alone the energy is not continuous.
(ii) is not in the book; it is what the continuity of Milnor's deformation $r_u$ needs (V10.7). The Lipschitz bound is also what makes Milnor's map $h$ of §17 discontinuous (V10.19′).

items.title: The ball $S$, subdivisions, and Milnor’s choices

milnor.label: §16, pp. 88–89
milnor.statement: $\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of paths $\omega$ with each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ a geodesic, and $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c = (\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c) \cap \Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ (p. 88). On p. 89: every $\omega \in \Omega^c$ lies in the ball $S$ of radius $\sqrt c$ about $p$, by $L^2 \le E \le c$; $S$ is compact since $M$ is complete; by 10.8 there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that two points of $S$ at distance less than $\varepsilon$ are joined by a unique geodesic of length less than $\varepsilon$, depending differentiably on them; and the subdivision is chosen with each $t_i - t_{i-1} < \varepsilon^2/c$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $c > 0$ and $S = \{x \in N : \rho(p, x) \le \sqrt c\}$. (i) Every $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) \le c$ maps $[0, 1]$ into $S$. (ii) $S$ is compact if $N$ is closed in $V$, or connected and complete. (iii) For every compact $K \subseteq N$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that points of $K$ at distance $< \delta$ are joined as in Corollary 10.8 at the scale $\delta$, and $\delta$ is at most a normal radius at every point of $K$. (iv) *Milnor's data* (V10.3): $p, q \in N$, $c > 0$ with $S = \{x \in N : \rho(p, x) \le \sqrt c\}$ compact, a scale $\delta$ as in Corollary 10.8 for $K = S$ that is also at most a normal radius on $S$ (Milnor's $\varepsilon$), and a subdivision $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_{m+1} = 1$ with $c\,(t_{i+1} - t_i) < \delta^2$. If $p, q \in N$ and $S$ is compact, every subdivision of small enough mesh, and some subdivision into equal parts, is part of such data. (v) For Milnor's data, $B = \operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ is the set of $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) < c$ that are geodesics on each $(t_i, t_{i+1})$, and $B^a = \{\omega \in B : E(\omega) \le a\}$.

diff: Completeness enters only as the compactness of $S$, which is the Hopf–Rinow theorem (Corollary 10.10, V7.27) and holds in particular when $N$ is closed in $V$.
$\delta$ is also asked to be at most a normal radius on $S$, which (iii) provides at no cost and which keeps the ends of each segment non-conjugate (V10.10).

items.title: Lemma 16.1: the manifold of broken geodesics

milnor.label: §16, Lemma 16.1
milnor.statement: Let $M$ be complete and $c > 0$ with $\Omega^c$ non-vacuous. Then for all sufficiently fine subdivisions $(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ of $[0, 1]$, $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ can be given the structure of a smooth finite dimensional manifold "in a natural way". Proof (p. 89): for a broken geodesic $(L_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega)^2 = (t_i - t_{i-1})E_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega < \varepsilon^2$, so each segment is determined by its end points, and $\omega$ by $(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_{k-1})) \in M \times \dots \times M$; this is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of the product, whose differentiable structure is taken over.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: fix Milnor's data. For $y = (y_1, \dots, y_m) \in V^m$ put $x_0 = p$, $x_j = y_j$, $x_{m+1} = q$, and $E'(y) = \sum_{i=0}^m\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})^2/(t_{i+1} - t_i)$; let $U$ be the set of $y \in N^m$ with every $\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})$ finite and $E'(y) < c$. (i) $U = N^m \cap O$ for an open $O \subseteq V^m$, and every such set is a slice submanifold of $V^m$, with tangent space $T_{y_1}N \times \dots \times T_{y_m}N$. (ii) For $y \in U$, the broken geodesic $\omega_y$, on $[t_i, t_{i+1}]$ the short geodesic from $x_i$ to $x_{i+1}$ run at constant speed, lies in $B$, has break points $y$, and $E(\omega_y) = E'(y)$. (iii) Every $\omega \in B$ has its break points $y$ in $U$, and $\omega_y = \omega$ on $[0, 1]$. So $y \mapsto \omega_y$ and $\omega \mapsto (\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_m))$ are inverse bijections between $U$ and $B$, paths compared on $[0, 1]$.

diff: Milnor's hypothesis that $\Omega^c$ is non-vacuous is not needed (an empty manifold is a manifold).
The manifold is the open subset $U$ of $N^m$, rather than a structure transported to $B$; the topologies are compared in V10.5.

Hidden: that the image is exactly the open set $U$ (the vertices of a point of $U$ lie in $S$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, consecutive ones at distance $< \delta$); that a geodesic segment is the radial geodesic of its initial vector (V9.9) and, that vector being shorter than $\delta$, the short geodesic; and that a broken geodesic is smooth up to the ends of its segments.

items.title: Broken geodesics and their break points: a homeomorphism up to distance $0$

milnor.label: §16, p. 89
milnor.statement: "Evidently" the correspondence $\omega \mapsto (\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_{k-1}))$ defines a homeomorphism between $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ and an open subset of $M \times \dots \times M$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data, $y \mapsto \omega_y$ is continuous from $U$ (topology of $V^m$) to $(\Omega, d)$, and $\omega \mapsto (\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_m))$ is continuous from $\Omega$ to $V^m$. For every $a$ they restrict to continuous maps between $B^a$ and $\{y \in U : E'(y) \le a\}$, inverse to each other up to paths at distance $0$; so the two sets are homotopy equivalent (for $a \ge c$, $B$ and $U$).

diff: A homotopy equivalence, indeed a homeomorphism up to the identification of paths at distance $0$, replaces the homeomorphism, since paths are maps on $\mathbb R$.

"Evidently" hides the continuity of $y \mapsto \omega_y$ for $d$: the uniform term needs the continuity of short geodesics in their end points (Corollary 10.8 and the continuity of $\exp$, V7.23), and the $L^2$ term that of the speeds $\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})/(t_{i+1} - t_i)$.

items.title: Theorem 16.2: $E'$ is smooth and $B^a$ is compact

milnor.label: §16, Theorem 16.2, pp. 90–91
milnor.statement: The function $E' : B \to \mathbb R$, the restriction of $E$, is smooth; for each $a < c$ the set $B^a = (E')^{-1}[0, a]$ is compact. On p. 90 $E'$ depends smoothly on the break points by the explicit formula $E'(\omega) = \sum_i\rho(\omega(t_{i-1}), \omega(t_i))^2/(t_i - t_{i-1})$; on p. 91 $B^a$ is homeomorphic to a set of $(k - 1)$-tuples in $S \times \dots \times S$ that is closed in a compact set.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data: (i) every $y_0 \in U$ has an open neighbourhood $O$ in $V^m$ with a function smooth on $O$ that equals $E'$ on $U \cap O$; hence $E'$ is continuous on $U$, and smooth on the manifold $N^m \cap O$ for every open $O \subseteq V^m$ with $N^m \cap O \subseteq U$. (ii) For $a < c$, $\{y \in U : E'(y) \le a\}$ is compact.

diff: $\rho$ is not smooth on the diagonal; $E'$ is smooth because $\rho(x, x')^2 = \|v(x, x')\|^2$ with $v$ the smooth initial vector of Corollary 10.8. The set of tuples is closed only because the distances are finite.

As reproduced in the scan, the condition defining the tuples reads $\rho(p_{i-1}, p_i)^c/(t_i - t_{i-1}) \le a$, with exponent $c$ and no summation sign; the formal condition is $E'(p_1, \dots, p_{k-1}) \le a$, the sum with exponent $2$.
Compactness is stated for the set of break points, which is homotopy equivalent to $B^a$ by V10.5.

items.title: Milnor’s deformation $r_u$ (Lemma 16.C)

milnor.label: §16, p. 91
milnor.statement: The retraction $r : \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c \to B$ sends $\omega$ to the broken geodesic which on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is the geodesic of length less than $\varepsilon$ from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(t_i)$; "clearly" $E(r(\omega)) \le E(\omega) < c$. For $t_{i-1} \le u \le t_i$, $r_u(\omega)$ is $r(\omega)$ on $[0, t_{i-1}]$, the minimal geodesic from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(u)$ on $[t_{i-1}, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; $r_0$ is the identity, $r_1 = r$, and "it is easily verified" that $r_u(\omega)$ is continuous as a function of both variables.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data, $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) < c$ and $t_i \le u \le t_{i+1}$, $r_u(\omega)$ is the broken geodesic of the break points of $\omega$ on $[0, t_i]$, the short geodesic from $\omega(t_i)$ to $\omega(u)$ at constant speed on $[t_i, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; the formulas of neighbouring segments agree at $u = t_{i+1}$. On $[0, 1]$: $r_u(\omega) \in \Omega$, $E(r_u(\omega)) \le E(\omega)$, $r_0(\omega) = \omega$, $r_1(\omega) = \omega_y$ for the break points $y$ of $\omega$, and $r_u(\omega) = \omega$ for $\omega \in B$. Completed by $\omega$ off $[0, 1]$, and by $\omega$ itself when $u \notin [0, 1]$ or $E(\omega) \ge c$, $(u, \omega) \mapsto r_u(\omega)$ is a map $\mathbb R \times \Omega \to \Omega$, continuous on $[0, 1] \times \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$.

diff: Milnor's minimal geodesic is the short geodesic of Corollary 10.8, which is minimal; it exists since $\rho(\omega(t_i), \omega(u))^2 \le (u - t_i)E(\omega) < \delta^2$.

Hidden: the formulas must agree where neighbouring intervals meet; $r_u$ fixes $B$ because a sub-arc of a short geodesic is the short geodesic between its ends; and $E(r_u(\omega)) \le E(\omega)$ holds segment by segment, by $\rho^2 \le (b - a)E_a^b$.

The continuity needs, for the uniform term, the continuity of short geodesics in their end points and the equicontinuity of the paths of energy $< c$, and, for the $L^2$ term near $u = t_i$, the bound $\rho(\omega(t_i), \omega(u))^2/(u - t_i) \le E_{t_i}^u(\omega)$ with Lemma 16.B (V10.2).

items.title: Theorem 16.2: $B^a$ is a deformation retract of $\Omega^a$

milnor.label: §16, Theorem 16.2, pp. 90–91
milnor.statement: For each $a < c$, $B^a$ is a deformation retract of $\Omega^a$; a footnote adds that $B$ itself is similarly a deformation retract of $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$. On p. 91: since $E(r_u(\omega)) \le E(\omega)$, "it is clear" that each $B^a$ is a deformation retract of $\Omega^a$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data and $a < c$, the deformation of V10.7 is continuous on $[0, 1] \times \Omega^a$, does not increase the energy (so each $r_u$ maps $\Omega^a$ into itself), starts at the identity, ends in $B$, and fixes every point of $B$ for $0 \le u \le 1$. So $B^a$ is a strong deformation retract of $\Omega^a$ and the inclusion $B^a \subseteq \Omega^a$ is a homotopy equivalence; likewise $B$ is a strong deformation retract of $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$.

diff: The strong deformation retraction is stated through the listed properties of $(u, \omega) \mapsto r_u(\omega)$, which hold exactly, not only on $[0, 1]$, thanks to the completion of V10.7; the hidden hypotheses are those of V10.7.

items.title: Theorem 16.2: the critical points of $E'$

milnor.label: §16, Theorem 16.2, pp. 90–91
milnor.statement: The critical points of $E'$ are precisely the critical points of $E$ in $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$, namely the unbroken geodesics from $p$ to $q$ of length less than $\sqrt c$. On p. 91: every geodesic is a broken geodesic, so every critical point of $E$ in $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$ lies in $B$, and with the first variation formula (12.2) "it is clear" that the critical points of $E'$ are the unbroken geodesics.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: fix Milnor's data. (i) Every tangent vector of a slice submanifold is the velocity of a smooth curve in it; for a smooth curve $y(u)$ in $U$, $(u, t) \mapsto \omega_{y(u)}(t)$ is a variation through broken geodesics, smooth on each strip, whose variation field takes the value $y'(0)_j$ at $t_j$. (ii) At $\gamma = \omega_y$ the first variation in the direction $X$ is $-\sum_j\langle X(t_j), \Delta_{t_j}\gamma'\rangle$. (iii) Let $O \subseteq V^m$ be open with $N^m \cap O \subseteq U$ and $F$ smooth on $V^m$ with $F = E'$ on $N^m \cap O$. Then $dF_y(w) = -2\sum_j\langle w_j, \Delta_{t_j}\omega_y'\rangle$ for tangent $w$, and $y$ is a critical point of $E' = F|(N^m \cap O)$ iff $\omega_y$ is an unbroken geodesic. (iv) Every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega$ with $E(\gamma) < c$ has its break points $y$ in $U$, $\omega_y = \gamma$ on $[0, 1]$, and $E'(y) = E(\gamma)$.

diff: The critical points of $E$ are the unbroken geodesics by Corollary 12.3; $E'$ is read through a smooth ambient extension $F$, as functions on submanifolds are in Part I, and the statement holds for every such $F$ and $O$.

Hidden: every tangent vector of $B$ at $\gamma$ must be the variation field of a variation through broken geodesics, smooth on the strips, which needs the smooth dependence of a geodesic segment on its end points over the whole segment (V9.9 (iii)); the test is one break point at a time, with the tangent vector $\Delta_{t_j}\gamma'$; and a broken geodesic without velocity jumps is unbroken (Corollary 12.3).

items.title: Lemma 15.4 for the subdivision of §16

milnor.label: §16, pp. 91–92
milnor.statement: On pp. 91–92 the tangent space $TB_\gamma$ is identified with the space $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ of broken Jacobi fields of §15, and the equality of the indices and nullities "is an immediate consequence of Lemma 15.4".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: fix Milnor's data and $y \in U$ with $\gamma = \omega_y$ an unbroken geodesic. (i) A Jacobi field along $\gamma$, restricted to a segment and reparametrized affinely, is a Jacobi field along the reparametrized segment. (ii) For every $i$, $t_i$ and $t_{i+1}$ are not conjugate along $\gamma$. (iii) The broken Jacobi fields along $\gamma$ with break points $t_1, \dots, t_m$ take arbitrary tangent values at the $t_j$ and are determined by them. (iv) For every $\omega \in \Omega$, $E'(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_m)) \le E(\omega)$; hence $E_{**}(W, W) \ge 0$ for $W \in T\Omega_\gamma$ vanishing at the $t_j$, and $> 0$ if moreover $W \ne 0$ vanishes off $[0, 1]$. (v) The fields of $T\Omega_\gamma$ vanishing off $[0, 1]$ are the direct sum of the broken Jacobi fields and of those vanishing at the $t_j$; the index of $E_{**}$ is that of its restriction to the broken Jacobi fields, and so is the nullity.

diff: Lemma 15.4 (V9.19) is proved for a subdivision chosen in §15, which the subdivision of §16 need not be; its proof needs (a) Jacobi fields on each segment with arbitrary, unique end values and (b) $E_{**}$ positive definite on the fields vanishing at the break points. For §16, (a) holds because each segment is the radial geodesic of a vector shorter than a normal radius (V9.11), and (b) because the broken geodesic minimizes the energy among the paths through its break points.
(iv)–(v) are therefore Lemma 15.4 proved anew for this subdivision; the "immediate consequence" is not immediate.

items.title: Theorem 16.2: the index and nullity of $E'$

milnor.label: §16, Theorem 16.2, pp. 90 and 92
milnor.statement: The index (or the nullity) of the Hessian $E'_{**}$ at each critical point $\gamma$ is equal to the index (or the nullity) of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma$. On p. 92: for a variation $\bar\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to B$ through broken geodesics the variation field is "clearly a broken Jacobi field" (compare 14.3); then Lemma 15.4.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $O$, $F$ be as in V10.9 (iii) and $y \in N^m \cap O$ with $\gamma = \omega_y$ an unbroken geodesic; let $x$ be the parametrization of a slice chart of $N^m \cap O$ at $y$, $z_0$ the chart point of $y$, and $\Lambda z$ the broken Jacobi field with values $dx_{z_0}(z)$ at the break points, a linear isomorphism onto the broken Jacobi fields. (i) For $G$ of class $C^2$ near $z_0$, the second derivative at $0$ of $u \mapsto G(z_0 + uz)$ is $G_{**}(z, z)$. (ii) $(F \circ x)_{**}(z, z') = E_{**}(\Lambda z, \Lambda z')$. (iii) **Theorem 16.2:** the index of $E'$ at $y$ equals the index of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma$ (V9.13), and the nullity of $E'$ at $y$ equals the nullity of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma$ (V9.6).

diff: The variation field of a variation through broken geodesics is, on each segment, a Jacobi field along the segment reparametrized to $[0, 1]$ (Lemma 14.3 with V10.10 (i)); that it is the broken Jacobi field with the same values at the break points needs their uniqueness (V10.10 (iii)).
The Hessians are compared first as quadratic forms, through Remark 13.5 along the variation $F(x(z_0 + uz)) = E(\omega_{x(z_0 + uz)})$, then polarized.

items.title: Theorem 16.3 in the finite-dimensional model

milnor.label: §16, Theorem 16.3, and §3.5
milnor.statement: Theorem 16.3 is proved in one line: "This follows from 16.2 together with §3.5." Theorem 3.5 is the description of a manifold with compact sublevel sets and no degenerate critical points as a CW-complex with one cell for each critical point.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $K \subseteq S'$ are subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space, $K$ compact, and $f$ agrees on $S'$ near each point of $K$ with a function smooth on an open set, then $f$ agrees on $K$ with a function smooth everywhere. (ii) (Theorem 3.5 for a compact sublevel set) for $f = F|N$ with $F$ smooth on $V$ and a level $a_0$ that is not a critical value, with $N^{a_0} = f^{-1}(-\infty, a_0]$ compact and every critical point in it non-degenerate, those critical points are finitely many and $N^{a_0}$ has the homotopy type of an iterated adjunction space with one cell of dimension the index for each. (iii) For Milnor's data and $a < c$, if $E'(y) \ne a$ for every $y \in U$ with $\omega_y$ a geodesic, and $E_{**}$ has nullity $0$ at every such $\omega_y$ with $E'(y) \le a$, then these $y$ are finitely many, and $\{y \in U : E'(y) \le a\}$ has the homotopy type of an iterated adjunction space with one cell of dimension the index of $E_{**}$ at $\omega_y$ for each, attached in order of non-decreasing energy.

chips: $a$ not the energy of a geodesic
diff: Theorem 3.5 concerns a function with compact sublevel sets and no degenerate critical point at all, while $B$ is not compact and only the critical points in $B^a$ are assumed non-degenerate. The formal proof extends $E'$ by (i) from the compact set $\{E' \le (a + c)/2\}$ to a smooth function on $V^m$ and applies (ii) there.
$a$ must not be a critical value of $E'$: Milnor's hypothesis does not exclude a geodesic of energy exactly $a$, and then $B^a$ is a critical sublevel set. The formal statement assumes it.
The CW-complex is an iterated adjunction space whose attaching maps need not be cellular (V2.11).

items.title: Theorem 16.3: the homotopy type of $\Omega^a$

milnor.label: §16, Theorem 16.3
milnor.statement: If $M$ is complete and $p, q \in M$ are not conjugate along any geodesic of length $\le \sqrt a$, then $\Omega^a$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex, with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each geodesic in $\Omega^a$ along which $E_{**}$ has index $\lambda$. In particular $\Omega^a$ contains only finitely many geodesics.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let Milnor's data be given with $c > a$ (they exist for every $c > 0$ when $N$ is closed in $V$, or connected and complete, V10.3), and suppose that no geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega$ has $E(\gamma) = a$ and that $E_{**}$ has nullity $0$ at every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega$ with $E(\gamma) \le a$. Then the geodesics in $\Omega^a$ are finitely many, and $\Omega^a$, with the metric $d$, has the homotopy type of an iterated adjunction space with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each geodesic in $\Omega^a$ of index $\lambda$, attached in order of non-decreasing energy.

chips: $a$ not the energy of a geodesic
diff: $a$ must not be the energy of a geodesic (as in V10.12); the case of a critical level is not formalized.
Non-conjugacy of $p$ and $q$ along the geodesics is stated as nullity $0$, equivalent by Theorem 14.1 (V9.6); completeness enters only through Milnor's data (the compactness of $S$).
The CW-complex is an iterated adjunction space (V2.11). The proof transports V10.12 along V10.5 and V10.8; every geodesic of $\Omega^a$ is some $\omega_y$ on $[0, 1]$ (V10.9 (iv)).

items.title: The Remark on p. 92: a minimum of $E'$

milnor.label: §16, Remark, p. 92
milnor.statement: As a consequence of Theorem 16.2, an alternative proof of the existence of a minimal geodesic joining two points $p, q$ of a complete manifold: if $\Omega^a(p, q)$ is non-vacuous, then $B^a$ is compact and non-vacuous, so the continuous function $E' : B^a \to \mathbb R$ takes on its minimum at some point $\gamma \in B^a$, and this $\gamma$ "will be the required minimal geodesic".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data, every $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) < c$ has its break points $y$ in $U$, with $E'(y) \le E(\omega)$; and if some $\omega_0 \in \Omega$ has $E(\omega_0) < c$, there is $y \in U$ such that $\omega_y$ is an unbroken geodesic and $E(\omega_y) \le E(\omega)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$.

chips: minimal for the energy, not length
diff: Minimality is proved for the energy on all of $\Omega$; that $\omega_y$ is then a minimal geodesic in the sense of V7.24 (shortest) is not stated.

Hidden: that $\gamma$ minimizes $E$ on all of $\Omega$ needs $E(\omega) \ge E'(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_m))$ for every $\omega$ (Schwarz's inequality), and that it is a geodesic, that a minimum is a critical point (V10.9).

items.title: The full path space $\Omega^*$ and the inclusion $i$

milnor.label: §17, p. 93
milnor.statement: $\Omega^*$ is the space of all continuous paths $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ from $p$ to $q$, with the compact-open topology, which can also be described as that induced by the metric $d^*(\omega, \omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t))$. Since $d \ge d^*$, the natural map $i : \Omega \to \Omega^*$ is continuous.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: $\Omega^*(N; p, q)$ is the set of continuous maps $\omega : [0, 1] \to V$ with values in $N$, $\omega(0) = p$ and $\omega(1) = q$, as a subspace of the continuous maps $[0, 1] \to V$ with the uniform distance $d^*(\omega, \eta) = \max_t\|\omega(t) - \eta(t)\|$, whose topology is the compact-open topology. The map $i : \Omega \to \Omega^*$ restricts a path to $[0, 1]$; $d^*(i\omega, i\eta) \le d(\omega, \eta)$, so $i$ is continuous.

diff: $d^*$ is measured with the norm of $V$ rather than with $\rho$; on $N$ the two distances define the same topology (V7.21), so both give the compact-open topology, and $\|x - y\| \le \rho(x, y)$ gives the inequality.

items.title: Convergence in $\Omega$ controls the velocities

milnor.label: §17, cf. p. 94
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. It is what the continuity, for $d$, of the maps in the proof of Theorem 17.1 needs, since $d$ involves only the speeds $\frac{ds}{dt}$, not the velocities.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $\omega_j \to \omega$ in $(\Omega, d)$, along any filter, then $\int_0^1\|\omega_j' - \omega'\|^2dt \to 0$. (ii) Conversely, if $\omega_j(s) \to \omega(s)$ for every $s \in [0, 1]$ and $\int_0^1\|\omega_j' - \omega'\|^2dt \to 0$, then $\omega_j \to \omega$ in $\Omega$. (iii) If $\Phi$ is of class $C^1$ on an open set containing $F([a, b])$, $F_j \to F$ uniformly on $[a, b]$, and the velocities $F_j'$ are bounded in $L^2$ and converge to $F'$ in $L^2$, then $(\Phi \circ F_j)' \to (\Phi \circ F)'$ in $L^2$.

diff: These are the analytic facts that make maps given pointwise by smooth formulas, such as the deformation of V10.18, continuous for $d$. (i) holds although $d$ involves only the speeds: the energies converge (V10.2), and the velocities converge weakly in $L^2$ by integration by parts on the smooth pieces.

items.title: Good balls and join systems (Lemma 17.B)

milnor.label: §17, p. 93
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 17.1, Milnor takes a continuous $f : M \to [0, \infty)$ with each $f^{-1}([0, r])$ compact, and lets $\varepsilon_1(r) \le \infty$ be the largest number such that any two points of $f^{-1}([0, r])$ at distance less than $\varepsilon_1(r)$ are joined by a unique minimal geodesic which varies differentiably with the end points.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $y, z \in V$ the minimal join vector $v(y, z)$ is the unique $v \in T_yN$ with $\exp_y(v) = z$, $\rho(y, z) = \|v\|$ and Corollary 10.8 holding at some scale $\delta > \|v\|$ ($0$ if there is none), and $\sigma_{yz}(s) = \exp_y(s\,v(y, z))$. A *good ball* (V7.10′) is an open $O$ such that, for one $\delta > 0$, any two points of $N \cap O$ are at distance $< \delta$ and joined as in Corollary 10.8 at the scale $\delta$, and $\sigma_{yz}([0, 1]) \subseteq N \cap O$. (i) Small balls of $V$ about points of $N$ are good. (ii) Compact subsets of $N$ have a Lebesgue number for good balls. (iii) In a good ball $\sigma_{yz}$ is the unique minimal geodesic from $y$ to $z$, its sub-arcs are minimal, and $(y, z, s) \mapsto \sigma_{yz}(s)$ is locally the restriction of a smooth map. (iv) Local smooth extensions glue, by a partition of unity, into a *join system*: open good sets, convex for the joins, with one smooth map of $(y, z, s)$ on each and a Lebesgue number for every compact subset of $N$.

chips: one smooth join on each whole ball
diff: The modified proof of Theorem 17.1 needs regions that are convex for the short geodesics (J. H. C. Whitehead's convex balls, as in Milnor's remark after Lemma 10.3, V7.10′), one smooth map of $(y, z, s)$ on each whole region, and a uniform scale; Milnor's $\varepsilon_1$ provides none of these.

Good balls are balls of $V$ intersected with $N$, not metric balls of $\rho$; their convexity is proved with the ambient distance, and the smoothness in $(y, z, s)$ uses the smoothness of $\exp$ on its whole domain (V11.1).

items.title: Dyadic broken geodesics as homotopy inverses (Lemma 17.C)

milnor.label: §17, p. 94
milnor.statement: For $\omega \in \Omega^*$, $h(\omega)$ is the broken geodesic which agrees with $\omega$ at $t = 0, A(\omega), 2A(\omega), \dots, kA(\omega)$ and $1$; "an argument similar to that in §16" shows that $h \circ i$ and $i \circ h$ are homotopic to the identity maps of $\Omega$ and $\Omega^*$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: fix a join system (V10.17). For $k \ge 0$ let $Y_k \subseteq \Omega^*$ be the set of paths each of whose dyadic pieces $\omega([j2^{-k}, (j + 1)2^{-k}])$ lies in a good set, and $X_k = i^{-1}(Y_k) \subseteq \Omega$. (i) The $Y_k$ are open, increasing, and cover $\Omega^*$. (ii) For $\omega \in Y_k$ let $b(\omega)$ be the broken geodesic with vertices $\omega(j2^{-k})$, joined by the joins, and $H(\omega, u)(s)$ the point at time $u$ of the join from $\omega(s)$ to $b(\omega)(s)$. Then $H$ is continuous from $Y_k \times [0, 1]$ to $Y_k$ for $d^*$ and from $X_k \times [0, 1]$ to $X_k$ for $d$, and $b$ is continuous from $(Y_k, d^*)$ to $(X_k, d)$. (iii) Hence $i : X_k \to Y_k$ is a homotopy equivalence with homotopy inverse $b$.

chips: points move along joins, not breaks
diff: The dyadic sets $Y_k$ and $X_k$, on each of which the subdivision is fixed, are not in the book; on them the broken geodesic $b$ is continuous for $d$, unlike Milnor's $h$, whose subdivision moves with $\omega$ (V10.19′).

The deformation moves every point $\omega(s)$ along the join to $b(\omega)(s)$, instead of moving a break point along the path as Milnor's $r_u$ does; it stays where the joins are defined by convexity (V10.17), and its continuity for $d$ needs V10.16. $b \circ i \simeq \mathrm{id}$ holds up to paths at distance $0$.

items.title: Theorem 17.1: $\Omega$ and $\Omega^*$ are homotopy equivalent

milnor.label: §17, Theorem 17.1
milnor.statement: Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold, not necessarily complete, and $p, q \in M$. The natural map $i : \Omega \to \Omega^*$ is a homotopy equivalence between $\Omega$, with the metric $d$, and the space $\Omega^*$ of continuous paths. The proof (pp. 93–94) builds a continuous $A : \Omega^* \to (0, 1]$ and the broken geodesic $h(\omega)$ through $\omega(0), \omega(A), \dots, \omega(kA), \omega(1)$, asserts "Clearly $h$ is continuous", and shows $h \circ i \simeq \mathrm{id}$, $i \circ h \simeq \mathrm{id}$ by "an argument similar to that in §16".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $Y$ is paracompact and Hausdorff, $B_0 \subseteq B_1 \subseteq \cdots$ are subsets of $Y$ such that every point lies in the interior of some $B_n$, and $g : X \to Y$ is continuous, then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of the sets $g^{-1}(B_n)$. (ii) For every join system, $i : \Omega(N; p, q) \to \Omega^*(N; p, q)$ is a homotopy equivalence. (iii) **Theorem 17.1:** for every slice submanifold $N$ of $V$, complete or not, and all $p, q$, the inclusion $i : \Omega \to \Omega^*$, with Milnor's metric $d$ on $\Omega$ and the compact-open topology on $\Omega^*$, is a homotopy equivalence.

chips: the theorem is true; the proof is not
proved by Theorem A on telescopes
diff: The statement is Milnor's, and it holds without completeness, as in the book. **One step of the printed proof does not hold as we read it**: "Clearly $h$ is continuous" fails for the metric $d$ (V10.19′), so what is verified is the theorem itself, by the exposition's modified proof.

The modified proof: the open sets $Y_k$ exhaust the metric, hence paracompact, space $\Omega^*$, which is therefore the homotopy direct limit of the $Y_k$ (Example 1 of the Appendix), and $\Omega$ is that of the $X_k = i^{-1}(Y_k)$ by (i); $i$ carries each $X_k$ into $Y_k$ by a homotopy equivalence (V10.18); Theorem A with no closedness hypothesis (VA.15) concludes.
$\Omega$ is not Hausdorff for $d$, so Example 1 is applied to $\Omega^*$ and pulled back by $i$; Theorem A is needed for open, not closed, pieces.

items.title: Milnor’s map $h$ is not continuous: a step in the proof of Theorem 17.1

milnor.label: §17, proof of Theorem 17.1, p. 94
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 17.1, with $\varepsilon(\omega) = \varepsilon_2(\max_tf(\omega(t)))$ and $F(\omega, \alpha) = (\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\omega) + \max_{|t - t'| \le \alpha}\rho(\omega(t), \omega(t'))$, the zero $\alpha = 2A(\omega)$ of $F(\omega, \cdot)$ defines a continuous $A : \Omega^* \to (0, 1]$. Then $h(\omega) \in \Omega$ is the path which agrees with $\omega$ at $t = 0, A(\omega), 2A(\omega), \dots, kA(\omega)$, $k$ the largest integer $\le 1/A(\omega)$, and at $t = 1$, and is a geodesic on each intermediate interval. Milnor writes: "Clearly $h$ is continuous."

lean.statement: Take $M = \mathbb R$, $p = q = 0$ (so $\rho(x, y) = |x - y|$), Milnor's $f(x) = |x|$ and the admissible choice $\varepsilon_2 \equiv 1$; $2A(\omega)$ is the unique zero of $F(\omega, \cdot)$ in $[0, 1]$, as Milnor claims, and $h(\omega)$ is the piecewise affine interpolation of $\omega$ at $0, A, \dots, kA, 1$, a map $h : \Omega^* \to \Omega$. Let $\omega_\lambda(t) = \lambda((1 - t)^{1/3} - (1 - t))$ and $\lambda_* = \sqrt3/2$. Then $\omega_\lambda \to \omega_{\lambda_*}$ uniformly as $\lambda \to \lambda_*$, while $E(h(\omega_\lambda)) \to \infty$ as $\lambda \downarrow \lambda_*$ ($E(h(\omega_{\lambda_*})) \le 1$). Since $\sqrt E$ is $1$-Lipschitz for $d$, $d(h(\omega_\lambda), h(\omega_{\lambda_*})) \to \infty$: **$h$ is not continuous at $\omega_{\lambda_*}$**, hence not continuous.

chips: a step of the book that does not hold as we read it
diff: This row records a step that does not hold as we read it, not a difference of formulation: Milnor's "Clearly $h$ is continuous" (p. 94) is false for the metric $d$ of $\Omega$, the topology in which Theorem 17.1 is stated; $h$ is continuous only for $d^*$. The counterexample is machine-checked for an admissible instance of Milnor's own choices: $f(x) = |x|$ and $\varepsilon_2 \equiv 1$, legitimate because on $\mathbb R$ any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending smoothly on them, so $\varepsilon_1 \equiv \infty$. Other constants $\varepsilon_2 \equiv c$ only rescale the family (a remark, not formalized).

The failure is in the $L^2$ term of $d$. When $1/A(\omega)$ crosses an integer, $h(\omega)$ acquires a new last segment of duration $\delta \to 0$ and length $\ell \to 0$, whose energy $\ell^2/\delta$ need not tend to $0$: here $\ell = \lambda(\delta^{1/3} - \delta)$ gives energy at least $\frac{27}{64}\delta^{-1/3}$. Milnor's $A$ is not at fault: $A(\omega_\lambda) = (1 - \lambda c_0)/2$, with $c_0 = 2\sqrt3/9$ the maximum of $(1 - t)^{1/3} - (1 - t)$ on $[0, 1]$, depends continuously on $\lambda$, and $k = 3$ for $\lambda_* \le \lambda \le \frac54\lambda_*$; what moves is the last break point $kA = 3A$, which leaves $1$.

Only this step fails: the theorem is proved by a different route (V10.17–V10.19), with subdivisions kept fixed on open sets and Theorem A of the Appendix. (Also, $A$ takes its values in $(0, \frac12]$, not $(0, 1]$.)

items.title: Relative cell complexes and the tower

milnor.label: §17, p. 95
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 17.3: by 16.2 together with 3.3 and 3.7, each $\Omega^{a_i}$ has the homotopy type of $\Omega^{a_{i-1}}$ with finitely many cells attached; "just as in the proof of 3.5", one constructs CW-complexes $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$ with cells of the required description and homotopy equivalences $\Omega^{a_i} \to K_i$, each extending the previous one, forming a commutative diagram.

lean.statement: (i) A map $\iota : A \to X$ is, *up to homotopy, the inclusion of $A$ with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ attached* if there are a space $K$ obtained from $A$ by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on, with $j : A \to K$ the inclusion, and a homotopy equivalence $e : X \to K$ with $e \circ \iota \simeq j$. (ii) (Lemma 3.7, relative and iterated) such attachments transport along homotopy equivalences, and the notion is invariant under homotopy-commutative squares of homotopy equivalences. (iii) (relative Theorem 3.5) for $f = F|N$ on a slice submanifold, $F$ smooth, and levels $b \le a_0$, neither critical, with $N^{a_0}$ compact and the critical points in it non-degenerate, $N^b \to N^{a_0}$ is, up to homotopy, $N^b$ with one cell of dimension the index for each critical point in $f^{-1}(b, a_0)$, in order of value. (iv) (the tower) if $E : X \to \mathbb R$ is continuous, $a_n \to \infty$, $X^{a_0}$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0$, and each $X^{a_n} \to X^{a_{n+1}}$ is, up to homotopy, the inclusion with cells $\mathrm{cells}_{n+1}$ attached, then $X$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \mathrm{cells}_1, \dots$ (VA.18).

chips: a tower up to homotopy suffices
diff: "Each extending the previous one" is not available: Lemma 3.7 extends a homotopy equivalence over the new cells, but $\Omega^{a_{i+1}}$ is only homotopy equivalent to $\Omega^{a_i}$ with cells attached, by retractions that move $\Omega^{a_i}$, so the extension holds only up to homotopy (strict compatibility would need nested subdivisions).

The Appendix's comparison of telescopes needs only homotopy-commutative squares (VA.16, VA.19), so the tower is built up to homotopy. The step also needs a relative form of Theorem 3.5, for pairs of sublevel sets, which the book does not state.

items.title: The step from $\Omega^a$ to $\Omega^b$

milnor.label: §17, p. 95
milnor.statement: Each $\Omega^{a_i}$ has the homotopy type of $\Omega^{a_{i-1}}$ with one $\lambda$-cell attached for each geodesic of index $\lambda$ with energy in $(a_{i-1}, a_i)$, by 16.2 together with 3.3 and 3.7.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) for Milnor's data and levels $a \le b < c$, if neither $a$ nor $b$ is $E'(y)$ for a $y \in U$ with $\omega_y$ a geodesic, and every such $\omega_y$ with $E'(y) \le b$ has nullity $0$, then $\Omega^a \to \Omega^b$ is, up to homotopy, $\Omega^a$ with one cell of dimension the index of $E_{**}$ at $\omega_y$ for each such $y$ with $a < E'(y) < b$, attached in order of energy; the homotopy equivalences $\Omega^t \simeq \{y \in U : E'(y) \le t\}$ are all given by $\omega \mapsto$ the break points of $r_1(\omega)$, so they commute with the inclusions. (ii) Under nullity $0$, such geodesics are finitely many; if $N$ is closed in $V$, $p, q \in N$, and every geodesic in $\Omega$ has nullity $0$, the energies at most $b$ of the geodesics in $\Omega$ are finitely many, for every $b$. (iii) The index of a geodesic, as a natural number, equals the index of $E_{**}$ at it (finite by Theorem 15.1).

chips: any finite number of critical values
diff: Each step uses its own manifold of broken geodesics, with an energy bound $c > b$, and allows any finite number of critical values between $a$ and $b$.

Hidden: the choice of levels needs the critical values of $E$ to be discrete, which follows from Theorem 16.3 (finitely many geodesics below each level); and the homotopy equivalences with the models must commute with the inclusions.

items.title: Theorem 17.3: the fundamental theorem of Morse theory

milnor.label: §17, Theorem 17.3
milnor.statement: If $M$ is complete and $p, q \in M$ are not conjugate along any geodesic, then $\Omega(M; p, q)$ (or $\Omega^*(M; p, q)$) has the homotopy type of a countable CW-complex which contains one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each geodesic from $p$ to $q$ of index $\lambda$. Proof: levels $a_0 < a_1 < \cdots$, not critical values, with "precisely one" critical value in each interval and $\Omega^{a_0}$ empty; the tower of CW-complexes; the direct limit map $\Omega \to K$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups, hence is a homotopy equivalence by Whitehead's theorem, $\Omega$ having the homotopy type of a CW-complex by 17.2. A different proof, not using 17.1, is referred to the Appendix.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric, closed in $V$, and $p, q \in N$: (i) suppose every geodesic in $\Omega$ has nullity $0$, and let $a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots$ be levels tending to $\infty$, $a_0 < 0$, none of which is the energy of a geodesic. Then there are finite lists $\mathrm{geo}_0 = \emptyset, \mathrm{geo}_1, \dots$ of geodesics, $\mathrm{geo}_{n+1}$ containing exactly one representative of each geodesic with energy in $(a_n, a_{n+1})$, ordered by energy, such that $\Omega$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex (VA.18) with one cell of dimension the index of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma$ for each entry $\gamma$. (ii) **Theorem 17.3:** if every geodesic in $\Omega$ has nullity $0$, there are finite lists of geodesics from $p$ to $q$ such that every geodesic agrees on $[0, 1]$ with exactly one entry of exactly one list, energies increase strictly from list to list and weakly within a list, and $\Omega(N; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each entry of index $\lambda$. (iii) The same holds if $q$ is not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic (V11.4).

diff: Completeness is replaced by the closedness of $N$ in $V$, which implies it (V7.30) and is used only through the compactness of the balls $S$ (V10.3).

The statement is for $\Omega$; for $\Omega^*$ it would follow by composing with Theorem 17.1 (V10.19), but is not stated. The countable CW-complex is the mapping telescope of a tower of cell attachments along arbitrary maps (VA.18).

The proof is Milnor's second route, Theorem A of the Appendix (VA.19), through V10.20 and V10.21; neither Whitehead's theorem nor Corollary 17.2 is used. "Precisely one" critical value per interval is impossible when there are finitely many geodesics, and "at most one" is not needed: several are attached in order of energy. The levels must tend to infinity.
Geodesics are counted by their values on $[0, 1]$, as paths are maps on $\mathbb R$.

items.title: The geodesics from $p$ to $q$ on $S^n$, and their indices

milnor.label: §17, pp. 95–96; §14, Example 2
milnor.statement: For $q \ne p, p'$ on $S^n$, $p'$ the antipode of $p$, the geodesics from $p$ to $q$ are $\gamma_0$, the short great circle arc, $\gamma_1$, the long arc $pq'p'q$, $\gamma_2 = pqp'q'pq$, and so on. The index $\lambda(\gamma_k)$ is $k(n - 1)$: $k$ is the number of times $p$ or $p'$ occurs in the interior of $\gamma_k$, and each of these points is conjugate to $p$ with multiplicity $n - 1$ (Example 2 of §14).

lean.statement: On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$: (i) for unit $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ of energy $L^2$ on $[0, 1]$, and every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(S^n; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with such a $c$, $L \ge 0$. (ii) The conjugate parameters along $c$ are as in V9.7″. (iii) Let $q \ne \pm p$, $\theta \in (0, \pi)$ the angle between $p$ and $q$, $u \perp p$ the unit vector with $q = \cos\theta\,p + \sin\theta\,u$; let $\gamma_{2j}$ be the great circle along $u$ with $L_{2j} = \theta + 2\pi j$, and $\gamma_{2j+1}$ the one along $-u$ with $L_{2j+1} = 2\pi(j + 1) - \theta$. These are geodesics in $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ with $E(\gamma_k) = L_k^2$ and $k\pi < L_k < (k + 1)\pi$; every geodesic in $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with some $\gamma_k$; $q$ is not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic; and the index of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma_k$, and at every geodesic that agrees with it on $[0, 1]$, is $k(n - 1)$.

chips: the list of geodesics shown complete
diff: Milnor's count of the interior occurrences of $p$ and $p'$ is the inequality $k\pi < L_k < (k + 1)\pi$; the index comes from Theorem 15.1.

Hidden: that $q \ne p, p'$ makes $p$, $q$ non-conjugate along every geodesic needs the conjugate points along every great circle through $p$ and the list of all geodesics from $p$ to $q$; that every geodesic is a great circle uses uniqueness after extending the segment past $t = 0$ (V9.9). Of the rephrasing of non-conjugacy as $q \ne p, p'$, the direction Theorem 17.3 needs is proved.
The Jacobi fields are checked directly with $R(x, y)z = \langle x, z\rangle y - \langle y, z\rangle x$, not by rotations and Lemma 14.3.

items.title: Corollary 17.4: the cells of the path space of $S^n$

milnor.label: §17, Corollary 17.4
milnor.statement: The loop space $\Omega(S^n)$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex with one cell each in the dimensions $0, n - 1, 2(n - 1), 3(n - 1), \dots$. It is derived from Theorem 17.3 and the example of the geodesics from $p$ to a point $q \ne p, p'$.

lean.statement: (i) Let $N \subseteq V$ be closed in $V$, $p, q \in N$, every geodesic in $\Omega$ of nullity $0$, and suppose the geodesics in $\Omega$ are, up to their values off $[0, 1]$, a sequence $g_0, g_1, \dots$ with strictly increasing energies tending to $\infty$, every geodesic agreeing with $g_k$ on $[0, 1]$ having index $d_k$. Then $\Omega$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with one cell of dimension $d_k$ at stage $k + 1$. (ii) **Corollary 17.4:** for $n \ge 2$ and $p, q \in S^n$ with $q \ne p$ and $q \ne -p$, the path space $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with one cell in each of the dimensions $0, n - 1, 2(n - 1), \dots$, attached in this order.

diff: The path space $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ with $q \ne \pm p$, which is what Milnor's argument gives, replaces the loop space: in the loop space $p$ is conjugate to itself along every great circle, and passing to loops needs that $\Omega^*(S^n; p, q)$ does not depend on $q$ up to homotopy (the exposition's Lemma 17.D) together with Theorem 17.1; that change of end point is V10.28, and the loop space is V10.30.
$n \ge 2$; the case $n = 1$, with every cell a point, is not stated. The cell complex is a countable cell complex in the sense of VA.18.

items.title: The homology of a path space read off from its geodesics

milnor.label: §17, p. 96
milnor.statement: For $n > 2$, the homology of $\Omega(S^n)$ "can be computed immediately" from the cell structure of Corollary 17.4.

lean.statement: Homology is singular homology with coefficients in a field $\Bbbk$, and $b_i = \dim_\Bbbk H_i$. (i) Let $A_0 \subseteq A_1 \subseteq \cdots$ be subsets of a space $X$ such that every compact subset of $X$ lies in some $A_k$. If $H_j(A_k, A_{k_0}) = 0$ for all $k \ge k_0$, then $H_j(X, A_{k_0}) = 0$; and if the steps $H_*(A_{k+1}, A_k)$ vanish in degrees $i$ and $i + 1$ for all $k \ge k_0$, then $b_i(X) = \dim H_i(A_{k_0})$. (ii) For Milnor's data and levels $a \le b < c$, neither the energy of a geodesic, with at most one energy of a geodesic in $(a, b)$ and every geodesic of energy at most $b$ of nullity $0$, $H_j(\Omega^b, \Omega^a)$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of geodesics with energy in $(a, b)$ and index $j$. (iii) In the situation of V10.24 (i) with $d_k = kr$, $r \ge 2$, $b_i(\Omega) = 1$ when $r$ divides $i$ and $0$ otherwise.

chips: filtration by energy, not cellular homology
diff: Reading the homology off the cells is cellular homology, which needs cellular attaching maps; here the homology is computed from the filtration of $\Omega$ by the $\Omega^a$, with the lacunary principle on the finite stages (Corollary 5.4), rather than from a cellular chain complex.

That the homology of $\Omega$ is the limit of that of the $\Omega^a$ needs every compact subset of $\Omega$ to have bounded energy, true for $d$ since $E$ is continuous, false for $d^*$; the vanishing is needed in degrees $i$ and $i + 1$. Coefficients are in a field.

items.title: The homology of the path space of $S^n$

milnor.label: §17, p. 96
milnor.statement: For $n > 2$ the homology of $\Omega(S^n)$ "can be computed immediately" from Corollary 17.4 (the cells lie in the dimensions $k(n - 1)$, no two of them consecutive, so every cell contributes a free generator); in particular $\Omega(S^n)$ has non-trivial homology in infinitely many dimensions, which is what Corollary 17.5 uses.

lean.statement: For $n \ge 3$, $p, q \in S^n$ with $q \ne p$ and $q \ne -p$, and every field $\Bbbk$, $\dim_\Bbbk H_i(\Omega(S^n; p, q); \Bbbk)$ is $1$ if $n - 1$ divides $i$ and $0$ otherwise.

diff: The path space with $q \ne \pm p$ replaces the loop space, as in V10.24, and coefficients are in a field, not the integers.
$n > 2$ is needed, so that no two cells have consecutive dimensions; for $n = 2$ there is a cell in every dimension and the lacunary principle does not apply.

items.title: Corollary 17.5 needs completeness

milnor.label: §17, Corollary 17.5
milnor.statement: Corollary 17.5: if $M$ has the homotopy type of $S^n$, $n > 2$, then any two non-conjugate points of $M$ are joined by infinitely many geodesics. Completeness is not among its hypotheses, although the proof rests on Theorem 17.3, which assumes it; the Remark that follows (p. 97) assumes it.

lean.statement: (i) An open subset of $V$ is a slice submanifold of codimension $0$, every tangent space being $V$. (ii) If every tangent space of $N$ is $V$, the induced metric is flat; every geodesic in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with the segment $t \mapsto p + t(q - p)$; no two parameters are conjugate along a curve in $N$, and every geodesic has index $0$ and nullity $0$; and if the segment from $p$ to $q$ lies in $N$, it is the unique geodesic in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ up to values off $[0, 1]$. (iii) For $n \ge 1$, $N = \mathbb R^{n+1} \setminus \{0\}$ with the induced metric is homotopy equivalent to $S^n$ and path-connected; it is neither closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ nor geodesically complete; no point of $N$ is conjugate to another along any geodesic; and there are $p \ne q$ in $N$ joined by exactly one geodesic.

diff: For $n \ge 3$, $\mathbb R^{n+1} \setminus \{0\}$ satisfies the hypotheses of Corollary 17.5 as printed and not its conclusion, so the hypothesis that $M$ is complete, which the book omits, cannot be dropped.

Corollary 17.5 itself, for complete $M$, is not formalized; nor is the fact that $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is not contractible here, which would contradict Theorem 17.3 without completeness for every $n \ge 1$. What is proved is that $N$ satisfies every hypothesis of the formal Theorem 17.3 except closedness in the ambient space.

items.title: $\exp$ is smooth on its whole domain

milnor.label: §18, p. 98
milnor.statement: A critical point is defined for a smooth map between manifolds of the same dimension and applied to $\exp = \exp_p : TM_p \to M$, so $\exp_p$ is treated as smooth on all of $TM_p$. $M$ is assumed complete so that $\exp$ is everywhere defined, "although this assumption could easily be eliminated".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) let $E$ be a real normed space, $U_0 \subseteq E$ open, $u_0 \in U_0$, and $c, w$ of class $C^\infty$ on $U_0$ with $c(u) \in N$, $w(u) \in T_{c(u)}N$. If $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u_0)}(t\,w(u_0))$ is a geodesic on $(-\delta, B + \delta)$, $B \ge 0$, there are $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$ such that every $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ with $\|u - u_0\| < \varepsilon$ is a geodesic on $(-\eta, B + \eta)$ and $(u, t) \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ is $C^\infty$ there. (ii) Every point of $N$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ in $V$ with a $C^\infty$ retraction $U \to N$. (iii) The domain of $\exp$ lies in $TN$, contains $(y, w)$ as soon as $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ is a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$, and equals $TN \cap O'$ for an open $O' \subseteq V \times V$; near each of its points $\exp$ is the restriction of a $C^\infty$ map on an open set of $V \times V$, and $(q, v) \mapsto \exp_q(v)$ is $C^\infty$ on it as a map on the manifold $TN$.

chips: the whole domain, not near the zero section
diff: §10 gives the smoothness of $\exp$ only near the zero section (Lemma 10.2, V7.8), and Chapter 7 only its continuity on the domain (V7.23); Milnor uses smoothness everywhere from §18 on without proof. It is the smooth dependence of geodesics on their initial data over a compact time interval.
The domain of $\exp$ is open in $TN$ and $\exp$ is smooth on it, with no completeness, as Milnor says could "easily" be arranged.

items.title: $\exp_q$, its derivative, and critical points of $\exp_q$

milnor.label: §18, p. 98
milnor.statement: A smooth map $f : N \to M$ between manifolds of the same dimension is *critical* at $x$ if $f_* : TN_x \to TM_{f(x)}$ is not one-to-one. This is applied to $\exp = \exp_p : TM_p \to M$, with $X \in T(TM_p)_v$ the tangent space at $v$ of $TM_p$ "considered as a manifold"; $\gamma_v$ is the geodesic $t \mapsto \exp(tv)$ from $p$ to $\exp v$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $q \in N$ let $\mathcal D_q \subseteq T_qN$ be the set of $v$ with $(q, v)$ in the domain of $\exp$. It contains $0$, contains $tv$ for $v \in \mathcal D_q$ and $0 \le t \le 1$, is open in $T_qN$, and $\exp_q$ is $C^\infty$ on it as a map from the vector space $T_qN$ to $V$. $d(\exp_q)_v : T_qN \to V$ is the derivative of this map at $v$, and $\exp_q$ is *critical* at $v$ if $d(\exp_q)_v$ is not one-to-one. For $v \in \mathcal D_q$, $\gamma_v(t) = \exp_q(tv)$ is a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$ and a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. If $N$ is geodesically complete, $\mathcal D_q = T_qN$.

diff: $T(TM_p)_v$ is identified with $T_qN$, as Milnor does on p. 99 (paths $v(u)$ in $TM_p$ with $\frac{dv}{du}(0) = X$), and $d(\exp_q)_v$ takes values in $V$; whether it is one-to-one does not depend on the target.
Without completeness, the domain of $\exp_q$ is shown open and star-shaped about $0$ (V11.1), which is what the statements of §18 need.

items.title: Theorem 18.1: conjugate points are critical values of $\exp$

milnor.label: §18, Theorem 18.1
milnor.statement: The point $q = \exp v$ is conjugate to $p$ along the geodesic $\gamma_v$ from $p$ to $\exp v$ if and only if the mapping $\exp$ is critical at $v$. Proof (pp. 98–99): if $\exp_*X = 0$ with $X \ne 0$, the variation $\alpha(u, t) = \exp tv(u)$ through geodesics, for a path $v(u)$ with $v(0) = v$ and $\frac{dv}{du}(0) = X$, has a variation field $W$ with $W(0) = 0$, $W(1) = \exp_*X = 0$ and $\frac{DW}{dt}(0) \ne 0$; conversely, if $\exp_*$ is non-singular at $v$, independent $X_1, \dots, X_n$ give $n$ Jacobi fields vanishing at $p$ with independent values at $\exp v$, and "clearly" no non-trivial Jacobi field vanishes at both ends.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $q \in N$ and $v \in \mathcal D_q$ (V11.2). For $X \in T_qN$ let $W_X(t) = t\,d(\exp_q)_{tv}(X)$ on $[0, 1]$, constant off $[0, 1]$. (i) $X \mapsto W_X$ is linear and each $W_X$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma_v$ with $W_X(0) = 0$, $\frac{DW_X}{dt}(0) = X$ and $W_X(1) = d(\exp_q)_v(X)$. (ii) $X \mapsto W_X$ is injective, and every Jacobi field along $\gamma_v$ vanishing at $0$ is a $W_X$. (iii) The Jacobi fields vanishing at $0$ and $1$ are the $W_X$ with $X \in \ker d(\exp_q)_v$, so the multiplicity of the conjugate parameters $0$ and $1$ is $\dim\ker d(\exp_q)_v$. (iv) **Theorem 18.1:** $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma_v$ iff $\exp_q$ is critical at $v$.

diff: The multiplicity of the conjugate point equals the dimension of the kernel of $d(\exp_q)_v$, which Milnor does not state (the exposition's form of 18.1); no completeness is assumed.

Hidden: the smoothness of $\exp_q$ on its domain (V11.1); $\frac{DW}{dt}(0) = \frac{D}{du}v(u)$ needs the symmetry lemma 8.7 along the constant curve $u \mapsto p$. The formal proof uses the straight line $v(u) = v + uX$ and $d(\exp_q)_0 = \mathrm{id}$ instead, and the uniqueness of Jacobi fields from initial data in place of the dimension count.
"$\exp v$ conjugate to $p$ along $\gamma_v$" is the conjugacy of the parameters $0$ and $1$ (V9.4).

items.title: The conjugate locus is the set of critical values of $\exp_p$

milnor.label: §18, p. 99
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. Milnor says that Corollary 18.2 "follows immediately from 18.1 together with Sard's theorem (6.1)", which needs every point conjugate to $p$ along some geodesic to be a critical value of $\exp_p$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $p \in V$, the conjugate locus $C(p)$ is the set of $q$ for which there is a geodesic $\gamma$ from $p$ (a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ that is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$, $\gamma(0) = p$) with $\gamma(1) = q$ along which $0$ and $1$ are conjugate. Let $p \in N$. For every geodesic $\gamma$ from $p$, its initial velocity $v$ lies in $\mathcal D_p$, $\exp_p(v) = \gamma(1)$, and $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma$ iff $\exp_p$ is critical at $v$. Hence $C(p) = \exp_p(\{v \in \mathcal D_p : \exp_p \text{ critical at } v\})$, the set of critical values of $\exp_p$; if $N$ is geodesically complete, $\mathcal D_p = T_pN$.

diff: The conjugate locus is named and identified as a set. "Follows immediately" hides that every geodesic from $p$ is a radial geodesic $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ (uniqueness of geodesics, and the extension of a segment past its end points, V9.9), and, without completeness, that the domain of $\exp_p$ is open (V11.1).

items.title: Corollary 18.2: almost every point is non-conjugate

milnor.label: §18, Corollary 18.2
milnor.statement: If $p \in M$, then for almost all $q \in M$, $p$ is not conjugate to $q$ along any geodesic. It follows "immediately from 18.1 together with Sard's theorem (6.1)".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $p \in N$, let $\sigma$ be a slice chart of $N$, and $\mu$ a Haar measure on the model space $Z$. Then the image of $C(p) \cap \operatorname{dom}\sigma$ under the chart is $\mu$-null: $C(p)$ has measure zero in $N$.

chips: measure zero read in every chart
diff: "Measure zero" in a manifold is not defined in the book (Theorem 6.1 uses the phrase for a manifold target); here it is read in every slice chart, for every Haar measure on the model space.

The proof applies the companion project's Sard theorem to $z \mapsto \sigma(\exp_p(e(z)))$, $e : Z \to T_pN$ a linear isomorphism: a derivative that is not one-to-one stays so after composing, and a linear map of $Z$ to itself is onto iff it is one-to-one.

items.title: Non-conjugate points exist, are dense, and are non-degenerate

milnor.label: §18, p. 98
milnor.statement: Theorem 17.3 describes $\Omega(M; p, q)$ when $p$ and $q$ are not conjugate along any geodesic, and "this section will justify this result by showing that such non-conjugate points always exist".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $p \in N$, the points of $N$ outside $C(p)$ are dense in $N$. If $q \notin C(p)$, then at every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ the nullity of $E_{**}$ is $0$.

diff: Milnor promises existence; density is proved, and the non-degeneracy that Theorems 16.3 and 17.3 actually use (nullity $0$, by Theorem 14.1).
From measure zero to existence needs that a null set has empty interior, a non-empty open subset of $Z$ having positive Haar measure.

items.title: Lemma 19.1: no conjugate points in non-positive curvature

milnor.label: §19, Lemma 19.1
milnor.statement: Suppose that the sectional curvature of $M$ is everywhere $\le 0$, i.e. $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$ for every pair of vectors $A, B$ in $TM_p$ and every $p$. Then no two points of $M$ are conjugate along any geodesic. Proof: $\langle\frac{D^2J}{dt^2}, J\rangle = -\langle R(V, J)V, J\rangle \ge 0$, so $\langle\frac{DJ}{dt}, J\rangle$ is monotonically increasing, strictly so unless $\frac{DJ}{dt} = 0$; if $J(0) = J(t_0) = 0$ it vanishes on $[0, t_0]$, so $J(0) = \frac{DJ}{dt}(0) = 0$ and $J \equiv 0$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: $N$ has *non-positive curvature* if $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$ for all $A, B \in T_qN$ and all $q \in N$; equivalently, every sectional curvature of $N$ is $\le 0$. (i) For a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and a Jacobi field $J$ along it, $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\frac{DJ}{dt}, J\rangle = \|\frac{DJ}{dt}\|^2 - \langle R(V, J)V, J\rangle$ on $(0, 1)$. (ii) If $N$ has non-positive curvature and $\gamma$ is a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ which is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$, a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ vanishing at two parameters $a < b$ of $[0, 1]$ vanishes on $[0, 1]$: no two parameters are conjugate along $\gamma$.

chips: the identity along any smooth curve
diff: Any two parameters $a < b$ in $[0, 1]$, where Milnor treats $0$ and $t_0$; conjugate parameters for points (V9.4). The identity (i) holds along any smooth curve.
$\frac{DJ}{dt}(0) = 0$ comes from $\frac{DJ}{dt} = 0$ on $(0, t_0)$ by continuity, a step the book leaves implicit.

items.title: Non-positive curvature: index $0$, and $\exp_p$ nowhere critical

milnor.label: §19, proof of Theorem 19.2, pp. 102–103
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 19.2: since there are no conjugate points, "it follows from the index theorem that every geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has index $\lambda = 0$" (p. 102); and "it follows from 18.1 that $\exp_p$ is non-critical everywhere" (p. 103).

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $N$ have non-positive curvature. At every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ the index and the nullity of $E_{**}$ are $0$, and $E_{**}(W, W) > 0$ for every $W \in T\Omega_\gamma$ that does not vanish identically on $[0, 1]$. For $p \in N$, $\exp_p$ is critical at no point of $\mathcal D_p$.

diff: Positive definiteness of $E_{**}$ is not in the book; neither completeness nor simple connectivity is assumed.

The proof is the index theorem (V9.24) with Lemma 19.1; a $W$ with $E_{**}(W, W) = 0$ is a null vector of the semi-definite form, hence a Jacobi field vanishing at $0$ and $1$ (V9.5), hence $0$; the last statement is Theorem 18.1 with Lemma 19.1.

items.title: Theorem 19.2 (Cartan–Hadamard)

milnor.label: §19, Theorem 19.2
milnor.statement: (Cartan.) Suppose that $M$ is a simply connected, complete Riemannian manifold, and that the sectional curvature $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$ is everywhere $\le 0$. Then any two points of $M$ are joined by a unique geodesic. Furthermore, $M$ is diffeomorphic to the Euclidean space $\mathbb R^n$. Proof (pp. 102–103): by the index theorem and 17.3, $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a $0$-dimensional complex with one vertex for each geodesic; it is connected since $M$ is simply connected, so there is precisely one geodesic from $p$ to $q$. Therefore $\exp_p : TM_p \to M$ is one-one and onto; by 18.1 it is non-critical, hence locally a diffeomorphism, hence a global diffeomorphism.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $N$ be geodesically complete (for instance closed in $V$), simply connected (as a topological space, with the topology of $V$), and of non-positive curvature. Then any two points $p, q \in N$ are joined by a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, and every geodesic in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees with $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$; and $N$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$, $n = \dim N$, for its manifold structure as a slice submanifold. More precisely, $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ is itself a diffeomorphism: it is a covering map (V11.19), injective because $N$ is simply connected, and onto by the Hopf–Rinow theorem.

chips: the argument runs in reverse order
diff: The statement is Milnor's. The order of the argument is reversed: Milnor deduces the uniqueness of geodesics from the connectedness of the path space and then the injectivity of $\exp_p$; here the covering $\exp_p$ (V11.19) gives injectivity directly (the image of a segment of $T_pN$ with both ends over one point is a null-homotopic loop, whose lift is closed), and uniqueness follows. Both routes rest on Lemma 19.1.

Milnor's route silently uses Theorem 17.1, to identify the components of $\Omega(M; p, q)$ with the homotopy classes of paths; the covering route needs instead the completeness of the metric pulled back to $T_pN$, his "it is clear" of p. 103.

"Hence a global diffeomorphism" is the fact that a bijective local diffeomorphism is a diffeomorphism (Mathlib); that $\exp_p$ is onto is the Hopf–Rinow theorem, which needs $M$ connected, part of "simply connected".

items.title: The path space in non-positive curvature

milnor.label: §19, proof of Theorem 19.2, p. 102
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 19.2: since every geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has index $0$, Theorem 17.3 asserts that the path space $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a $0$-dimensional CW-complex, with one vertex for each geodesic. The hypothesis that $M$ is simply connected implies that $\Omega(M; p, q)$ is connected, and a connected $0$-dimensional CW-complex must consist of a single point.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric, of non-positive curvature: (i) if $N$ is closed in $V$ and $p, q \in N$, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex (VA.18) all of whose cells are $0$-cells, one for each geodesic from $p$ to $q$ (Theorem 17.3 with all indices $0$). (ii) If $N$ is geodesically complete, the fibre of $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ over $q$ is discrete and countable, its points $v$ correspond bijectively to the geodesics $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ from $p$ to $q$, and $\Omega(N; p, q)$, with Milnor's metric, is homotopy equivalent to it. (iii) If moreover $N$ is simply connected, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is contractible, and (for $N$ closed) it has the homotopy type of a cell complex with exactly one cell, a $0$-cell.

chips: a discrete space, through the covering
diff: The homotopy type is obtained for every complete $N$ of non-positive curvature, simply connected or not: lifting a path from $p$ to $q$ from $0 \in T_pN$ and taking the end point is a homotopy equivalence of $\Omega^*$ with the fibre of $\exp_p$ over $q$, and $\Omega \simeq \Omega^*$ by Theorem 17.1.

That a countable cell complex with only $0$-cells, in the sense of VA.18 (a mapping telescope of finite stages), is homotopy equivalent to a discrete space is not formalized; (ii) reaches the discrete space directly.
For simply connected $N$ the contraction is explicit: $\Omega^*$ contracts onto a geodesic through the diffeomorphism $\exp_p$, and $\Omega \simeq \Omega^*$.

items.title: $\exp_p$ is a covering map

milnor.label: §19, p. 103
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. At the end of the proof of 19.2 Milnor notes that by 18.1 $\exp_p$ is non-critical everywhere, "so that $\exp_p$ is locally a diffeomorphism". For a complete $M$ of curvature $\le 0$ that is not simply connected, Theorem 19.2 is applied to the universal covering space $\tilde M$, which, "it is clear", inherits from $M$ a Riemannian metric that is geodesically complete and of curvature $\le 0$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) the Gauss lemma holds on the whole domain of $\exp_p$: $\langle d(\exp_p)_w(w), d(\exp_p)_w(x)\rangle = \langle w, x\rangle$ for $w \in \mathcal D_p$, $x \in T_pN$. (ii) $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ is a local diffeomorphism at every point where $d(\exp_p)$ is one-to-one. Now let $N$ be geodesically complete and $\exp_p$ nowhere critical. (iii) A lift $\Gamma$ through $\exp_p$ of a smooth curve of speed $\le L$ on $[0, T]$ satisfies $\|\Gamma(t)\| \le \|\Gamma(0)\| + 1 + Lt$. (iv) Smooth curves in $N$ lift through $\exp_p$, uniquely, from any point over the initial point. (v) $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ is a covering map. In non-positive curvature (V11.8) all of this applies.

chips: Gauss lemma beyond a normal ball
diff: The universal covering of p. 103 and of Corollary 19.3 is $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ itself, so no abstract covering space and no metric on it are needed; the covering argument is the standard proof of the Cartan–Hadamard theorem, not Milnor's, who works with the path space.

The only analytic input beyond Lemma 19.1 is the completeness of the metric pulled back to $T_pN$ — Milnor's "it is clear" — used in the form (iii): by the Gauss lemma the radius of a lift grows no faster than the length of the curve. This needs the Gauss lemma on the whole domain of $\exp_p$, while Milnor states it only in a normal neighbourhood (Lemma 10.5).
"Locally a diffeomorphism" is the inverse function theorem on manifolds (the companion project's): the derivative of $\exp_p$ into $N$ is one-to-one, and onto because $\dim T_pN = \dim N$.

items.title: Each homotopy class of paths contains exactly one geodesic

milnor.label: §19, p. 103
milnor.statement: More generally, suppose that $M$ is complete with sectional curvature $\le 0$ but not simply connected (for example a flat torus, or a compact surface of genus $\ge 2$ with constant negative curvature). Theorem 19.2 applies to the universal covering space $\tilde M$; given two points $p, q \in M$, it follows that each homotopy class of paths from $p$ to $q$ contains precisely one geodesic.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $N$ be geodesically complete and of non-positive curvature, and $p, q \in N$. Every continuous path $c$ in $N$ from $p$ to $q$ is homotopic, relative to its end points, to a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$; and two geodesics in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ that are both homotopic to $c$ agree on $[0, 1]$.

diff: The statement is Milnor's, for every complete $N$ of curvature $\le 0$. The geodesics from $p$ are the images of the segments from $0$ in $T_pN$, which are their lifts through the covering $\exp_p$ (V11.19); homotopic paths have lifts from $0$ with the same end point, and two paths of $T_pN$ with the same end points are homotopic.

items.title: Corollary 19.3: the homotopy groups in non-positive curvature

milnor.label: §19, Corollary 19.3
milnor.statement: If $M$ is complete with $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$, then the homotopy groups $\pi_i(M)$ are zero for $i > 1$, and $\pi_1(M)$ contains no element of finite order other than the identity. Proof: clearly $\pi_i(M) = \pi_i(\tilde M) = 0$ for $i > 1$, $\tilde M$ being contractible; and since the cohomology of $M$ is that of the group $\pi_1(M)$ (Hu), a non-trivial finite cyclic subgroup $G$ would give a covering $\hat M$ with $H^k(G) = H^k(\hat M) = 0$ for $k > n$, while the cohomology of a finite cyclic group is non-trivial in arbitrarily high dimensions.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: if $N$ is geodesically complete and of non-positive curvature, then $\pi_i(N, x) = 0$ for every $i > 1$ and every base point $x \in N$ (Mathlib's homotopy groups); on the way, every map of the cube $I^i$, $i \ge 2$, constant on the boundary, is null-homotopic relative to the boundary.

diff: Only the first half is formalized. That $\pi_1(M)$ has no non-trivial element of finite order needs the cohomology of groups ($H^k(M) \cong H^k(\pi_1(M))$ for $M$ with contractible universal covering) and the cohomology of finite cyclic groups, which are not available.

"Clearly $\pi_i(M) = \pi_i(\tilde M)$" is proved by lifting: a map of the cube lifts through the covering $\exp_x$ because the cube is simply connected and locally path connected, and the lift is constant on the boundary because the fibre is discrete and the boundary of the cube is connected for $i \ge 2$ — which is where the argument, and the statement, stop for $i = 1$.

items.title: The Ricci tensor and Milnor’s Assertion

milnor.label: §19, p. 104
milnor.statement: Definition: the Ricci tensor at a point $p$ of a Riemannian manifold is the bilinear pairing $K : TM_p \times TM_p \to \mathbb R$, $K(U_1, U_2)$ the trace of the linear transformation $W \mapsto R(U_1, W)U_2$ of $TM_p$; "it follows easily from 9.3 that $K$ is symmetric". Assertion: for an orthonormal basis $U_1, \dots, U_n$ of $TM_p$, $K(U_n, U_n)$ is the sum of the sectional curvatures $\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_i\rangle$, $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$, because the $n$-th diagonal term of the matrix $(\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_j\rangle)$ is zero.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $q \in N$ and $U_1, U_2 \in T_qN$, $K(U_1, U_2)$ is the trace of $W \mapsto R(U_1, W)U_2$ on $T_qN$. For an orthonormal basis $E_1, \dots, E_n$ of $T_qN$, $K(U_1, U_2) = \sum_i\langle R(U_1, E_i)U_2, E_i\rangle$, and $K(U_1, U_2) = K(U_2, U_1)$. **Assertion:** for an orthonormal basis $U_1, \dots, U_n$, $K(U_n, U_n) = \sum_{i \ne n}\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_i\rangle$.

items.title: A geodesic as a smooth curve with a parallel frame

milnor.label: §19, proof of Theorem 19.4, p. 104
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 19.4: for a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ of length $L$, choose parallel vector fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $\gamma$ which are orthonormal at one point, and hence everywhere, with $P_n$ pointing along $\gamma$, so that $V = \frac{d\gamma}{dt} = LP_n$ and $\frac{DP_i}{dt} = 0$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic of length $L$. (i) There are a $C^\infty$ curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$ equal to $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$ and a $C^\infty$ tangent field $V$ along $c$, equal to $\gamma'$ on $(0, 1)$, with $\|V\| = L$ and $L^{-1}V$ parallel along $c$. (ii) If $L > 0$, there are such $c$ and $V$ and $n - 1$ parallel unit fields $P_1, \dots, P_{n-1}$ along $c$ such that, for every $r$ for which $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$, $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\langle R(V, P_i)V, P_i\rangle \ge L^2(n - 1)/r^2$ at every $t$.

chips: frames need $\gamma$ extended past its ends
diff: Parallel fields along $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ (Lemma 8.2) are formalized for curves on $\mathbb R$, so $\gamma$ is first extended past its ends (the radial geodesic of $\gamma'(0)$, composed with a smooth clamp).
$V = LP_n$ needs the constant speed $L$ and that $V$ itself is parallel; the frame must be orthonormal at every $t$, parallel translation being an isometry, for the Assertion (V11.9) to apply.

items.title: The test fields $\sin(\pi t)P_i(t)$

milnor.label: §19, proof of Theorem 19.4, p. 105
milnor.statement: With $W_i(t) = (\sin\pi t)P_i(t)$, $\frac12E_{**}(W_i, W_i) = -\int_0^1\langle W_i, \frac{D^2W_i}{dt^2} + R(V, W_i)V\rangle\,dt = \int_0^1(\sin\pi t)^2(\pi^2 - L^2\langle R(P_n, P_i)P_n, P_i\rangle)\,dt$. Summing for $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$ gives $\int_0^1(\sin\pi t)^2((n - 1)\pi^2 - L^2K(P_n, P_n))\,dt$, which is negative if $K(P_n, P_n) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ and $L > \pi r$; hence $E_{**}(W_i, W_i) < 0$ for some $i$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ agree on $[0, 1]$ with a $C^\infty$ curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$, $P$ a parallel unit field along $c$, and $V$ a field equal to $\gamma'$ on $(0, 1)$. Then $W(t) = \sin(\pi t)P(t)$ lies in $T\Omega_\gamma$ and $\frac12E_{**}(W, W) = \int_0^1(\pi^2\cos^2(\pi t) - \sin^2(\pi t)\langle R(V, P)V, P\rangle)\,dt$. (ii) If $n \ge 2$, $r > 0$, $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$, and $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ is a geodesic of length $> \pi r$, then $E_{**}(X, X) < 0$ for some $X \in T\Omega_\gamma$.
