items.title: Theorem 19.4 (Myers)

milnor.label: §19, Theorem 19.4
milnor.statement: (Myers.) Suppose that the Ricci curvature $K$ satisfies $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit vector $U$ at every point of $M$, where $r$ is a positive constant. Then every geodesic on $M$ of length $> \pi r$ contains conjugate points, and hence is not minimal. On p. 105: $E_{**}(W_i, W_i) < 0$ makes the index of $\gamma$ positive, the index theorem gives conjugate points, and a variation with variation field $W_i$ decreases the energy.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $n = \dim N \ge 2$, $r > 0$, and $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$. Then every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ of length $> \pi r$ has a parameter $t \in (0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$, and is not minimal: some path of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is shorter (V8.6).

chips: does not hold as printed for $n = 1$
diff: $n \ge 2$ is a hypothesis the book leaves silent, and it is needed: for $n = 1$ the Ricci tensor vanishes, Milnor's hypothesis holds for every $r$, and a segment of a line longer than $\pi r$ has no conjugate points and is minimal.

"Contains conjugate points" is "has a parameter in $(0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$"; minimality is among the paths of $\Omega(N; p, q)$. The proof is Milnor's: the index is positive (V11.11), the index theorem (V9.24) gives the conjugate parameter, and Lemma 13.6 (V8.18) excludes minimality.

items.title: Corollary 19.5: compactness and diameter

milnor.label: §19, Corollary 19.5
milnor.statement: If $M$ is complete, and $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2 > 0$ for all unit vectors $U$, then $M$ is compact, with diameter $\le \pi r$. Proof: a minimal geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has length $\le \pi r$, and closed bounded sets in a complete manifold are compact.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$ (V7.24) is a geodesic of $\Omega(N; \gamma(0), \gamma(1))$ minimal in the sense of V8.6. Let $N$ be (pre)connected, $(N, \rho)$ complete, $r > 0$ with $(n - 1)/r^2 > 0$, and $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$. Then $\rho(p, q) \le \pi r$ for all $p, q \in N$, and $N$ is compact.

diff: Connectedness (Milnor's standing assumption) is needed for minimal geodesics to exist; $n \ge 2$ is forced by $(n - 1)/r^2 > 0$. The proof is Hopf–Rinow (V7.29) with V11.12.

items.title: Example: the sphere

milnor.label: §19, Example, p. 105
milnor.statement: If $M$ is a sphere of radius $r$ then every sectional curvature is equal to $1/r^2$, hence $K(U, U)$ takes the constant value $(n - 1)/r^2$. It follows from 19.4 that every geodesic of length $> \pi r$ contains conjugate points: "a best possible result".

lean.statement: On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$ with the induced metric, $K(U, U) = (n - 1)\|U\|^2$, so the hypothesis of Theorem 19.4 holds with $r = 1$. For $n \ge 2$, every geodesic of $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ of length $> \pi$ has a parameter in $(0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$ and is not minimal, and $\rho(p, q) \le \pi$ for all $p, q \in S^n$.

diff: Only the unit sphere, not a sphere of radius $r$; and "best possible" (that a geodesic of length $\pi$ has no interior conjugate point) is not stated here, although it follows from the computation of the conjugate points along great circles in Chapter 10 (V9.7″).

items.title: Test fields on disjoint pieces

milnor.label: §19, proof of Theorem 19.6, p. 106
milnor.statement: For a geodesic of length $> k\pi r$, "a similar argument" gives, for each $i = 1, \dots, k$, a vector field $X_i$ along $\gamma$ which vanishes outside the interval $(\frac{i-1}k, \frac ik)$ and has $E_{**}(X_i, X_i) < 0$; "clearly" $E_{**}(X_i, X_j) = 0$ for $i \ne j$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$, $c$, $V$ be as in V11.11 (i), $V$ smooth and tangent along $c$, $P$ parallel along $c$, and $0 \le a < b \le 1$. The field $X$ equal to $\sin(\kappa(t - a))P(t)$, $\kappa = \pi/(b - a)$, on $[a, b]$ and to $0$ elsewhere lies in $T\Omega_\gamma$, and if $\|P\| = 1$, $\frac12E_{**}(X, X) = \int_a^b(\kappa^2\cos^2(\kappa(t - a)) - \sin^2(\kappa(t - a))\langle R(V, P)V, P\rangle)\,dt$. Two such fields on $[a, b]$ and $[a', b']$ with $b \le a'$ have $E_{**}(X, X') = 0$. If $n \ge 2$, $r > 0$, the $P_i$ are as in V11.10 (ii) and $L(\gamma)(b - a) > \pi r$, the field built on $[a, b]$ from some $P_i$ has $E_{**}(X, X) < 0$.

items.title: Theorem 19.6: the index estimate

milnor.label: §19, proof of Theorem 19.6, p. 106
milnor.statement: Since the space of all unit vectors $U$ on the compact $M$ is compact, the continuous function $K(U, U) > 0$ takes on a minimum, which can be denoted by $(n - 1)/r^2 > 0$. Then every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(M; p, q)$ of length $> \pi r$ has index $\lambda \ge 1$; more generally one of length $> k\pi r$ has index $\lambda \ge k$, since $X_1, \dots, X_k$ span a $k$-dimensional subspace of $T\Omega_\gamma$ on which $E_{**}$ is negative definite.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $N$ is compact, $n = \dim N \ge 2$, and the Ricci tensor is positive definite at every point, there is $r > 0$ with $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$. (ii) Let $n \ge 2$, $r > 0$ and $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$; let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic and $k \ge 0$ an integer. If $L(\gamma) > k\pi r$, the index of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma$ is at least $k$, and the parameters $t \in (0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$, counted with multiplicity, number at least $k$. Equivalently, a geodesic of index $< k$ has length $\le k\pi r$.

diff: The continuity of $K(U, U)$ on the unit tangent bundle is used without proof: the Ricci tensor is a trace over the moving subspace $T_qN$; it equals the trace over the fixed space $V$ of $W \mapsto R(U, P_qW)U$, which is continuous in $(q, U)$. The compactness of the unit tangent vectors (a closed subset of $N \times S$, $S$ the unit sphere of $V$) is also made explicit.
$n \ge 2$ is needed, as in Theorem 19.4; and the $X_i$ are linearly independent because they are non-zero with disjoint supports.
The verified Chapter 11 took the bound $(n - 1)/r^2$ as a hypothesis; the first step of Milnor's proof, (i), is now proved (`Morse/Chapter11/PositiveRicci.lean`).

items.title: Theorem 19.6: positive Ricci curvature and the path space

milnor.label: §19, Theorem 19.6
milnor.statement: If $M$ is a compact manifold, and if the Ricci tensor $K$ of $M$ is everywhere positive definite, then the path space $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex having only finitely many cells in each dimension. Proof: by the index estimate a geodesic of length $> k\pi r$ has index $\ge k$; if $p$ and $q$ are not conjugate along any geodesic, then by 16.3 there are only finitely many geodesics of length $\le k\pi r$, hence only finitely many with index $< k$; together with 17.3 this completes the proof.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $N$ be compact, $n = \dim N \ge 2$, with Ricci tensor positive definite at every point, and $p, q \in N$ with $q$ not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic ($q \notin C(p)$, V11.4). Then $\Omega(N; p, q)$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex (VA.18) in which each dimension $d$ occurs at only finitely many of the stages, each stage attaching finitely many cells: only finitely many cells of each dimension. The same holds for $N$ closed in $V$ with $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$ for some $r > 0$; on the way, a geodesic of index $\le d$ has energy $\le ((d + 1)\pi r)^2$.

diff: Milnor's proof covers only end points not conjugate along any geodesic, while the theorem is stated for all $p, q$. This item is that case; the general case, through a nearby non-conjugate $q'$ (Corollary 18.2) and the change of end point $\Omega(M; p, q) \simeq \Omega(M; p, q')$ (the exposition's Lemma 17.D, through Theorem 17.1), is V11.24.

Counting the cells: Theorem 16.3 gives finitely many energy values below each level, the stages of the complex of 17.3 are ordered by energy, and a geodesic of index $\le d$ has length $\le (d + 1)\pi r$, hence energy $\le ((d + 1)\pi r)^2$, energy being length squared at constant speed.
$n \ge 2$ is needed (for $n = 1$ the Ricci tensor vanishes, so the hypothesis cannot hold on a nonempty $N$); the CW-complex is a countable cell complex with arbitrary attaching maps (VA.18).

items.title: The homology of the path space in positive Ricci curvature

milnor.label: §19, cf. Theorem 19.6, p. 106
milnor.statement: The book draws no homological consequence from Theorem 19.6; with cellular homology it would be immediate that each $H_i(\Omega(M; p, q))$ is finitely generated, as on p. 96 Milnor reads the homology of $\Omega(S^n)$ off its cells.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric, closed in $V$, and $p, q \in N$ with every geodesic in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ of nullity $0$: for levels $a \le b$ that are not energies of geodesics, $H_j(\Omega^b, \Omega^a; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional, and zero if no geodesic with energy in $(a, b)$ has index $j$. Hence, if $n = \dim N \ge 2$, $r > 0$, $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$, and $q \notin C(p)$, then $H_i(\Omega(N; p, q); \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional for every $i$ and every field $\Bbbk$; in particular under Milnor's hypotheses of Theorem 19.6 (compact $N$, positive definite Ricci tensor).

diff: The cell complexes of VA.18 have non-cellular attaching maps, so cellular homology is not available; the homology is computed from the energy filtration of $\Omega$: above the energy $((i + 2)\pi r)^2$ every geodesic has index $\ge i + 2$, so the slabs there have no homology in degrees $i$ and $i + 1$, and $H_i(\Omega^a) \cong H_i(\Omega)$ for a regular level $a$ above it.
As in V11.22, end points conjugate along some geodesic are not treated.

items.title: Theorem 19.6 for all end points

milnor.label: §19, Theorem 19.6
milnor.statement: If $M$ is a compact manifold, and if the Ricci tensor $K$ of $M$ is everywhere positive definite, then the path space $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex having only finitely many cells in each dimension — stated for all $p, q$; the proof treats $p, q$ not conjugate along any geodesic.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $N$ be compact, $n = \dim N \ge 2$, with Ricci tensor positive definite at every point. Then for all $p, q \in N$, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex (VA.18) with only finitely many cells of each dimension, and $H_i(\Omega(N; p, q); \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional for every $i$ and every field $\Bbbk$. On the way, $q$ is joined in $N$ to a point $q'$ not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic, and $\Omega(N; p, q) \simeq \Omega(N; p, q')$.

No connectedness of $N$ is needed: $q'$ lies in a small Riemannian ball about $q$.
As in V11.22, $n \ge 2$ and the cell complex is a countable telescope (VA.18).

items.title: The telescope and homotopy direct limits

milnor.label: Appendix, p. 149
milnor.statement: For a topological space $X$ and a sequence $X_0 \subset X_1 \subset X_2 \subset \cdots$ of subspaces, it is convenient to consider the infinite union $X_\Sigma = X_0 \times [0, 1] \cup X_1 \times [1, 2] \cup X_2 \times [2, 3] \cup \cdots$, "to be topologized as a subset of $X \times \mathbb R$". Definition: $X$ is the *homotopy direct limit* of the sequence $\{X_i\}$ if the projection map $p : X_\Sigma \to X$, $p(x, \tau) = x$, is a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; for subsets $X_0, X_1, \dots$ of $X$, the telescope is $X_\Sigma = \bigcup_nX_n \times [n, n + 1] \subseteq X \times \mathbb R$, with the subspace topology; the $n$-th strip is the map $X_n \times [0, 1] \to X_\Sigma$, $(x, t) \mapsto (x, n + t)$; $p(x, \tau) = x$; and $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ if $p$ is a homotopy equivalence. **(T1)** For a monotone sequence, $(x, \tau) \in X_\Sigma$ iff $x \in X_n$ for some integer $0 \le n \le \tau$; so raising $\tau$ stays in $X_\Sigma$.

diff: The definition is Milnor's; the elementary fact (T1), that a point of the telescope may be raised, is used throughout his proof without comment and is stated here.

items.title: Pasting maps along the strips (T3)

milnor.label: Appendix, pp. 151–153
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. Every map and homotopy on a telescope in the proof of Theorem A (pp. 151–153) is given strip by strip, by formulas in $(x, n + t)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, and its continuity is taken for granted.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; if every $X_n$ is closed in $X$, then for every space $P$ a function $F$ on $P \times X_\Sigma$ is continuous as soon as each $(p, x, t) \mapsto F(p, (x, n + t))$ is continuous on $P \times X_n \times [0, 1]$. Hence, for a monotone sequence of closed sets, maps $\Phi_n : P \times X_n \times [0, 1] \to Z$ with $\Phi_{n+1}(p, x, 0) = \Phi_n(p, x, 1)$ define a continuous map on $P \times X_\Sigma$; in particular maps on $X_\Sigma$, and homotopies between them, may be given strip by strip.

diff: This is where closedness enters, a hypothesis Milnor never states: when the $X_n$ are closed, the strips are closed in $X_\Sigma$ and form a locally finite family, and pasting is legitimate. Without it Milnor's maps can be discontinuous (VA.10); the device that removes the hypothesis altogether is the mapping telescope (VA.13, VA.15).

items.title: The map of telescopes, and “clearly sufficient”

milnor.label: Appendix, proof of Theorem A, p. 150
milnor.statement: Define $f_\Sigma : X_\Sigma \to Y_\Sigma$ by $f_\Sigma(x, t) = (f(x), t)$. Then "it is clearly sufficient to prove that $f_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence".

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; if $f : X \to Y$ carries each $X_n$ into $Y_n$, then $f_\Sigma(x, \tau) = (f(x), \tau)$ is a map $X_\Sigma \to Y_\Sigma$ with $p_Yf_\Sigma = fp_X$. If $X$ and $Y$ are the homotopy direct limits of $\{X_i\}$ and $\{Y_i\}$ and $f_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence, then so is $f$.

diff: No hidden hypothesis: neither closedness nor monotonicity is needed. The proof is $f \simeq fp_Xs = p_Yf_\Sigma s$ for a homotopy inverse $s$ of $p_X$.

items.title: Truncations of the telescope (T2)

milnor.label: Appendix, p. 152
milnor.statement: In Case 2, $X_\Sigma^n$ is the subset of $X_\Sigma$ of pairs $(x, \tau)$ with $\tau \le n$, i.e. $X_0 \times [0, 1] \cup \dots \cup X_{n-1} \times [n - 1, n] \cup X_n \times [n]$. "In fact $X_\Sigma^n$ contains $X_n \times [n]$ as deformation retract", and the composition $Gf_\Sigma$ carries $X_\Sigma^n$ into itself.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; the truncation $X^n_\Sigma = \{(x, \tau) \in X_\Sigma : \tau \le n\}$ is closed in $X_\Sigma$, and $X^0_\Sigma \subseteq X^1_\Sigma \subseteq \cdots$, whatever the $X_i$. For a monotone sequence, $x \mapsto (x, n)$ is a homotopy equivalence $X_n \to X^n_\Sigma$ with homotopy inverse $(x, \tau) \mapsto x$, the homotopy raising $\tau$ to $n$; and a function on $X_\Sigma$ that sends the $n$-th strip to levels $\le n + 1$ and $X_n \times \{n\}$ to levels $\le n$ sends each $X^m_\Sigma$ to levels $\le m$.

That truncations are always closed, with no closedness of the $X_i$, is what lets Case 2 need closedness only of the $Y_i$ (VA.11).

items.title: A level function makes a homotopy direct limit (Lemmas 2.1, 2.2)

milnor.label: Appendix, Example 1, p. 149
milnor.statement: In Example 1, given $f : X \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) \ge i + 1$ for $x \notin X_i$ and $f \ge 0$, the correspondence $x \mapsto (x, f(x))$ maps $X$ homeomorphically onto a subset of $X_\Sigma$ "which is clearly a deformation retract". Then using a partition of unity one can construct a map $f : X \to \mathbb R$ so that $f(x) \ge i + 1$ for $x \notin X_i$ and $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$; and $X$ is a homotopy direct limit.

items.title: Milnor’s maps $h_1$ and their homotopy inverse $g$

items.title: Theorem A, Case 2: $f_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence

milnor.label: Appendix, Case 2, pp. 152–153
milnor.statement: Now let $X$ and $Y$ be arbitrary. With homotopy inverses $g_n$ of the $f_n$, $i_ng_n \simeq g_{n+1}f_{n+1}i_ng_n = g_{n+1}j_nf_ng_n \simeq g_{n+1}j_n$; with a homotopy $h^n_u$ from $i_ng_n$ to $g_{n+1}j_n$, $G(y, n + t) = (g_n(y), n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$ and $(h^n_{2t-1}(y), n + 1)$ for $t \ge \frac12$. $Gf_\Sigma$ carries $X^n_\Sigma$ into itself by a map homotopic to the identity, so "we can apply Case 1 to the sequence $\{X_\Sigma^n\}$, and conclude that $Gf_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence"; similarly $f_\Sigma G$; so $f_\Sigma$ has a left and a right homotopy inverse.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; (i) let $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ be monotone, closed or not, and $F : X_\Sigma \to X_\Sigma$ a map carrying each truncation $X^m_\Sigma$ into itself, with $F(x, m) = (e_m(x), m)$ for maps $e_m : X_m \to X_m$ homotopic to the identity. Then $F$ is a homotopy equivalence. (ii) Let $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ in $X$ and $Y_0 \subseteq Y_1 \subseteq \cdots$ in $Y$, the $Y_n$ closed, and let $f : X \to Y$ carry each $X_n$ into $Y_n$ by a homotopy equivalence $f_n$. Then $f_\Sigma : X_\Sigma \to Y_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence.

diff: The $Y_n$ must be closed, for the continuity of $G$ (VA.3), where Milnor's Case 2 has no hypothesis; this is removed for Theorem A in VA.15.
Conversely, the $X_n$ need not be closed, and no homotopy direct limit hypothesis is used: Case 1 is applied only to the truncations, which are always closed (VA.5).

Hidden: the return from Case 1, which is about the induced map of the telescope of $\{X^n_\Sigma\}$, to $Gf_\Sigma$ itself needs $X_\Sigma$ to be the homotopy direct limit of its truncations (VA.6 (ii)); and "$Gf_\Sigma$ on $X^m_\Sigma$ is homotopic to the identity" is a chain of homotopies through the maps of VA.5.

items.title: Theorem A, by Milnor’s proof

milnor.label: Appendix, Theorem A
milnor.statement: Suppose that $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ and $Y$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{Y_i\}$. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a map which carries each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence. Then $f$ itself is a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; let $X$ be the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ and $Y$ that of $Y_0 \subseteq Y_1 \subseteq \cdots$, the $Y_i$ closed in $Y$, and let $f : X \to Y$ carry each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence $f_i : X_i \to Y_i$. Then $f$ is a homotopy equivalence.

diff: Milnor's proof, as written, needs the $Y_i$ closed (VA.11), and only these: Case 1 as written needs closed sets, but Case 2 applies it only to truncations, which are closed. The hypothesis is removed in VA.15, by running the same proof on mapping telescopes.

items.title: The mapping telescope

milnor.label: Appendix, pp. 149–153
milnor.statement: The book has no such construction. The Appendix works with the telescope $X_\Sigma$ of a sequence of subspaces of one space $X$, and the application to Theorem 17.3 with a union $K = \bigcup K_i$ of complexes $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$.

lean.statement: For a sequence of spaces and maps $K_0 \xrightarrow{c_0} K_1 \xrightarrow{c_1} \cdots$, the mapping telescope $T$ is the quotient of the disjoint union of the blocks $K_n \times [0, 1]$ by $(k, 1)_n \sim (c_n(k), 0)_{n+1}$; $(k, t)_n$ is at level $n + t$, a continuous function on $T$. Maps out of $T$, and out of $P \times T$ for locally compact $P$, may be given block by block, compatibly with the gluing, with no closedness condition. The truncations $T_n = \{\text{level} \le n\}$ are closed and increasing, $T$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{T_n\}$, and $k \mapsto (k, 0)_n$ is an embedding $K_n \to T$ and a homotopy equivalence $K_n \to T_n$. For subsets $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ of $X$, the mapping telescope of the inclusions is homotopy equivalent to $X_\Sigma$ (homeomorphic when the $X_n$ are closed).

chips: stands for a union of complexes
diff: This is the device that removes the closedness hypotheses (VA.15), pasting being automatic in a quotient, and that replaces a union of complexes which are not subspaces of one space (VA.16, VA.17).
The product of a quotient map with a locally compact space is a quotient map, which is what makes homotopies on $T$ definable block by block.

items.title: Theorem A, exactly as Milnor states it

milnor.label: Appendix, Theorem A
milnor.statement: Suppose that $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ and $Y$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{Y_i\}$. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a map which carries each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence. Then $f$ itself is a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; let $X$ be the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ and $Y$ that of $Y_0 \subseteq Y_1 \subseteq \cdots$, arbitrary subsets, and let $f : X \to Y$ carry each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence $f_i : X_i \to Y_i$. Then $f$ is a homotopy equivalence.

diff: The statement is Milnor's, with no closedness hypothesis. The proof departs from his only in the space on which it is run: the induced map of the mapping telescopes of the inclusions carries each closed truncation into the corresponding one by a map homotopic to a composite of homotopy equivalences, so Milnor's proof (VA.12) applies, and the mapping telescopes are homotopy equivalent to $X$ and $Y$ by maps commuting with $f$ (VA.13).
This general form is what Theorem 17.1 needs, its pieces being open sets (V10.19).

items.title: Monotone unions, and the final step of Theorem 17.3

milnor.label: Appendix, p. 150
milnor.statement: Assuming Theorem A, the alternative proof of Theorem 17.3: the constructed homotopy equivalences $\Omega^{a_i} \to K_i$ form a commutative diagram with $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$; since $\Omega = \bigcup\Omega^{a_i}$ and $K = \bigcup K_i$ are homotopy direct limits (Examples 1 and 2), the limit mapping $\Omega \to K$ is also a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; (i) if $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$, the $Y_i \subseteq Y$ are closed and increasing, and $f : X \to Y$ carries each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence, then $X$ is homotopy equivalent to the telescope $Y_\Sigma$. (ii) If $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ (closed or not), $K_0 \xrightarrow{c_0} K_1 \xrightarrow{c_1} \cdots$ is a sequence of spaces and maps, and $g_n : X_n \to K_n$ are homotopy equivalences with $c_ng_n \simeq g_{n+1}$ on $X_n$, then $X$ is homotopy equivalent to the mapping telescope of the $K_n$.

chips: squares commute only up to homotopy
diff: The conclusion is a homotopy equivalence with the mapping telescope of the $K_n$, which stands for the union $K$ with the weak topology; the two are homotopy equivalent by Example 2, which needs Whitehead's theorem and is not formalized.

The squares need only commute up to homotopy, and the $K_n$ need not be subspaces of one space: Milnor's limit mapping exists only because each map extends the previous one, which is not available in the proof of Theorem 17.3 (V10.20).
The proof is Milnor's map $G$ of Case 2, built from homotopy inverses of the $g_n$ and defined from the mapping telescope, where it is continuous block by block.

items.title: The Corollary: homotopy direct limits of CW-complexes

milnor.label: Appendix, Corollary, p. 153
milnor.statement: Suppose that $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$. If each $X_i$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex, then $X$ itself has the homotopy type of a CW-complex. "The proof is not difficult".

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; (i) if $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ and each $X_n$ is homotopy equivalent to a space $K_n$, there are maps $K_0 \to K_1 \to \cdots$ such that $X$ is homotopy equivalent to their mapping telescope. (ii) If each $X_n$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $\mathrm{cells}_n$ (an iterated adjunction space, V2.11), $X$ is homotopy equivalent to the mapping telescope of a sequence of iterated adjunction spaces $K_n$ with these cells. No closedness of the $X_n$ is assumed.

chips: a mapping telescope, not a CW-complex
diff: The conclusion is a mapping telescope of the $K_n$, not a CW-complex: that a telescope of CW-complexes is a CW-complex needs cellular maps (cellular approximation) and the CW structure of mapping telescopes, neither of which is in Mathlib. For finite complexes, iterated adjunction spaces replace CW-complexes.

items.title: Countable cell complexes

milnor.label: Appendix, pp. 149–150
milnor.statement: Each $\Omega^{a_i}$ has the homotopy type of "a certain CW-complex", and the union $\Omega$ should have the homotopy type of a CW-complex (p. 149); in the final step of Theorem 17.3 the complexes form a nested sequence $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$ with union $K$ (p. 150).

lean.statement: A space $K$ is obtained from $L$ by attaching cells of dimensions $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is obtained by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell to $L$, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on, each along an arbitrary map of its boundary sphere into the space built so far. A *cell tower* with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \mathrm{cells}_1, \dots$ (finite lists of dimensions) is a sequence $K_0 \to K_1 \to \cdots$ in which $K_0$ is an iterated adjunction space with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0$ and $K_{n+1}$ is obtained from $K_n$ by attaching the cells $\mathrm{cells}_{n+1}$. A space *has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex* with these cells if it is homotopy equivalent to the mapping telescope of such a tower; this is invariant under homotopy equivalence.

chips: attaching maps need not be cellular
a telescope stands for the union
diff: Weaker than a CW-complex: the attaching maps need not be cellular, and the mapping telescope of the tower stands for the union of the $K_n$ with the weak topology, to which it is homotopy equivalent by Example 2, not verified. Every "CW-complex" of Theorems 17.3, 19.6 and Corollary 17.4 in the formalization is of this kind.

items.title: The topological part of Theorem 17.3

milnor.label: Appendix, p. 150
milnor.statement: The alternative final step of Theorem 17.3: a commutative diagram of homotopy equivalences $\Omega^{a_i} \to K_i$, Examples 1 and 2, and Theorem A make the limit mapping $\Omega \to K$ a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; (i) if $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ and $g_n : X_n \to K_n$ are homotopy equivalences to the stages of a cell tower with $c_ng_n \simeq g_{n+1}$ on $X_n$, then $X$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex. (ii) Let $E : X \to \mathbb R$ be continuous, $a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots$ with $a_n \to \infty$, and $g_n : \{E \le a_n\} \to K_n$ homotopy equivalences to the stages of a cell tower with $c_ng_n = g_{n+1}$ on $\{E \le a_n\}$. Then $X$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \mathrm{cells}_1, \dots$.

diff: No paracompactness: the sublevel sets of a continuous function with levels tending to infinity always form a homotopy direct limit (VA.7 (ii)). The levels must tend to infinity, so that the sublevel sets exhaust $X$, which the book leaves implicit.
"CW-complex" is read in the sense of VA.18; the application to the path space is Chapter 10 (V10.20–V10.22).

items.title: Moving the end point

milnor.label: §17, p. 96; §19, p. 106
milnor.statement: The loop space of $S^n$ is treated through the paths from $p$ to a point $q \neq p, p'$, and Theorem 19.6 is stated for all $p, q$ but proved for non-conjugate ones; that the end point may be moved is not said.

lean.statement: Let $N$ be a slice submanifold of $V$ and $p, q \in N$. (i) Two points of $N$ at finite Riemannian distance are joined by a path in $N$, and $q$ is joined by a path in $N$ to a point $q' \in N$ which is not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic. (ii) A path in $N$ from $q$ to $q'$ gives a homotopy equivalence $\Omega(N; p, q) \simeq \Omega(N; p, q')$ of path spaces with Milnor's metric. (iii) Homotopy equivalent spaces have isomorphic homology over a field, hence the same Betti numbers.

diff: Every $q$ is joined in $N$ to a point $q'$ not conjugate to $p$ (V11.6), and a path from $q$ to $q'$ gives a homotopy equivalence of the path spaces with Milnor's metric, through Theorem 17.1 (V10.19) and composition of paths.

items.title: Corollary 17.2

milnor.label: §17, Corollary 17.2
milnor.statement: "It is known that the space $\Omega^*$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex" (Milnor, 1959). Therefore $\Omega$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex.

lean.statement: Let $N$ be closed in $V$ and $p, q \in N$. Then $\Omega(N; p, q)$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex (VA.18), and so does the space $\Omega^*(N; p, q)$ of continuous paths with the compact-open topology.

diff: The end point is moved to a non-conjugate one (V10.28) and Theorem 17.3 (V10.22) gives the complex; so $N$ must be complete, which Milnor's corollary does not assume, but the complex is countable and explicit. The same holds for $\Omega^*$.

items.title: Corollary 17.4 for the loop space

milnor.label: §17, Corollary 17.4
milnor.statement: The loop space $\Omega(S^n)$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex with one cell each in the dimensions $0, n - 1, 2(n - 1), 3(n - 1), \dots$.

lean.statement: Let $n \ge 2$ and $p \in S^n$. The loop space $\Omega(S^n; p, p)$ is homotopy equivalent to $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ for some $q \neq \pm p$, and it has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with one cell in each of the dimensions $0, n - 1, 2(n - 1), 3(n - 1), \dots$, attached in this order. For $n \ge 3$ and every field $\mathbb k$, $\dim H_i(\Omega(S^n; p, p); \mathbb k)$ is $1$ if $n - 1$ divides $i$ and $0$ otherwise.

diff: $p$ is conjugate to itself along every great circle, so Theorem 17.3 does not apply to loops: $\Omega(S^n; p, p) \simeq \Omega(S^n; p, q)$ for some $q \neq \pm p$ (V10.28), and V10.24 applies. For $n \ge 3$ the Betti numbers over a field are $1$ in the degrees divisible by $n - 1$.

notFormalized.title: Geodesics and path spaces on an abstract Riemannian manifold
notFormalized.book: Milnor's §§10–19 are written for an abstract Riemannian manifold $M$: the Levi-Civita connection of §8, geodesics and the exponential map, the distance and completeness, the path space $\Omega(M; p, q)$ with its energy, Jacobi fields, the index theorem, and the topology of $\Omega$.
notFormalized.instead: **Everything in Chapters 7–11 is proved for a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$ with the induced metric** (V7.1). Mathlib has no Levi-Civita connection, geodesics or exponential map on an abstract manifold, and the Christoffel-symbol form of the geodesic equation is not formalized (V7.3). Every Riemannian manifold is isometric to such an $N$ by Nash's embedding theorem, which is quoted in the Lean files but neither proved nor used, so the formal results reach an abstract manifold only through it. Within the setting, completeness is often obtained from closedness of $N$ in $V$, which implies it (V7.30, V10.22).

notFormalized.title: The remarks on minimal geodesics
notFormalized.label: §10, p. 62
notFormalized.book: Theorem 10.4 asserts that any sufficiently small segment of a geodesic is minimal. On the other hand a long geodesic may not be minimal: a great circle arc on the unit sphere of length greater than $\pi$ is certainly not. In general minimal geodesics are not unique: two antipodal points of a unit sphere are joined by infinitely many.
notFormalized.instead: Not stated as such. The short geodesics of Lemma 10.3 and Corollary 10.8 are shortest (V7.15, V7.20), from which the first remark follows for every geodesic, but the step is not written. For long arcs, every geodesic of $S^n$, $n \ge 2$, of length $> \pi$ is not minimal (V11.14, from Myers' theorem). The non-uniqueness of minimal geodesics between antipodal points is not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Geodesics of surfaces, and the footnote on $U(n)$
notFormalized.label: §10, pp. 57 and 65–66
notFormalized.book: Among the familiar examples of p. 65: meridians of a surface of revolution are geodesics; the geodesics of a right circular cylinder are the generating lines, the circles cut by perpendicular planes, and the helices, so that two points of the cylinder are joined by infinitely many; antipodal points of $S^n$ are joined by a continuum of minimal geodesics. A footnote on p. 57 explains the name "exponential": on the group of unitary matrices, $\exp_I(A) = I + A + \frac1{2!}A^2 + \dots$.
notFormalized.instead: The geodesics of $\mathbb R^n$ and of $S^n$ are V7.30′. Surfaces of revolution, the cylinder, the continuum of minimal geodesics between antipodal points, and the identification of the Riemannian exponential of $U(n)$ with the matrix exponential (which needs a bi-invariant metric) are not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Induced maps and Hessians of functions on $\Omega$
notFormalized.label: §§11 and 13, pp. 68–69 and 74
notFormalized.book: To motivate the definitions, Milnor defines the induced map $F_* : T\Omega_\omega \to T\mathbb R_{F(\omega)}$ of a real function $F$ on $\Omega$ through variations, noting that without hypotheses on $F$ there is no guarantee that it exists or is independent of the variation; and he observes that if $F$ takes its minimum at $\omega_0$ and the derivatives $dF(\bar\alpha(u))/du$ are all defined, then $\omega_0$ is a critical path (p. 69). On p. 74 he recalls the Hessian $f_{**}$ of a function on a finite-dimensional manifold, defined through 2-parameter maps.
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized: critical paths are defined only for the energy (V8.4), and the Hessian only for $E$ (V8.14), where Theorem 13.1 shows it to be well defined. The Hessian of a function on a finite-dimensional manifold is that of Part I.

notFormalized.title: Corollary 17.2 by Milnor's route
notFormalized.label: §17, Corollary 17.2
notFormalized.book: The path space $\Omega$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex: by Theorem 17.1 it is homotopy equivalent to $\Omega^*$, which has the homotopy type of a CW-complex by Milnor's theorem (*On spaces having the homotopy type of a CW-complex*, 1959). It is used with Whitehead's theorem in the first proof of Theorem 17.3.
notFormalized.instead: **Proved for $N$ closed in $V$** (V10.29), by moving the end point to a non-conjugate one and Theorem 17.3, which gives a countable cell complex in the sense of VA.18. What remains: Milnor's theorem of 1959 and Whitehead's theorem, which are not in Mathlib, and the corollary for manifolds that are not complete. Theorem 17.3 does not use it (V10.22).

notFormalized.title: Corollary 17.5: infinitely many geodesics
notFormalized.label: §17, Corollary 17.5
notFormalized.book: Let $M$ have the homotopy type of $S^n$, $n > 2$. Then any two non-conjugate points of $M$ are joined by infinitely many geodesics: the homotopy type of $\Omega^*(M)$, and hence of $\Omega(M)$, depends only on that of $M$, so there must be at least one geodesic of index $0$, at least one of index $n - 1$, $2(n - 1)$, and so on.
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized. It needs the homotopy invariance of $\Omega^*$ (the path spaces of homotopy equivalent spaces are weakly equivalent, with the same homology) and the homology of the countable cell complex of Theorem 17.3 in each dimension. What is formalized is that the corollary as printed omits a hypothesis: $\mathbb R^{n+1} \setminus \{0\}$ has the homotopy type of $S^n$ and no conjugate points, yet two of its points are joined by a single geodesic (V10.27), so $M$ must be complete. For $M = S^n$ itself the geodesics and the homology of $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ are computed (V10.23, V10.26).

notFormalized.title: Serre's remark, and the suspension theorem
notFormalized.label: §17, Remark, p. 97
notFormalized.book: More generally, if $M$ is any complete manifold which is not contractible, then any two non-conjugate points of $M$ are joined by infinitely many geodesics (compare Serre, *Homologie singulière des espaces fibrés*, 1951). As another application of 17.4 one can give a proof of the Freudenthal suspension theorem (compare §22.3).
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized: Serre's theorem on the homology of loop spaces (the spectral sequence of the path fibration) and the passage to the universal covering are not available. The suspension theorem belongs to §22, which is not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Corollary 19.3: no torsion in $\pi_1$
notFormalized.label: §19, Corollary 19.3
notFormalized.book: If $M$ is complete with $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$, then $\pi_1(M)$ contains no element of finite order other than the identity. Proof: the universal covering $\tilde M$ being contractible, $H^k(M)$ is the cohomology of the group $\pi_1(M)$ (Hu); a non-trivial finite cyclic subgroup $G$ would give a covering $\hat M$ with $H^k(G) = H^k(\hat M) = 0$ for $k > n$, while the cohomology groups of a finite cyclic group are non-trivial in arbitrarily high dimensions.
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized: the cohomology of groups, of finite cyclic groups in particular, and the identification $H^k(M) \cong H^k(\pi_1(M))$ are not available. The first half of the corollary, $\pi_i(M) = 0$ for $i > 1$, is V11.21, where the universal covering is $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ (V11.19).

notFormalized.title: Finiteness of $\pi_1$ in positive Ricci curvature
notFormalized.label: §19, p. 105
notFormalized.book: Corollary 19.5 applies also to the universal covering space $\tilde M$ of $M$. Since $\tilde M$ is compact, the fundamental group $\pi_1(M)$ is finite.
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized: universal coverings with a lifted metric are not formalized. In non-positive curvature the universal covering is $\exp_p$ itself (V11.19), but in positive Ricci curvature $\exp_p$ has critical points (Myers' theorem), so it is no covering. Corollary 19.5, compactness and the bound $\pi r$ on the diameter, is V11.13.

notFormalized.title: Sectional curvature as a Gaussian curvature
notFormalized.label: §19, Remark, p. 100
notFormalized.book: If $A$ and $B$ are orthogonal unit vectors at $p$, the sectional curvature $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$ is equal to the Gaussian curvature of the surface $(u_1, u_2) \mapsto \exp_p(u_1A + u_2B)$ spanned by the geodesics through $p$ with velocity vectors in the plane of $A$ and $B$ (Laugwitz).
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized: the Gaussian curvature of this surface is not defined. The sectional curvature is that of Chapter 6, and the hypothesis of Lemma 19.1 is shown equivalent to all sectional curvatures being $\le 0$ (V11.7).

notFormalized.title: The optics of curvature, and examples of curvature $\le 0$
notFormalized.label: §19, pp. 101–102
notFormalized.book: Intuitively, curvature can be described through "optics", geodesics being the paths of light rays: a short segment of length $L$ at $\exp_p(rU)$ in the direction $W$ appears to have length $L(1 + \frac{r^2}6\langle R(U, W)U, W\rangle + \dots)$, and a small object of volume $v$ appears to have volume $v(1 + \frac{r^2}6K(U, U) + \dots)$. Examples of complete manifolds of curvature $\le 0$: Euclidean space, the paraboloid $z = x^2 - y^2$, the hyperboloid of rotation $x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 1$, the helicoid. The pseudo-sphere has constant curvature $-1$ and no conjugate points, but is not complete; by a theorem of Hilbert no complete surface of constant negative curvature can be imbedded in $\mathbb R^3$, although complete, even compact, ones exist, such as surfaces of genus $\ge 2$.
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized; none of these statements is used later in the book.

notFormalized.title: The remarks after Theorem 19.6
notFormalized.label: §19, pp. 106–107
notFormalized.book: Milnor does not know whether Theorem 19.6 remains true for $M$ complete but non-compact; the proof breaks down on the paraboloid $z = x^2 + y^2$, where $K(U, U)$ is not bounded away from $0$. The product $S^m \times S^k$, $m, k \ge 2$, has positive definite Ricci tensor while some sectional curvatures vanish; it is not known whether it can be remetrized with all sectional curvatures positive, and by a theorem of Synge such a metric could not be invariant under $(x, y) \mapsto (-x, -y)$.

notFormalized.title: Example 2 of the Appendix: CW-complexes
notFormalized.label: Appendix, Example 2
notFormalized.book: Let $X$ be a CW-complex and let the $X_i$ be subcomplexes with union $X$. Since $p : X_\Sigma \to X$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in all dimensions, it follows from Whitehead's theorem that $X$ is a homotopy direct limit.
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized: it needs Whitehead's theorem, the fact that a compact subset of a CW-complex lies in a finite subcomplex, and the CW topology of products, none of which is in Mathlib. Hence the mapping telescope of a cell tower is not compared with the union of its stages in the weak topology, and the "countable CW-complexes" of Theorems 17.3 and 19.6 are mapping telescopes of iterated adjunction spaces (VA.18). Example 1, the case used for the path space, is VA.7.

notFormalized.title: The Remark on Case 1 of Theorem A
notFormalized.label: Appendix, Remark, p. 150
notFormalized.book: Under the conditions of Case 1 it would be natural to conjecture that $f_\Sigma$ must actually be homotopic to the identity; however counterexamples can be given.
notFormalized.instead: Not formalized: the exposition's counterexample, a phantom map, needs cellular cohomology and $\mathbb{CP}^\infty$. Case 1 itself is VA.10.
